articles.title: Comelec building electoral sabotage case over pre-shaded ballots in Basilan
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections has identified those behind the pre-shaded ballots found in Basilan during the Bangsamoro elections, its chairperson George Garcia said Wednesday, September 30.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 3:22pm
The Bangsamoro regional capitol in Cotabato City.
Philstar.com / John Unson

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections has identified those behind the pre-shaded ballots found in Basilan during the Bangsamoro elections, its chairperson George Garcia said Wednesday, September 30.
Garcia declined to name its suspected culprits but confirmed the poll body is already eyeing the possible filing of an electoral sabotage case.

"There might be accusations that we're just pointing fingers. But we are building an airtight case, because remember, life imprisonment is the penalty [for electoral sabotage]," Garcia said at a forum in mixed English and Filipino.
Sixteen subpoenas have been issued asking explanations from officials in Maluso, Basilan, where 16,543 ballots for 36 of 68 precincts were found pre-shaded, Garcia confirmed.

Those asked to explain include the mayor, the municipal treasurer, the town's election officer and the police chief. The provincial police commander and Comelec's own provincial election supervisor were also subpoenaed.
Garcia said being issued a subpoena does not automatically mean the individuals are guilty or considered the accused.
Electoral sabotage is an offense under Republic Act 9369, the automated election law. Vote tampering counts as electoral sabotage when more than 10,000 votes are involved.
The poll chief said they are tracing who had ultimate custody of the ballots, as investigators do in drug cases.
"Sino ba ang may hawak ng mga balota?" he said. (Who was holding the ballots?)
Garcia said the tampering could not have been done by one person. "Mga mahigit pong 15 na tao po 'yung gumawa no'n," he said. (More than 15 people did it.)
The Comelec wants the case resolved before candidates file for the next elections, he added.

The poll body filed electoral sabotage charges against former President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo in 2011. The charges were over alleged cheating in the 2007 senatorial elections. A Pasay court dismissed the case in 2018.
Voting delayed by a day
The pre-shaded ballots were discovered on the night of September 13, the eve of the Bangsamoro region's first parliamentary elections.
Garcia said the Comelec stopped their distribution and had the National Printing Office reprint new ballots.
The replacement ballots were flown in from Zamboanga City and arrived on the night of election day.
Voting in the 36 precincts took place the next day.
None of the region's 5,212 precincts had a failure of elections, he said.
Comelec placed Maluso under its control on election day, along with Cotabato City, where violence broke out.

articles.title: In the Public Square: Taking the fight to the dynasties
articles.summary: How did Philippine politics get this way? And what can be done to change it?

blocks.text: How did Philippine politics get this way? And what can be done to change it?

In the ongoing drama of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the Senate sits as the impeachment court—and also as a representative of the general public. But the Senate also represents the country in a different and darker way: It is the practice of dynasty politics taken to the extreme.

Eight seats in the 24-person Senate are occupied by four pairs of siblings. At least four are held by senators who have family members in national elective or appointive positions. At least two belong to political families.
It is time to take the fight to the dynasties.

In this new episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by former Supreme Court senior associate justice Antonio Carpio, and lawyer Alex Lacson, the chair and vice chair, respectively, of the People’s Initiative Coalition Against Dynasties.
Watch the episode on Wednesday, September 30, at 8 pm. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [In This Economy] Investment options sa panahon ng mataas na inflation
articles.summary: Marami nang options ngayon sa pag-iinvest. Piliin ang produktong bagay sa goals mo at sa kung kailan mo kailangan ang pera.

items: Ang mataas na inflation rate na 6.1% ay nagiging sanhi ng pagbaba ng purchasing power ng mga tao, kaya't mahalagang suriin ang mga investment options na may mas mataas na interes.
Maraming tao ang lumilipat sa online bank accounts na nag-aalok ng mas mataas na interest rates, ngunit dapat maging maingat sa mga terms at conditions ng mga ito.
Sa pagtaas ng interest rates, mahalaga ang pagpapanatili ng inflation sa mababang antas upang hindi maapektuhan ang kakayahan ng mga tao na mag-ipon at makabili ng mga pangunahing pangangailangan.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Habang sumasama ang lagay ng ekonomiya, saan magandang mag-invest?

Mahalagang tingnan ang statistics sa inflation o bilis ng pagtaas ng presyo. Ayon sa Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), nasa 6.1% ang inflation noong Agosto 2026. Medyo bumaba ito mula 6.2% noong Hulyo, pero mataas pa rin kumpara sa kinikita ng savings natin sa bangko.

Ang problema, kapag masyadong mabilis ang inflation kumpara sa interes sa bangko, lumalaki nga ang pera mo sa bank account ngunit kumukonti naman ang puwede o kaya nitong bilhin. In other words, bumababa ang halaga ng piso mo dahil sa inflation.

Sabihin nating may P100,000 ka sa typical savings account na may 0.625% interest kada taon. Sa simpleng kuwenta, P625 ang kikitain mo after one year. May 20% tax pa sa interest, kaya P500 na lang ang matitira, bago ang anumang fees. So magiging P100,500 ang pera mo.

Ngunit kung tumaas nang 6.1% ang presyo sa loob ng taong iyon (dahil sa inflation), aabot sa P106,100 ang dating P100,000 na halaga ng mga bilihin. Magkukulang talaga ang savings at tinubo mo para mabili ang parehong dami ng produkto at serbisyo.

Ito ang tinatawag na “negative real return”: nabawasan ang purchasing power, o kayang bilhin, ng ipon mo dahil sa inflation. Sa example natin, katumbas na lang ng P97,267 sa dating presyo ang pera mo.

Dahil sadyang mababa ang interes sa mga normal savings account sa bangko, maraming na-eengganyo ngayon na maglagay ng savings sa online bank accounts na nag-ooffer ng mas mataas na interest rates. Kabilang sa mga ito ang Maya Savings, BanKo TODO Savings, at MariBank.
Ngunit sabi nga sa economics, “there’s no such thing as a free lunch.” I-research muna nang mabuti kung ano ang terms and conditions sa online accounts na ito.

Halimbawa, tignan natin ang Maya Savings. Sa official mechanics nito para sa Setyembre 2026, 3% kada taon ang base rate, ‘di hamak na mas mataas kumpara sa normal na savings account sa bangko. May bonus interest para sa qualified transactions, pero hanggang P100,000 lang ng savings balance ang sakop ng bonus.

May hiwalay ding offer na hanggang 15% kada taon para sa qualified new users, sa hanggang P100,000 na deposito. Limited-time promo ito at may requirements. Tandaan din na ang “per annum” o “p.a.” ay kada taon. So kung isang buwan lang ang promo, bahagi lang ng annual interest ang maaari mong kitain.

Kaya naman, icheck muna kung hanggang kailan ang promo, magkano ang covered na deposito, at anong transactions ang counted. Puwedeng magbago ang rates, at magkaiba rin ang offers para sa new at existing users.

Huwag ding gumastos sa hindi kailangan para lang makakuha ng bonus. Halimbawa, may P10,000 ka at tataas ang interest rate mo mula 3% papuntang sa 5% kada taon. Sa loob ng 30 araw, mga P13 lang ang dagdag na kita after the 20% tax. Kung bibili ka ng P500 na bagay na hindi mo naman kailangan para makuha iyon, lugi ka.
‘Di hamak na mas sulit kung bills o mahalagang purchases ang gagamitin para ma-meet ang requirements. By the way, kilangan mo ring isama sa kuwenta ang transfer at withdrawal fees.
Siguraduhin ding bank deposit talaga ang produkto. Magkaiba kasi ang savings account at e-wallet balance kahit nasa iisang app. Walang deposit insurance ang e-wallet balance mismo.

Mula Marso 2025, hanggang P1 milyon per depositor, per bank ang sakop ng Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC). Pinagsasama ang personal deposits na nasa parehong pangalan at capacity sa iisang bangko, kahit magkakahiwalay ang accounts. Kaya huwag ilagay ang lahat ng iyong pera sa iisang bangko.

Note din na ang deposit insurance ay proteksiyon kapag nagsara ang bangko. Hindi nito automatic na sasagutin ang perang nawala sa scam o dahil nanakaw ang password mo. Huwag ibigay ang password o one-time PIN, at sa official app at customer-service channels lang makipagtransaksiyon.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] Should Filipinos’ ‘consumption culture’ be blamed for the weak peso?

blocks.text: Ang paglalagay ng pera sa savings account (traditional or online bank) ay nakadepende rin sa pangangailangan mong gumastos sa mga susunod na buwan. Magtira ng extra savings para sa mga emergencies at iba pang mahalagang gastusin.

Unahin ang emergency fund o perang madaling makuha kapag may nagkasakit o nawalan ng trabaho sa pamilya. Usual na starting target ang 3 hanggang 6 na buwang basic expenses, depende sa kung gaano ka-stable ang income mo at kung ilan ang umaasa sa iyo. Kung mabigat iyon, magsimula sa halagang kaya mo.

Puwedeng ilagay ang bahagi nito sa high-interest savings account. Mag-iwan din ng madaling ma-access na pera sa ibang bangko para may magamit kapag may aberya sa isang app. Kung may utang na mataas ang interest, isama mo sa plano ang pagbabayad nito.

Para sa perang hindi mo agad kailangan, ikumpara ang time deposits. May fixed period ang paglalagay ng pera rito. Puwedeng may penalty o mas mababang interest kapag nag-withdraw nang maaga. Hangga’t maaari, itapat ang maturity (o pagtatapos ng period na iyon) sa petsa kung kailan mo kailangan ang pera.

Puwede ring tingnan ang Treasury bills at retail Treasury bonds (RTBs), kung saan effectively ay nagpapautang ka sa national government. Ikumpara ang kita nga mga ito after tax and fees, pati ang maturity. Puwede ka pa ring malugi kung kailangan mong ibenta bago mag-mature at mas mababa ang market price.

Kung kayang maghintay ng 5 taon, may Modified Pag-IBIG 2 (MP2) para sa qualified members. Tax-free ang dividends o bahagi ng kita na napupunta sa nag-iipon. Nagbabago ang dividend rate nito bawat taon, at may conditions sa pag-withdraw nang maaga.

Para sa long-term goals naman, puwede ring pag-aralan ang low-cost, diversified stock index funds. Sinusundan ng mga pondong ito ang isang stock-market index at nakakalat ang investments sa maraming kumpanya. Ngunit may risk pa rin ng malaking pagkalugi, kaya huwag ilagay rito ang pambayad sa tuition sa susunod na semester.

Sa kabuoan, marami nang options ngayon sa pag-iinvest. Piliin ang produktong bagay sa goals mo at sa kung kailan mo kailangan ang pera. Tingnan mo rin lagi ang take-home na kita matapos ang lahat ng gastos.

Ang trend ngayon (at maaaring hanggang sa susunod na taon) ay ang pagtaas ng interest rates, dahil nagsisimula nang magtaas ng interest rates ang Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) bilang tugon nito sa inflation.

Oo, ibig sabihin nito na mas maraming maeengganyo na mag-save dahil asahang tataas din ang interes sa iba’t-ibang investment opportunities, tulad ng mga deposito at government securities. Pero ang mataas na interes ay pambawi lang din dahil sa pagkawala ng halaga ng pera. Kung lalong lalala ang inflation, maaari pa ngang kainin nito ang kinikitang interes.

At siyempre, maraming pamilya ang wala nang naitatabi matapos bumili ng pagkain at magbayad ng kuryente. Hindi nila basta mapapakinabangan ang mas mataas na interes sa savings. Kung may utang pa sila, maaari ring madagdagan ang gastos nila sa pangungutang.
Kaya para sa maraming Pilipino, importante ang pagpapanatili ng inflation sa mababang antas, dahil ang inflation ay mistulang tax o buwis din para sa masa at middle class.

Dito papasok ang mga polisiya ng gobyerno para pigilan ang masyadong mabilis na pag-arangkada ng mga presyo. Kabilang dito ang pagtugon sa mga kakulangan sa suplay at mga hakbang ng BSP. – Rappler.com

articles.title: David Shoebridge wants the Greens to ‘seize this moment’. Is his more combative style the answer?
articles.summary: New leader says his party must connect with millions of disaffected voters and ‘make them believe in politics again’

blocks.text: As One Nation’s polling surged this year, and Pauline Hanson ate away at the votes of first the Coalition and then Labor, one curious mainstay emerged; the Greens remained seemingly anchored to the 10-12% range, no matter which poll you look at.

That’s despite the fact that, arguably, there’s rarely been more fertile political ground for the Greens leader to reap rewards; a centrist Labor government with a big majority but increasingly on the nose, a resurgent anti-immigration populist party backed by Australia’s richest mining billionaire, a Coalition in disarray, a cost-of-living crisis set ablaze by rising interest rates and inflation, and a public increasingly alarmed about the nexus of big tech, big datacentres and shadowy AI oligarchs operating with impunity.
David Shoebridge, in his first comments as the new Greens leader, seemed to acknowledge the party should, and could, be doing better.
“The Greens need to seize this moment because politics demands it of us,” he said.
“This is an extraordinary moment in politics, and we can all feel it. We can feel that politics as usual is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for now.”

Moments after winning Wednesday’s party-room ballot, Shoebridge, a former corporate lawyer, councillor from Woollahra in Sydney’s affluent eastern suburbs and state upper house MP, signalled he would take a more combative approach to not only One Nation, but the government as well. He argued the Greens were “not here to reform the Labor party. We are here to replace the Labor party.”
Arguably a message about cost of living should resonate better when it comes from a party that didn’t receive a private plane as a gift.

Progressives in Australia have been buoyed up by the successes of socialist outsider candidates in the US and UK, but there have been quiet frustrations inside the Greens that they haven’t managed to emulate the likes of Zohran Mamdani, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zack Polanski in the United Kingdom.
Shoebridge says the Greens must both fill a “vacuum” left by Labor and “recognise” the factors driving disaffected voters to Hanson.

“Our task in this moment is to connect with those millions of Australians who have quite legitimate and real anger with politics, and make them believe in politics again, and not believe in the politics of hate and division,” he said.

blocks.caption: Shoebridge will preside over a critical period of renewal for the Greens. Photograph: George Chan/AAP

blocks.text: Another task, of course, is internal. The Greens usually decide leaders by consensus, but Shoebridge won a rare contested party-room vote. He saw off challenges from Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young, initially winning six of 11 votes. Shoebridge was last to publicly declare his hand, and the optics of a white man besting two women more experienced in federal politics will surely be dissected by some in the party.

Faruqi, shortly after the result was decided, said she was “disappointed the party chose another direction” and claimed “many others will feel the same way”. She said ordinary party members felt “frustration” the leadership was decided by politicians, not grassroots membership; Shoebridge earlier had said he supported grassroots involvement in choosing leaders, and will be held to this.

He also will preside over a critical period of renewal for the Greens, with the veteran senator Peter Whish-Wilson already having left parliament, and South Australian senator Barbara Pocock not contesting the next election.
There is a push on from some in the party’s more activist ranks for those spots to be given to younger, digitally savvy, vigorous campaigners in the mould of the US “democratic socialist” movement.
after newsletter promotion

One key point to look out for is Shoebridge’s strategy for negotiating with Labor on legislation. Bandt campaigned at the 2022 election on pushing Labor to go further, but government sources pinned his unexpected defeat in 2025 on the Greens playing hardball on housing legislation. Larissa Waters took a more constructive approach, seeming more open to negotiations. Judging from past performance, and his pledge to “replace” not “reform” Labor, Shoebridge may take the tougher line.

Waters is well-liked, both among colleagues and more broadly across federal politics, seen as more conciliatory and pragmatic than some in her party room. There was genuine remorse and upset in the Greens as she stood down from the leadership to focus on managing a chronic kidney issue, and she must be given ample credit for holding the party together after the unexpected losses of leader Adam Bandt and rising stars Max Chandler-Mather and Stephen Bates at the 2025 election.

On a personal level, it must be acknowledged Shoebridge is not the most popular guy across the parliament or among Labor types, but much of that stems from his relentless style of questioning, needling and interrogation of political opponents and government officials.

Politico reported last week that the government offered the Greens a spot on a new AI committee, but with the proviso that it couldn’t be Shoebridge; clips of him forensically drawing answers out of public servants on Aukus, AI and the bureaucracy have gone viral online.
As one Greens source said: “He does act like the smartest guy in the room, but often, he actually is.”

Or as the Liberal senator James Paterson told the Guardian in 2025: “David Shoebridge and I don’t agree on much, but he’s easily the most effective Green and one of the most impactful crossbenchers in the Senate.”
With parliament returning in mid-October, it won’t be long before we see how effective he can be as leader.

articles.title: Treeless urban areas may face 50 degrees Celsius heat index as Super El Niño looms
articles.summary: Heat index in cities and towns with limited tree cover could reach 45 to 50 degrees Celsius during Super El Niño, the Climate Change Commission said.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 3:02pm

A dog drinks from a water container as residents line up their containers in Tondo, Manila on March 18, 2024 amid aniticipations of a reduction of the water pressure of Metro Manila concessionnaires due to the continuous decline of water levels at the Angat Dam as a result of the effects of El Nino.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa
MANILA, Philippines — Heat index in cities and towns with limited tree cover could reach 45 to 50 degrees Celsius during Super El Niño, the Climate Change Commission said.

Climate Change Commissioner Albert Dela Cruz said on Wednesday, September 30, that the Super El Niño phenomenon expected to start in October this year is so far the “most severe” that the Philippines may experience.
“Ito po 'yung pinaka-bad at ito ‘yung pinakamatindi sa tala ng history,” Dela Cruz said.
(This is the worst and most severe in the records of history.)
The commissioner noted that sea surface temperatures could increase by 1.5 degrees Celsius during Super El Niño, which could exacerbate atmospheric conditions and drive up the heat index.
From this, residents of urban areas where there is little greenery to deflect the heat may experience dangerous levels of heat index.

“Kasama na diyan 'yung mga lumot. ‘Yung mga nasa pader na lumot, kasama ‘yung mga grasses, kailangan hindi inaalis ‘yan. Kapag walang puno, walang grasses, walang lumot at walang tubig, walang sasalo. Ang sasalo diyan ay mga tao at mga animals,” Dela Cruz said.

(That includes moss as well. The moss growing on walls, along with grasses, should not be removed. When there are no trees, grasses, moss, and water, there is nothing to absorb the heat. The ones that will bear the heat will be people and animals.)
Preserving greens in urban jungles
Dela Cruz explained that heat bounces off concrete walls in urban jungles, making people living in cities more vulnerable to heat stroke during Super El Niño.
Due to this, he urged the public to preserve any remaining “greens” in the urban jungle, including moss and grasses.

“Kung meron kayong nakitang pader na mayroong green, dati-dati nililinis natin 'yung lumot. Huwag nating alisin 'yan. Kasama na 'yung mga sa sidewalk. Kung minsan sa mga sidewalk natin makikita natin may mga lumot huwag ho nating alisin 'yan,” Dela Cruz said.
(If you saw walls with greens, which we used to clean before, let’s not remove those. Including the sidewalks. Sometimes we see moss on the sidewalks, let’s not remove them.)
He also pushed for the installation of misting systems and public cooling and hydration systems in busy and populated areas.
Stay indoors

Dela Cruz cited a study by the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab, saying there could be 6,500 fatalities in the Philippines from the impacts of Super El Niño, to describe the severity of its potential impact.
The commissioner suggested implementing a shifting schedule for classes and work once Super El Niño starts to peak to avoid heat-related health issues.
He proposed moving the class schedule from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 a.m., to make students stay inside their homes at 10:00 a.m.
Senior citizens with pre-existing conditions and other vulnerable sectors, meanwhile, were also advised to stay indoors during peak heat hours from 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.

articles.title: Sixteen English councils spend more than 80% of core funding on social care
articles.summary:
Councils collectively spent record 71.9% of core spending on adult and children’s care last year, analysis shows

Sixteen English councils spent more than 80% of their core funding on adult…

blocks.text: Sixteen English councils spent more than 80% of their core funding on adult and children’s social care last year, highlighting the growing financial pressure on other local services.

Guardian analysis of government figures found that councils responsible for social care spent a net £42.8bn on adult and children’s services in 2025-26, equivalent to a record 71.9% of their combined core spending. Adult social care took 44.5% and children’s services accounted for 27.4%. In 2017-18, care costs made up 62.4% of councils’ core spending.

The overspending, which is driven by an ageing population with increasingly complex care needs, rising inflationary pressures and growing children’s social care demand, is pushing many councils to the brink of bankruptcy.
These challenges have led Andy Burnham to make reform of the care system key to his government’s ambitions.

Speaking at the Labour conference on Tuesday, the prime minister announced that the government would begin laying the groundwork for a National Care Service to be introduced after the next election, paid for in part by changing the earnings element of the triple lock.

He has already accelerated a government-commissioned independent review of adult social care carried out by Louise Casey, which initially was due to be published in 2028 but is now expected next year. That review will now shape the form the new care service takes.

Lady Casey delivered a withering critique of the state of the English social care system earlier this year, describing it as held together by “sticking plasters and glue”. She said the country faced a “moment of reckoning” over its failure to meet growing care needs.

Halton in Cheshire had the highest net spending on social care relative to its spending power at 92.9% in 2025-26. Just over half of its core spending was spent on adult social care and 42% was spent on child social care, which includes fostering services.

An official audit of the council published last month found its finances were unsustainable, despite it making cuts and selling off council assets. Halton received £35m in government-approved exceptional financial support this year.

A spokesperson for the council said the demand for services continued to place pressure on their finances. “The council is making necessary changes to drive down spending and improve its long-term financial sustainability,” the spokesperson said. “This includes introducing new ways of working that reduce costs while continuing to deliver good outcomes for vulnerable residents.”

Many of the 16 councils spending the largest proportions of their budgets on social care were forced to apply to the government this year for permission to borrow money to meet the day-to-day costs of running services and balance their budgets. Some cover among the most deprived areas in England, including Blackpool, Middlesbrough and Hartlepool.
Adult care alone consumed more than half of core spending power at 19 councils. That number has more than tripled since 2017-18, when six authorities crossed the same threshold.

Core spending power is the government’s measure of the money councils can use to provide services, combining locally raised income such as council tax and business rates with central government grants. It is not ringfenced, meaning councils can choose how to use it.

Councils in England overspent their 2025-26 adult social care budgets by £715m, and in response have drawn up plans to save £909m, according to the Association of Directors of Adult Social Services. These will include higher charges for care and cuts to adult care services such as daycentres.

Analysis by the King’s Fund found that the recent rise in spending reflected a rise in the number of people being supported – contrasting with 2015-20 when, during a period of cuts to council budgets, increased social care costs were mainly going on the fees to social care providers. As of March this year, 684,920 adults were in long-term care, up from a low of 613,360 in 2021-22.
The King’s Fund’s senior fellow for social care, Simon Bottery, said demand for social care had risen due to England’s ageing population as well as more adults living longer with complex needs.

He said: “Councils are meeting some of the extra costs faced by care providers, while also supporting more people. Those two factors combined account for the extra expenditure and the rising proportion of council funding going on care.

“A higher proportion of council budgets is being spent on adult social care than a few years ago, which means services such as refuse collection, libraries and roads get squeezed. Only about 2% of the population receives adult social care in any one year, but councils are spending a huge proportion of their budgets providing it.
“We need to move to a national system for funding social care to avoid the variation we’re seeing. At the moment, someone may receive support in one local authority but not in the next.”

Dr Wendy Taylor, the chair of the Local Government Association’s health and wellbeing committee, said: “Overall overspend has decreased slightly this year, but it remains high and is impacting spending on other council services. At the same time, councils’ capacity to spend on planned prevention is shrinking, with knock-on effects elsewhere in health and care services.

“Sustained and predictable funding and infrastructure will be essential for the future of adult social care, if councils are to successfully meet growing demand, deliver on their duties under the Care Act and support people to live the independent lives they want to lead.”
The Guardian excluded six councils that had not submitted their spending data for 2025-26.

articles.title: Carlo Paalam earns shot at ending PH’s 16-year wait for Asian Games boxing gold
articles.summary: Cagayan de Oro pride Carlo Paalam squeaks past reigning world champion Makhmud Sabyrkhan of Kazakhstan to advance to the final of the men's 55kg division in the 2026 Asian Games

blocks.text: POWER. Boxer Carlo Paalam in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Cagayan de Oro pride Carlo Paalam squeaks past reigning world champion Makhmud Sabyrkhan of Kazakhstan to advance to the final of the men's 55kg division in the 2026 Asian Games
MANILA, Philippines – Carlo Paalam moved on the cusp of ending the Philippines’ 16-year drought for a boxing gold medal in the Asian Games.

That is after the pride of Cagayan de Oro overcame reigning world champion Makhmud Sabyrkhan of Kazakhstan, pulling off a razor-thin split decision win to advance to the final of the men’s 55kg division at the Nishio Gymnasium in Japan on Wednesday, September 30.

Paalam did just enough to earn the nod of three of the five judges, winning with scores of 29-27, 29-27, 28-28, 27-29, 26-30 to stay on track of becoming the first Filipino boxing champion in the Asian Games since Rey Saludar reigned in the 2010 edition.

The last Filipino boxer standing, Paalam won the opening round with four judges ruling in his favor before Sabyrkhan flashed the form that netted him two world titles, turning up the heat and drawing level in the second round.
But Paalam, an Olympic silver medalist and an Asian champion, stayed composed and landed crisp counters, clinching the third round with a 3-2 score to secure the win.

Paalam will face home bet Rui Yamaguchi in the title match on Friday, October 2 — the Japanese registering a unanimous decision win over Mongolia’s Bilguunsaikhan Kharkhuu in the other final four duel.
By reaching the final, the 28-year-old is guaranteed to eclipse his bronze finish in the 2018 Asian Games, where he competed in the 49kg class.

Paalam hopes to get the job done for Philippine boxing after teammate Eumir Marcial fell short of the gold in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China, losing a contentious unanimous decision loss to a home fighter. – Rappler.com

articles.title: El Nino is a 'postcard from the future' — and could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths
articles.summary: The current El Nino could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths. Researchers warn it offers a glimpse of temperatures that may become normal within 20 years.

image.caption: India is among the countries projected to suffer a high death toll during the current El Niño An elderly woman is carried into a crowded hospital in Ballia, northern India, during a severe heat wave (FILE; 20/06/2023)Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Peruvian fishermen gave El Nino its name — "the little boy," or Christ Child — after noticing unusually warm Pacific waters around Christmas that caused the fish they depended on to suddenly become scarce.

But what those fishermen observed locally can have consequences thousands of kilometers away. El Nino can shift temperature and rainfall patterns around the world, bringing extreme heat and drought to some regions and heavy rain and flooding to others.
Researchers now estimate that the unusually high temperatures linked to the current El Nino could cause around 451,000 excess deaths worldwide from June 2026 to February 2027.

The event is a "postcard from the future," Tamma Carleton, head of research at the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab, told DW. Land temperatures over the coming months are forecast to run about 1.2 degrees C (2.1 F) above normal.
"For the average person, that's roughly the warming climate change is projected to bring about 20 years from now, arriving all at once," Carleton said.
How does El Nino affect weather worldwide?

Normally, winds blowing west across the Pacific push warm surface water towards Asia and Australia, allowing colder water to rise near South America. During El Nino, which occurs erratically every two to seven years, those winds weaken. Less cold water then rises, and much more of the Pacific stays unusually warm.
The warmer water heats the air above it and fuels rainfall over the central and eastern Pacific. The rising air spreads high in the atmosphere, sending waves that disrupt weather worldwide.

"It is like throwing a stone into a lake," climate researcher Fred Kucharski told DW. "Initially the surface perturbation is local, but then the energy spreads all over the lake through wave propagation."
Kucharski said the effects can cross the tropics within one week and reach higher latitudes in about two. Where the waves travel determines whether a region becomes hotter, cooler, wetter or drier.
The current El Nino developed in June and has strengthened rapidly since. It is now on course to become an exceptionally strong — sometimes called "super" — El Nino.

The Climate Impact Lab says its estimate covers only the first nine months of El Nino, as far as the current seasonal forecasts allow. The event is expected to continue into Northern Hemisphere spring, and its effect on global temperatures could last longer.
"We expect the final number to be meaningfully higher than what we are currently reporting here," Carleton said.
Why can El Nino be so deadly?
The estimate of 451,000 excess deaths covers deaths linked to the direct health effects of unusually high temperatures associated with El Nino.

Extreme heat strains the heart and kidneys, makes it harder for the body to maintain a safe temperature and can worsen cardiovascular, respiratory and other illnesses. As a result, the underlying condition is often recorded as the cause of death rather than the heat that aggravated it.
"Most heat deaths never show up in official statistics as heat deaths," Carleton said.
Could El Nino cause half a million heat-related deaths?
El Nino can also alter rainfall, contributing to drought in some regions and heavy rain and flooding in others.
Floods can kill, contaminate drinking water and spread disease. Drought can damage harvests and cause water and food shortages.
Deaths from these other indirect effects are not included in the 451,000 projection.
Where will the toll be greatest?

The Climate Impact Lab expects some of the largest increases in deaths in the Sahel, South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America. The highest numbers of fatalities are predicted for Nigeria, Sudan, Niger, Chad, India, Indonesia and Brazil.
Many are projected to occur between December and February, meaning much of the expected toll still lies ahead.

"Heat headlines usually focus on Europe and North America," Carleton said. "This event's toll is overwhelmingly in lower-income, already-hot countries, where people have the fewest ways to adapt and where these deaths are least likely to be counted."
Are these lives being significantly shortened?

Some people who die during extreme heat are already frail. This raises an important question: Is the heat cutting their lives substantially short, or merely bringing forward deaths that would have occurred days or weeks later — an effect known as mortality displacement?
What happens when El Nino meets climate change?
The underlying research uses annual rather than daily death rates, which largely filters out deaths brought forward by only days or weeks.

Ben Armstrong, an emeritus professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said he could not verify the 451,000 figure. But because the estimate is based on annual mortality data, it largely excludes deaths brought forward by only days or weeks. If the figure is correct, he said, most of those counted "would have lived at least six months longer."
Why predict deaths before they happen?
Scientists have long estimated the death toll from extreme temperatures retrospectively. Better seasonal forecasting is increasingly allowing researchers to look ahead instead.

To produce the estimate, researchers used earlier work showing how death rates change during hot weather in different parts of the world. They combined it with seasonal forecasts showing how hot each place is expected to become.
El Nino, regional wars fuel global food crisis
"Putting the two together lets us estimate the human cost of this event while there's still time to do something about it, rather than counting the deaths after the fact," Carleton said.
Heat warnings, cooling centers and hydration stations, home visits to vulnerable people, protections for outdoor workers and additional health care capacity could all reduce mortality.
The researchers believe targeted interventions could save tens of thousands of lives.
For Carleton, the forecast is a warning to prepare now for the heat that climate change could make commonplace.

"This El Nino gives us a look at future weather in the 2040s," Carleton said. "These temperatures will become normal in 20 years, giving us time and reason to begin investing in adaptive capacity now."

articles.title: Somali pirates killed oil tanker crew before rescue, official tells BBC
articles.summary: Piracy off the Somali coast has increased in recent years after dropping when international naval operations began in 2011.

blocks.text: Five crew members of an oil tanker seized by pirates off the coast of Somalia were killed before local security forces retook the vessel, a senior regional official has told the BBC.
Puntland Deputy Information Minister Bile Qabowsade said the five were killed by pirates before regional forces boarded MT Hoarner 25.
He said the dead included three Pakistani nationals, one Indian and one national of Myanmar. Four other crew members were injured, including three Pakistanis and one Indian.
The tanker, which was carrying about 18,500 barrels of oil destined for the Somali capital, Mogadishu, was seized in April by six armed men while sailing off the coast of Somalia.
Sixteen suspected pirates have been arrested, while others escaped and were being pursued, officials said.

Qabowsade rejected suggestions that forces from Puntland, a semi-autonomous region of Somalia, had helped some of the pirates escape. The authorities have not given further details how the five crew members were killed or how the pirates took control of the vessel.
The hijacked tanker was anchored near the Somali coast between the fishing towns of Xaafun and Bander Beyla.
In April, officials had said there were 17 crew members on board when the vessel was hijacked. They included 10 Pakistanis, four Indonesians, one Indian, one Sri Lankan and a Myanmar national.
Piracy off the Somali coast fell sharply after 2011 following international naval operations, but attacks and hijackings have increased again in recent years.

articles.title: Marcos institutionalizes DBM public funds tracker
articles.summary: The digital platform COMPASS, launched in late June this year, allows the public to track the movements of government funds from its approval to release, obligations incurred, and actual…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 2:41pm
PRESIDENT Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. signed the General Appropriations Act for Fiscal Year 2026 during a ceremony at Malacañan Palace on Monday, Jan. 5.
Noel B. Pabalate / PPA Pool
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Budget and Management’s (DBM) platform, where the public can monitor and track government funds has been made permanent and embedded into government systems.

This comes after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order No. 126 on Tuesday, September 28, to institutionalize DBM’s Centralized Open Monitoring Platform for Appropriations and Spending Statistics (COMPASS).
The digital platform COMPASS, launched in late June this year, allows the public to track the movement of government funds from approval to release, obligations incurred, and actual disbursements.
The information can also be filtered by agency, department, purpose, fiscal year and other categories.

“There is a need to institutionalize the COMPASS portal to enhance public access to information on government budget, procurement, and fund utilization through a unified digital platform,” the executive order read.
COMPASS Council

The order directed all government agencies, government-owned and controlled corporations, and state financial institutions to publish and disclose information that may be required by the DBM on the COMPASS Portal.
Local government units, meanwhile, were encouraged to do the same.

For its implementation, the COMPASS Council, composed of the DBM as the chairperson, the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) as the co-chairperson, and the Department of Finance and Department of the Interior and Local Government as members, will be established.

The COMPASS portal will be embedded in existing government digital systems such as the Budget and Treasury Management System, Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System, Digital Information for Monitoring and Evaluation and E-Gov App.

articles.title: Poor planning at resettlement sites pushing schools past capacity
articles.summary: Poor planning in the government's mass resettlement program is pushing public schools past capacity, with one Cavite town needing 135 new classrooms from the surge in a single year alone.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 2:23pm
The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development unveils new housing sites in Naic, Cavite on May 6, 2026.
Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development

MANILA, Philippines — Poor planning in the government's mass resettlement program is pushing public schools past capacity, with one Cavite town needing 135 new classrooms from the surge in a single year alone.
This is according to data shared Tuesday, September 29, during the deliberations of the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD)'s proposed 2027 budget.

Data from the department, compiled by EDCOM 2, lists 64 NHA resettlement sites in 30 cities and municipalities, as of August 24, where elementary and high school enrollment has surged without enough school facilities planned for the new students.
In Naic, Cavite, enrollment rose by 5,405 learners in one school year, from 52,394 in school year 2025-2026 to 57,799 in 2026-2027, EDCOM 2 data show.
Public schools in the town serve students from at least 48 housing sites run by the National Housing Authority (NHA) and the Pag-IBIG Fund.
Under the Department of Education's (DepEd) standard of 40 learners per classroom, that one-year increase requires at least 135 more classrooms.
The NHA told the Senate committee it is about to sign an agreement under which DepEd will fund schools in its resettlement sites.
However, EDCOM 2 said the commitment covers only a fraction of what Naic alone needs.

"In Naic alone, the 50 classrooms committed represents only a fraction of the need, considering the exponential increase in student enrolment," EDCOM II Executive Director Karol Mark Yee said during the hearing.
EDCOM II first raised the Naic example at a July hearing by the Senate basic education committee, where it said lack of planning has "overwhelmed" the public schools near resettlement areas.
For instance, this school year, enrollment at Muzon Elementary School in Naic, Cavite more than doubled, to 1,510 learners from 605, even as it only has seven classrooms.
At the elementary school of Timalan Hillsview Integrated School, enrollment rose to 7,459 from 6,515. It has 32 classrooms.
A much larger surge in students had already taken place in school year 2022-2023, when the municipality of Naic saw enrollment increase by 10,794 in that school year alone.
That increase came around the recorded start year of the Naic View Residences housing development and required 270 more classrooms, Sen. JV Ejercito said.
Yee urged the department to coordinate better with the Department of Education on the availability of school facilities when pursuing housing developments.

articles.title: US troops exit Iraq after more than a decade
articles.summary: The current deployment began in 2014 in an effort to combat 'Islamic State' extremists. Iran, which has sought a complete removal of the US military from the Middle East, celebrated the withdrawal.

image.caption: The coalition troops deployed to Iraq in 2014 (FILE PHOTO: May, 15. 2011)Image: Ali Al-Saadi/AFP

blocks.text: After more than ten years, US forces are to withdraw from their remaining military bases in Iraq on Wednesday.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi declared that October 1, the day following the coalition's departure, should be celebrated as Sovereignty Day.

It is "a national occasion that affirms the completion of Iraq's path toward sovereignty and consolidates the presence of the state and its institutions," the heads of the executive, legislative and judicial branches said on Monday.
What will the US troop withdrawal from Iraq mean for Kurds?
The troops were delpoyed in Iraq and Syria in 2014, to tackle the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group, which had taken over large swathes of both countries.
The IS was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group's remnants.
The complete departure of US troops from Iraq comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled Saddam Hussein, triggering widespread upheaval and chaos, before the rise of IS.
Iran celebrates US withdrawal from Iraq

Iran and its allies celebrated the withdrawal of US forces, which was agreed upon in 2024 by then-US President Joe Biden. The agreement has now been executed under Donald Trump's term even as US continues to wage a war against Iran.
Iran, which wants a US-free Middle East, sees the US pullout from Iraq as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of ​allied armed groups across the region.
The withdrawal of the US troops from Iraq has raised threats of diminished security in the region as Iran-backed Shi'ite militias are vying to gain more control and potentially regroup 'IS'.

articles.summary: 'I do not know Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., nor have I ever received any money from him,' says Vice President Duterte

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte, who is in the middle of an impeachment trial that could oust her from office, is facing yet another allegation.
This time, the so-called revelation comes from a former member of the Philippine National Police (PNP).

In his eight-page affidavit, former police corporal Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., 36, claimed he had delivered suitcases containing millions of pesos to Duterte on different occasions. He also claimed he had served as former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco’s security detail.

Duterte, in a statement, denied knowing Gracioso or receiving money from him. The Vice President also said they were still waiting for a copy of his affidavit before considering possible legal action against him.

“Once we are done dismantling the lies contained in his testimony, it will end up in the trash bin—just like the one from Ramil Madriaga. This is nothing more than another media stunt, an attempt to breathe life into a faltering impeachment case,” said Duterte.
“No amount of political maneuvering, propaganda, or manufactured distractions can ultimately silence the Filipino people,” she added.

On Monday, September 28, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. confirmed that Gracioso used to be a policeman until he was dismissed from service due to a case. He also confirmed that the former police corporal used to be part of Velasco’s security detail.
We have reached out to the other individuals mentioned in the affidavit. We will update this story once they respond.

According to Gracioso, he became a member of the PNP in 2015. Two years later, in 2017, he was deployed to Marawi during the siege and worked under his battalion commander, Police Brigadier General Segundo Lagundi.

After the Marawi siege, the former cop said he and other Marawi veterans were assigned as close-in security aides of Velasco and his wife, Rowena Amara. He said he became Velasco’s head of security in 2018 and served as the lawmaker’s security aide until 2024.

As the security head, Gracioso said he was tasked to greet and give protection to the couple’s visitors. He claimed that Velasco told him that the most important guest was Duterte, who was the then-Davao City mayor.

Gracioso said he first met Duterte in 2018 at a hangar in Pasay City where she had landed in a private plane. He claimed he drove Duterte to a hotel in Manila in a white Ford Savannah van. During the trip, the former cop alleged that he told Duterte that Rowena had a gift for her, which was stored in a paper bag and a small suitcase.
The former cop alleged that Duterte took the paper bag and ordered him to give the suitcase to Jefry Tupas, a former Davao City information officer.

“Ang laman ng inabot kong paper bag ay Royce chocolates na paborito daw ni Ma’am Sara at ang maliit na maleta naman ay naglalaman ng [P20-million] cash (The paper bag contains Royce chocolates said to be Ma’am Sara’s favorite, while the small suitcase contained P20-million cash),” he alleged in his affidavit.
Gracioso alleged that there were similar incidents like this, almost 10 times, from 2018 to 2020. He also claimed that whenever Duterte arrived at the Pasay City hangar, he would fetch her.

“Pinaabutan siya ni Boss Allan ng pasalubong na Royce Chocolate at maleta na naglalaman ng nasa sampu hanggang dalawampung milyong piso (P10-20 million) na ‘budget’ niya sa pagiikot. Personal ko itong inaabot kay Ma’am Sara o minsan kapag kasama niya ang katiwala na si Jepoy (Tupas) ay dito niya ito pinaaabot,” the former cop claimed.

(Boss Allan always gave Duterte Royce chocolates and suitcases containing between P10 million and P20 million, which was Duterte’s budget for “going around.” I personally handed these to Ma’am Sara, or sometimes through Tupas..)

blocks.caption: GROUFIE. Former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. (second from right) poses for a photo with Vice President Sara Duterte and former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco. Gracioso attached this photo in his NBI affidavit.

blocks.text: Before the campaign for the 2019 midterm elections, Gracioso alleged that Velasco ordered him to deliver a Toyota Grandia van and a Cadillac Escalade containing money and gifts to Duterte in Davao. Gracioso alleged they delivered these to Duterte’s residence and told her that they were from Rowena.

He also alleged that he gave the paper bag to Duterte, who supposedly told him to give the suitcase to Tupas. He said he and Tupas then went to the vehicles and gave Duterte’s aide a suitcase containing P50 million in cash, along with the keys to the two vehicles.
During the 2019 election campaign, Gracioso alleged, he gave Duterte kakanin (rice cakes) and two large suitcases while they were in Marinduque. He said each suitcase contained P50 million.

“Sabi ni Ma’am Sara na ibigay kay Jepoy ang dalawang (2) malaking maleta at mga kakanin (rice cakes). Inabot ko ‘yong dalawang malaking maleta na naglalaman ng [P50-million] cash bawat isa at ‘yong mga kakanin kay Jepoy bago sila sumakay ng eroplano,” the former cop claimed.
(Ma’am Sara told me to give the two big suitcases and the kakanin to Jepoy. I gave him the two suitcases, each containing P50 million in cash, and the rice cakes before they boarded the plane.)

Gracioso also claimed that after the Moriones Festival in 2019, they went to Velasco’s house in Valle Verde 2, Pasig City, to get money before flying to Davao from the private hangar in Pasay City. The former cop said they brought two large suitcases containing about P100 million, which was supposedly intended for the additional expenses of Duterte’s regional party, Hugpong ng Pagbabago (HNP).

On one occasion, Gracioso said, they went to Davao to deliver two brand new Toyota Super Grandia vans, one of them bulletproof. He claimed they stuffed the vehicles with cash and gifts stored in various boxes and suitcases. The smallest suitcase contained around P20 million, while the larger suitcases contained P50 million each.
The bulletproof van allegedly contained the cash, while the other vehicle carried gifts such as watches, Royce chocolates, and branded bags.

Before the May 2019 elections, Gracioso alleged, Velasco told them to pack money into about 20 balikbayan boxes and suitcases. They also brought boxes of cigarettes and noodles. He claimed the money came from former Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co.

Gracioso alleged that Velasco ordered them to set aside one suitcase containing about P20 million, which would be used to buy motorcycles for HNP’s election caravan. After packing the money and gifts into two Grandia vans, he claimed that they traveled from Samar to Davao City.
The former cop alleged that he handed Royce chocolates and a Patek Philippe watch to Duterte, while he left the keys to the vehicles with Tupas.

Gracioso also claimed that he met Ramil Madriaga, a self-confessed bagman of Duterte. He alleged that Duterte introduced Madriaga to him, and the Vice President supposedly told him to give the money for the motorcycles to Madriaga.

“Iniabot ko nga ang maleta ng pera na naglalaman ng higit kumulang [P20 million] kay Sir Ramil sa utos ni Ma’am Sara. Noong nabili na ni Sir Ramil ang mga big bike para kay Ma’am Sara, sumama ako kay Ma’am Sara para sa election caravan ng HNP sa Mindanao,” the affidavit reads.
(I gave the suitcase containing around P20 million to Sir Ramil based on Ma’am Sara’s order. When Ramil bought the big bikes for Ma’am Sara, I joined her for the HNP’s election caravan in Mindanao.)

blocks.caption: Who is Ramil Madriaga and what’s behind his accusations vs Sara Duterte?

blocks.text: He narrated that he once saw Madriaga in Velasco’s home because Duterte allegedly ordered Madriaga to get P20 million for a motorcycle-riding course in Davao. Gracioso alleged that he personally handed over the money to Madriaga.

Gracioso also listed other alleged deliveries to Duterte. He claimed he gave two suitcases containing P50 million each on September 21, 2019. He also said that during the dry season in 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, he allegedly delivered three suitcases to Duterte in Cebu.

When Velasco became the House speaker in 2020, Gracioso said, the alleged deliveries of money to Velasco’s house became more frequent. The money allegedly came from different personalities like Co, now Marikina 2nd District Representative Miro Quimbo, and a lawyer named Honey Sipin.

“Kay Sir Miro Quimbo ko din narinig noong nasa Starbucks Katipunan, malapit sa Miriam College, na galing ang pera kila Curlee Discaya at Sarah Discaya at iba pang DPWH contractor (I’ve heard from Sir Miro Quimbo while we’re in Starbucks Katipunan near Miriam College that the money came from Curlee and Sarah Discaya, and other DPWH contractors),” the former cop claimed.

Gracioso alleged that in 2021, he went to Davao to deliver a suitcase containing P20 million intended for a riders’ training and to buy motorcycles for Duterte’s security people. The former policeman also alleged that he went to Davao on another occasion to deliver about 10 large suitcases that he said came from Co’s security detail.

When Velasco supposedly bought a house in Valle Verde 2, Duterte made frequent visits there. During the Vice President’s alleged first visit there, Velasco allegedly asked to bring out two big suitcases with cash that allegedly came from the collections of Quimbo.
The suitcases allegedly contained more or less P100 million, according to Gracioso. Tupas allegedly received the money on Duterte’s behalf.

Gracioso also alleged that he delivered around P80 million in two suitcases to Duterte at the Quezon Memorial Circle. In Subic Safari in Subic Bay Freeport, the former cop also alleged that he delivered two suitcases with P50 million each to the Vice President.
In 2021, Gracioso claimed that Velasco allegedly told them to pack more than P200 million cash into suitcases and boxes for Duterte. Again, he said, Tupas allegedly received the delivery.

“Nagkaron na din ng pagkakataon na sabay akong nag-deliver ng maleta ng pera sa Davao para kay Ma’am Sara at para kay Cong. Paolo Duterte. Sa utos pa [rin] ni Boss Allan, nag deliver din ako ng maleta ng pera para kay Congressman Paolo Duterte sa isang bar sa Davao at sa iba’t iba pang lugar sa Metro Manila,” Gracioso claimed.

(There were also times when I delivered money to Davao for Ma’am Sara and Congressman Paolo Duterte. Based on Boss Allan’s order, I delivered a suitcase to Congressman Paolo Duterte at a bar in Davao and in different places in Metro Manila.)

blocks.caption: BIG BIKE. Former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. (extreme left) poses for a photo with Vice President Sara Duterte. Gracioso attached this photo in his NBI affidavit.

blocks.text: Gracioso’s statements, in the affidavit submitted to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), are just allegations. It’s up to the government’s investigative bodies to assess if there’s merit in these claims and pursue investigations, if warranted, into those mentioned.
On Tuesday, September 29, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that Velasco was out of the country.

“Based on the Bureau’s records, there was no existing Hold Departure Order (HDO) or derogatory alert that would have prevented his departure from the Philippines. The BI cannot disclose further details concerning an individual’s immigration records due to data privacy concerns,” the BI said.

For Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla, Gracioso needs to be examined to determine if his statements are factual. But, for now, the Ombudsman thinks the allegations would eventually reach his office.

“Hindi pa ako puwedeng mag-judge e. Kailangang masubukan pa siya nang husto sa mga tanong na matindi para malaman natin kung totoo ang kanyang sinasabi (I cannot judge for now. We need to examine him more with tough questions to check if he’s telling the truth),” Remulla said in a chance interview.

The NBI is currently in the process of validating Gracioso’s claims. On September 28, NBI Director Melvin Matibag said his office will invite, not subpoena, the people mentioned in the affidavit, like the Vice President and Velasco, among others.

Catholic priest Father Flavie Villanueva, who was with Gracioso on Monday when he appeared before the NBI, said Gracioso reached out to him due to his father’s passing as well as the ex-cop’s anger toward the Velascos.

“Pitong taon siyang nagtrabaho bilang security, driver, head security sa mag-asawa. Pero sa panahon ng kagipitan, na kumakatok siya sa pinto ng mag-asawa para mapagamot ang kanyang sarili, mapagamot ang kanyang ama na may sakit, walang tulong na dumating,” Villanueva said in a Facts First interview with Christian Esguerra.

(He worked as security, driver, head of security for the couple for seven years. But in his time of need, when he needed the Velascos for help for his medical treatment, treatment for his father who’s suffering from an illness, no help arrived.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Rear View] DDS senators have the numbers to acquit. Why aren’t they cheering?
articles.summary: The Senate minority's survival now depends on the Ombudsman, the justice department, The Hague, and the Supreme Court

blocks.text: Following last week’s vote by the impeachment court to lower the conviction threshold in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, House prosecutor Gerville Luistro reminded everyone, particularly those cheering at the looming certainty of conviction, that the lower conviction threshold also meant a lower threshold for acquittal.

With 20 senators as the denominator, conviction needs 14 votes, which means seven “not guilty” votes will acquit the Vice President. Seven. That’s exactly how many DDS-minority senators are physically present at the moment. (Editor’s note: DDS is a common reference to Duterte Diehard Supporters.)

But the minority senators aren’t high-fiving each other. Minority leader Alan Peter Cayetano, the blessed bearded one, hasn’t fallen on his knees to thank the heavens or shaved off his facial hair, which he said he grew in protest over injustice and oppression. The DDS talking heads and their troll armies haven’t flooded our feeds with victory statements and memes.
Why is that? Allow me to offer two possibilities.
One, they can’t celebrate a formula they’re calling unconstitutional.

It shatters the oppression narrative, which portrays the Vice President as a victim of a vindictive Marcos administration — one that, in collusion with majority senators, will go to extremes to take her out of the 2028 presidential race by securing her conviction, even put her in jail.

The vote has converted the Vice President, the Dutertes, the minority senators, and the DDS to latter-day constitutionalists. For them, the Constitution is a covenant written in stone, sacred and inviolate. What the majority senators and one minority senator did, they insist, was unconstitutional.
It’s classic DDS sleight of hand.

During the reign of Duterte the father, charter provisions mandating the protection and respect for human rights were willfully ignored in the name of the drug war. The former president himself, now detained at The Hague on charges of crimes against humanity, once likened the Constitution to toilet paper.

True to the narrative, Vic Rodriguez, a former Marcos official turned DDS, has asked the Supreme Court to void the ruling as unconstitutional and restrain its enforcement. Thus, cheering the new formula would mean accepting the very premise they’re asking the tribunal to strike down.
Two, and more practical: The minority’s seven isn’t a solid seven.

Senator Mark Villar, who has replaced Senator Lito Lapid as the Senate’s quiet one, surprisingly broke from the minority twice during the September 23 session: first abstaining on his bloc’s bid to defer the threshold vote, then joining the majority to lower the threshold for conviction.

Both Mark and Senator Camille Villar are among the family members named in criminal and administrative complaints filed by the Ombudsman on September 18 over PrimeWater’s water district deals, five days before the vote. Senator Imee Marcos, the President’s elder sister and a member of the minority, hinted that Mark’s vote could have been linked to the family’s legal troubles, saying “we know what he’s going through.”

Cayetano insisted that Villar remains with the minority, but he offered the assurance without his usual cocksure bluster. The minority has zero margin, and the quiet Villar has already broken ranks twice.
And the seven may become six without anyone switching sides.

The new formula counts only senators who are “legally and factually” able to participate when the verdict is rendered, tentatively in December. The denominator isn’t frozen at 20. It can shrink every time another senator-judge lands in detention or goes into hiding.

Senator Robin Padilla faces a preliminary investigation at the Department of Justice for allegedly helping Senator Ronald “Bato” de la Rosa slip out of the Senate in May. Cayetano is under investigation for alleged ghost flood control projects and illegal reclamation in Taguig, his home turf. Let’s not forget the former Duterte aide, Senator Bong Go, named in February by International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors as an alleged co-perpetrator, along with senator-in-hiding de la Rosa and other former police chiefs, in the crimes against humanity case against the elder Duterte.

Lose one more minority senator and the denominator drops to 19. Conviction then needs 13 “guilty” votes. Acquittal still needs seven “not guilty” votes. Impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero pointed this out when he cast the lone dissenting vote: a shrinking denominator lowers the bar for conviction faster than it lowers the bar for acquittal.
The minority’s best shield was the full 24-member count, and that shield is gone. Its survival now depends on the Ombudsman, the justice department, The Hague, and the Supreme Court.
So no, there’s no cheering. Seven is a number you celebrate only if you’re sure you’ll still have it when the votes are cast. – Rappler.com
Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

articles.title: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January
articles.summary:
Cap poised to rise by 16% to equivalent of £1,999 for dual-fuel bill as impact of Iran war puts squeeze on homes

Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to soar by £276 a year…

blocks.text: Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to soar by £276 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East war continues through the coldest months of winter.

The government’s cap on energy prices is poised to jump by 16% to the equivalent of £1,999 for the average annual dual-fuel bill in a further blow to struggling households, according to figures from the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.

The increase for the January to March quarter is well above the consultancy’s previous prediction of a 9% rise, with analysts blaming the uptick on the recent rise in gas market prices to three-year highs.
It would take the cap to its highest level for four years.

Gas prices in Europe have doubled in recent months as the continent prepares to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years after the US-Israel war on Iran triggered an increase in global market prices.

Buyers have delayed refilling storage facilities after a cold end to last winter, and extra gas power generation during the summer heatwaves, depleted stocks while oil and gas exports from the Gulf remain severely disrupted.

The gloomier outlook for energy bills was published as millions of households brace for energy charges to rise by 4% from Thursday as the quarterly energy bill cap, which is set by the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, climbs to its highest level in three years this winter.
after newsletter promotion

The unit cost of electricity will rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.32p, while gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.97p – equivalent to £1,723 a year for a typical home’s gas and electricity use. However, actual household bills will depend on how much each consumes.

articles.title: 'Alternative Nobel' honors women's rights activists, AI researcher
articles.summary: The Right Livelihood Award has gone to a female AI researcher and women fighting repression. The Sweden-based prize has been dubbed an "alternative Nobel."

image.caption: The Right Livelihood Award honors people trying to make the world better and more peacefulImage: Right Livelihood Foundation/dpa/Right Livelihood Foundation/picture alliance

blocks.text: A leading AI researcher, together with a woman lawyer from Pakistan and two women-led rights groups, on Wednesday received a Sweden-based rights award that honors work seen as contributing to a more just and peaceful world.

The Right Livelihood Award was created by Swedish-German philanthropist Jakob von Uexkull in 1980 to celebrate achievements in the fields of environment and international development disregarded by the Nobel Prizes.
It is usually awarded a week before the Nobel Prizes.

Right Livelihood said this year's winners, from 200 nominations from 72 countries, were being honored "resistance to systems that push people to the margins, and a shared insistence on putting people back at the center."
Who won the Right Livelihood Award in 2026?
An AI researcher fighting bias

blocks.caption: Timnit Gebru has highlighted the biases affecting AI systemsImage: Right Livelihood/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: AI researcher Timnit Gebru, the founder of the Distributed AI Research Institute, received her prize for her work in examining how artificial intelligence is influenced by biases.

In a statement, Right Livelihood said she was being honored "for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency."

In 2020, Gebru, who was born in Ethiopia to a family of Eritrean origin, was one of the authors behind a paper on the risks of biases in so-called large language models (LLMs) while co-leading tech giant Google's Ethical AI team.
According to the jury, Google dismissed her after she refused to retract the paper or remove her name as requested unless certain guarantees were given.
A Pakistani lawyer fighting repression

blocks.caption: Jalila Haider defends vulnerable communities in PakistanImage: Right Livelihood/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another winner was Jalila Haider of Pakistan, who the jury said was awarded the prize "for breaking barriers, as the first female lawyer from her Hazara community, to challenge ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that no human being is illegal."
Haider is known for her work defending some of her country's most vulnerable communities against repression by the state, discrimination against women and ethnic violence.
"Haider has secured justice for thousands targeted or ignored by those in power, specifically ethnic, gender and religious minorities, as well as refugees," the organization said.
A Southern African rural women's group defending land rights

blocks.caption: Mercia Andrews is the regional coordinator of the Rural Women's AssemblyImage: Right Livelihood/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Rural Women's Assembly, which brings together more than 178,000 small-scale farmers in 11 Southern African countries, was another winner of the prize.
The Right Livelihood jury said the group had created "a united force defending land, seed and bodily autonomy against corporate and patriarchal dispossession."
Among other things, the Assembly has worked to reproduce and preserve local seed varieties to help protect a long traditional practice of saving and exchanging such seeds, the foundation said.
A Georgian human rights group protecting civic power

blocks.caption: Nona Kurdovanidze (L) is the former GYLA chairperson and Tamar Oniani the current oneImage: Leli Blagonravova/Right Livelihood Award Foundation/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The prize also went to the Georgian Young Lawyers' Association (GYLA), which the foundation said it was honoring "as the moral compass of Georgian society."
The jury said the group, founded in 1994, received the award for its efforts in "building and safeguarding Georgian democracy and sustaining civic power in the face of an autocratic crackdown."
