articles.title: Iran urges US voters to vote out Trump’s allies in election
articles.summary: While it is unlikely to sway US voters, Iran identifies issues that US political analysts say are working against Donald Trump and the Republicans ahead of November 3 congressional elections

blocks.text: DONALD TRUMP. US President Donald Trump gestures after his speech during the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, USA, September 9, 2026.
Jessica Koscielniak/Reuters
While it is unlikely to sway US voters, Iran identifies issues that US political analysts say are working against Donald Trump and the Republicans ahead of November 3 congressional elections

items: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps called on Americans to vote out Trump allies in Congress, linking the US withdrawal from Iraq to their political agenda.
Qatar is mediating efforts to end the conflict between the US and Iran, with ongoing negotiations failing to yield a resolution despite recent talks.
Trump's administration faces criticism over handling the war and economic issues, with a significant portion of the public disapproving of his policies ahead of the upcoming elections.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps urged Americans to vote out US President Donald Trump’s allies in Congress as US forces were due to withdraw from their remaining bases in neighboring Iraq on Wednesday, September 30, in a departure celebrated by Tehran.
Meanwhile, Qatar continued to promote its shuttle diplomacy aimed at ending the seven-month-old war between Iran and the United States. Trump once again predicted a swift surrender for Iran.

The 26-page letter by the Guards, published on Tuesday, September 29, urges Americans to use their political power to remove current leaders from office and reject US support for Israel and military intervention abroad.

blocks.caption: US forces exit Iraq, emboldening Iran’s proxies and Islamic State

blocks.text: While the missive was unlikely to sway US voters who may not even see the text published by Iranian media, it identifies issues that US political analysts say are working against Trump and the Republican Party ahead of November 3 congressional elections, when the opposition Democrats could retake control of one or both legislative chambers, potentially impeding Trump’s political agenda.
“Remove from power the evil, deceitful, and violent politicians who are responsible for America’s current state,” the letter said. “Make sure your politicians understand that the world has changed.”

Trump campaigned in 2024 pledging to avoid new wars, end existing conflicts and bring down inflation, but the war with Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel, has contributed to higher global fuel prices and spread in the Middle East.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll published September 21 found just 17% of respondents approved Trump’s handling of the cost of living – the top issue Americans say will determine how they vote in November. Only 34% approved of the strikes on Iran.

blocks.caption: Trump approval falls to record low as high costs bite, poll finds

blocks.text: Trump, who broke with Republican orthodoxy in 2016 when he called the US invasion of Iraq a major mistake, allowed the final withdrawal from Iraq on Wednesday, which was agreed in 2024 by former President Joe Biden.
The withdrawal comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled Saddam Hussein, then triggered upheaval that culminated with the rise of Islamic State.

The US war in Iran has drawn in Iranian allies in the region, including the Houthis in Yemen, Hezbollah in Lebanon and militias in Iraq, which Riyadh blamed for the September 10 attack that knocked the East-West Pipeline in Saudi Arabia offline.

Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the US withdrawal from Iraq as a triumph for its “axis of resistance” of allied armed groups across the region.
The US and Iran have not found an off-ramp from the war despite rounds of talks and several ceasefires.

Negotiations appeared to intensify during last week’s UN General Assembly meeting in New York, but have so far not yielded any agreement to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil and liquefied natural gas passed before the war started in February.

Qatar has again emerged as would-be peacemaker after previously playing a supporting role in producing a June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire. US and Iranian officials spoke separately with Qatari mediators on Monday, but it was unclear if exchanges took place on Tuesday.

“We are exchanging messages between the parties, and we’re working towards establishing a common ground in order to get into a deal that would save all of us from the repercussions of the conflict,” Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari told reporters.
Trump meanwhile repeated his position that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon and that the war would be over soon.

The conflict has degraded Iran’s conventional forces and damaged its already ailing economy, but Tehran has fought back with missile and drone strikes on US allies in the Gulf and by restricting oil tanker traffic in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which has pushed up world energy prices.
“I don’t know if they are going to give up yet but they’ll give up,” Trump told reporters on Tuesday.
“They are doing very poorly,” he added.
At the United Nations General Assembly last week, Iran floated a peace proposal that would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in fighting.
Trump on Saturday rejected the plan although Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that Washington had not officially relayed a US rejection through mediators.

Trump has cited weakening Iran’s nuclear capabilities as one of his war objectives, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbors and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.

Iran, which does not have nuclear weapons, denies seeking them. The US is nuclear-armed. Tehran says it has the right to develop nuclear technology for peaceful purposes as a party to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Inflation leaps to 4% stoking fears of fifth interest rate hike before Christmas
articles.summary: Jim Chalmers says ‘higher global oil prices flowing through to oil prices in Australia’ are to blame for inflation rising from 3.5%

blocks.text: Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, as Jim Chalmers was again forced to defend Labor’s economic management amid fears the Reserve Bank will need to hike interest rates again before Christmas.

The increasingly embattled treasurer was accused of “gaslighting” Australians by insisting that government spending was not responsible for high inflation, blaming instead higher fuel costs associated with the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran.

“We can see in today’s inflation figures that the overwhelming reason why annual headline inflation has come up in August compared to July is because of the impact of higher global oil prices flowing through to oil prices in Australia,” Chalmers told reporters in Sydney.
“That’s not an opinion. It’s a fact.”

Fuel prices surged by 15% last month, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said, after a worsening Middle East conflict triggered a rebound in global oil prices and the government ended its cut to the fuel excise.
Rising transport costs were the prime contributor to price increases in the month, the ABS confirmed.

But a 5.4% increase in home building costs over the 12 months to August was one of the prime drivers of high annual inflation “as builders passed on higher costs for materials and labour”, the ABS said.
Electricity bills were also higher than this time last year when households were still receiving government rebates.
The rise in headline inflation was slightly less than economists had anticipated, while underlying inflation – which removes the most volatile prices swing – was steady at 3.6% in the year to August.
Both were still well above the RBA’s 2.5% target. Cherelle Murphy, EY’s chief economist, said “another rate hike looks likely by the end of the year”.
A day after the RBA lifted its cash rate to 4.6% – the fourth increase in 2026 – Murphy said “they [the RBA] have an ongoing fight on their hands”.
“This is not the end of it.”

Chalmers on Wednesday afternoon denied that he was at odds with Michele Bullock, the central bank governor, who at her press conference the previous day said “inflation is too high and has been driven by domestic capacity pressures”.
after newsletter promotion
But Bullock also pointed to the worsening Middle East conflict and the sudden boom in AI-related spending on datacentres.
“These developments suggest that inflationary pressures will persist for longer than previously expected,” she said.
Murphy said it was a fact that spending by governments, at the commonwealth and state levels, was high, and that this was adding to demand in the economy.
She said this meant the government should be extremely careful with any new spending – including additional cost of living relief – for fear of making the RBA’s job harder.
But she said it was impossible to quantify exactly to what extent government spending was responsible for persistently high inflation in 2026.
“Do I think this is the biggest part of the inflation problem right now? No, the biggest part of the problem is that we have these global supply shocks.
“What we are witnessing is the accumulation of a number of events happening together, and none of them are good for inflation.”

articles.title: Hungary's reckoning with Orban's corrupt system picks up speed with high-profile arrests
articles.summary: Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar vowed to dismantle Orban's corrupt networks. High-profile figures are being arrested and many Hungarians are pushing for swift accountability, but the rule of…

image.caption: Prime Minister Peter Magyar addresses an extraordinary session of the National Assembly on MondayImage: Zsolt Szigetvary/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: One of the new Hungarian government's key pledges was to investigate corruption under Viktor Orban, recover embezzled assets, and hold those responsible accountable. Or, in the words of Prime Minister Peter Magyar, it is time to "liquidate Orban's mafia state." During his election campaign, Magyar had already announced a "program for the road to prison." As prime minister, he launched "Operation Purgatory" at the end of June 2026.

Measured against his fighting talk, little has happened so far. There have been no sweeping purges of the state apparatus, although some government funds flowing to Orban-aligned businessmen have been cut off. Police and prosecutors have summoned a handful of relatively unknown individuals for questioning, and a few people were arrested. The governing majority also established an agency to recover assets, but it is is not yet up and running.

But at the beginning of the week, Hungarians witnessed the first significant development in the promised reckoning with the Orban system. Two prominent lawmakers and former ministers were arrested over corruption allegations.

On Monday, Magyar's Tisza Party parliamentary faction used its two-thirds majority to lift the immunity of two lawmakers from the opposition Orban camp: Balazs Hanko, formerly minister for culture and innovation and a lawmaker from Orban's Fidesz party, and Miklos Sesztak, a former development minister who is now a lawmaker for the small Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP), which has been a Fidesz affiliate since 2010. Both are the subject of corruption investigations.

blocks.caption: Former Minister Miklos Sesztak in 2017Image: Robert Szaniszlo/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Illegal party financing, bribery

Balazs Hanko was not among those in Orban's system who enriched themselves on a large scale. But he is seen as a symbol of the common practice under Orban of systematically using public money to fund the ruling party, Orban's network of allies, election campaigns, and propaganda efforts. Specifically, as minister, Hanko allegedly unlawfully allocated around 50 million euros from the National Cultural Fund (NKA), which he oversaw, in 2025 and 2026, including funds intended for election campaign purposes.

The case of Miklos Sesztak is different. He is one of the wealthiest lawmakers in Hungary and has made headlines for more than a decade with his personal corruption scandals — another typical trait of the Orban system. As minister, Sesztak allegedly accepted around €30 million ($34 million) in bribes with an accomplice between 2015 and 2018. The alleged payments involved contracts related to the state-owned Hungarian bus company Volanbusz and the construction sector.
Barricaded in parliament with his family

Sesztak went straight to the prosecutor's office on Monday after his immunity was lifted, where he was taken into pretrial detention. Balazs Hanko took a different route. He arrived at Parliament on Monday morning with his wife and four teenage children and, after his immunity was lifted, said he was waiting for the authorities to make a decision. In practice, it appeared that he was barricading himself inside. Only after Parliament Speaker Agnes Forsthoffer formally ordered Hanko in writing that evening to leave the building, and he received a summons from the prosecutor's office, did he finally head for the exit, accompanied by his family and Fidesz lawmakers protesting what they called Magyar's "arbitrary rule."

The entire episode was livestreamed on Viktor Orban's Facebook page. After Hanko said goodbye to his family outside, a misunderstanding occurred. His SUV driver, apparently believing Hanko was already inside the vehicle, drove off without him. Hanko ran after the SUV, and the livestream on Orban's Facebook page then cut out. Later that evening, Hungarian media reported that Hanko had also been placed in pretrial detention.

blocks.caption: Balazs Hanko talks to press after walking out of the National AssemblyImage: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prime Minister Magyar's immunity lifted

Earlier that afternoon, Prime Minister Peter Magyar delivered a sharp speech in Parliament on the two cases. His own immunity had also been lifted beforehand — over a case that is classified in the records as theft.

In June 2024, Magyar took a phone from a man who had been filming him without permission at a nightclub and threw it into the Danube, where it was later found. Magyar had explicitly asked for his immunity to be lifted in the case. It is a calculated PR move intended to show that the same standards apply to everyone. But it is also a risky maneuver — if convicted, Magyar could lose his seat in Parliament.

In his parliamentary speech, he offered Fidesz and KDNP lawmakers a stark comparison: "How many hundreds of thousands of phones would you have to throw into the Danube to come close to the trillions allegedly stolen by the Fidesz-KDNP mafia?"
Dispute over Prosecutor General

Magyar has also spoken forcefully about Hungary's justice system. He has praised rank-and-file judicial employees while criticizing the leadership of the prosecutor's office, accusing them of repeatedly covering up corruption cases as "collaborators of the Orban system." At the center of the dispute is a fight over the appointment of a new prosecutor general.

The Tisza faction rejected Zoltan Szathmary, the candidate proposed by President Andras Baka, because his brother works for the Office for Constitutional Protection and, in that role, is a suspect in an ongoing politically sensitive case known as the "Gold Convoy" affair. In March 2026, Viktor Orban ordered the detention of a legal Ukrainian money shipment. The escorts were arrested in dramatic fashion, and cash and gold bars were seized. Orban and other Fidesz politicians indirectly accused Magyar's Tisza Party of receiving funding from Ukraine. Several people involved in the operation are now under investigation for abuse of office. Orban himself is not currently part of the proceedings, but could be in the future.
How much Orban influence remains in Hungary's politics?
Hungarians seek a swift reckoning

Although Magyar has formally emphasized the independence of the judiciary, his comments in the current debates have given the impression that he is getting ahead of judicial decisions or becoming too deeply involved. At the same time, expectations among many Hungarians for a swift reckoning are high — and public debate's often return to the topic of how people want to "hear the handcuffs click." A recent poll found that a large majority of Hungarians consider the former Orban order "systemically corrupt" and a "mafia state."

Overall, Magyar and his government face the challenge of balancing the rule of law with public expectations. Many former critics of Orban are also calling for the reckoning with the Orban system to be handled properly. Prominent attorney Gyorgy Magyar, for example, who represented people in numerous human rights and rule-of-law cases under Orban, called for "prudence, patience, calm, discipline, and professionalism" in an interview with the news outlet Hirklikk.
Questions remain about whether "Operation Purgatory" will be merely spectacle, or whether the justice system will investigate corruption cases independently and in keeping with the rule of law.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: North Korea denies South's claim, calls DMZ blast a 'farce'
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong has accused Seoul of conspiracy after it blamed Pyongyang for the blast in the DMZ.

image.caption: The DMZ is a fortified buffer zone between the two countries that has been in place since 1953Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea on Wednesday denied a South Korean claim that blamed Pyongyang for a mine blast in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that left three South Korean soldiers injured.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un, accused Seoul of coming up with false evidence after blaming Pyongyang for last week's explosion.
"It is ​too low and dirty as befitting the tribes of South Korea," Kim said in a statement carried by state media KCNA.
"Such a farce is by no means ​new."
What did South Korea say?
After the incident occured, South Korean authorities launched an investigation.
Cranes in the Demilitarized Zone

South Korea's Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said on Tuesday that North Korean mines caused the blast and that it would take "corresponding" action. He ​also ‌said North Korea likely planted mines to fortify the border.
He said the South Korean military "has a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages."
The South Korean military has also demanded an apology from North Korea for the explosion.

"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, .... and we strongly urge an apology and responsible measures," an official from Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff told reporters.
Violation of the Korean War armistice, says UN Command
The South Korean joint chiefs said South Korean and UN investigators found another North Korean mine Tuesday during a follow-up inspection.
Two Koreas mark 70 years since suspension of war
The UN Command said the investigation has "identified an active Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea's) anti-personnel mine on the ROK side of the Military Demarcation Line."
The UNC concluded thatNorth Korea violated the armistice agreement that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War.
The UNC is a US-led multinational military force that oversees the Korean armistice agreement and administers the southern side of the DMZ.

articles.title: Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
articles.summary: The owner said he chose the name because he wanted to run the "best Chinese restaurant" in South Korea.

blocks.text: A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say.
Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer.
The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent".
The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported.

The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said.
"People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent."

In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues.
The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; £8,400).
Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery.
Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province.

Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition.

Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars.

articles.title: AFP: BRP Sierra Madre troops have sufficient supplies despite China's interference
articles.summary: Troops aboard the BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal still have sufficient supplies despite the rescheduling of a rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission following interference from Chinese vessels, the…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 12:17pm

Troops aboard the BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal still have sufficient supplies despite the rescheduling of a rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission following interference from Chinese vessels, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said Wednesday.
In a virtual interview, AFP spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said the troops' morale also remains high despite the rescheduling.

“Ang kasundaluhan naman sa BRP Sierra Madre have sufficient supplies. At yung moral naman nila, mataas naman kahit hindi pa sila, sanay naman sila na kapag hindi kaagad makauwi, sanay sila doon,” he said.
(The soldiers in the BRP Sierra Madre have sufficient supplies. And their morale is high. They are used to not being able to go home right away.)
Chinese vessels interfered with the Philippine RoRe mission to Ayungin Shoal on September 24.

According to Trinidad, Philippine vessels had previously been able to approach BRP Sierra Madre within about 15 nautical miles before encountering China Coast Guard (CCG) and People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) vessels.
During the latest mission, however, Trinidad said Chinese vessels were detected when the Philippine ships were about 16 nautical miles.
The Chinese vessels also closed in less than one nautical mile from the Philippine vessel, while sending threatening messages.

“There were reports of the engine of the [BRP Lapu-Lapu] not performing well. Hindi naman siya bumigay. Maalon, madikit yung mga barko ng PLA at ng China Coast Guard. It was a judgment call of the commander of Western Command to reschedule the RoRe,” Trinidad said.

(There were reports of the engine of the BRP Lapu-Lapu not performing well. It did not break down. The PLA and China Coast Guard ships were close, so it was a judgment call of the commander of Western Command to reschedule the RoRe.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: AFP says China possibly behind fake Teodoro letter
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Wednesday said China could be behind a fake letter allegedly signed by Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. that recently circulated online.

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 12:16pm

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said Wednesday that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) could be behind the circulation of a fake letter allegedly signed by Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., possibly with the involvement of some Filipinos.
The fake letter was dated July 31 and contained claims about alleged maritime law enforcement in the West Philippine Sea, as well as issues concerning Philippine politics.

“Sa military, we look at indicators, and indicators will point na ito ay galaw ng Chinese Communist Party or yung kanilang mga galamay na minsan may kasamang Pilipino doon,” AFP spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said in a virtual interview.
(In the military, we look at indicators, and the indicators point to this being a move by the Chinese Communist Party or its tentacles, which sometimes include Filipinos.)
According to Trinidad, the fabricated document could be intended to discredit government officials and weaken the Philippines' alliance with the United States.

“We don't have to look far. Sino ba ang may makinabang kapag lumabas ito at nag-away-away ang Pilipino at nasira ang reputasyon ng ating SND at na-discredit ang alliance with the US? Kaninong interest ang ma-advance nito? Yung interest ng Chinese Communist Party,” he said.

(We don't have to look far. Who will benefit if this comes out, Filipinos fight among themselves, the reputation of our SND [Secretary of National Defense] is damaged, and the alliance with the US is discredited? Whose interests will this advance? The interests of the Chinese Communist Party.)
GMA News Online has sought comment from the Chinese Embassy in Manila, but the office had yet to provide a statement as of posting time.
On Tuesday, the Department of National Defense (DND) warned the public against a fabricated letter supposedly signed by Teodoro and addressed to a person identified as Peter Enzminger.

“The Department unequivocally states that the document and its content are obviously and absolutely false and fake. The matter has been referred to the National Bureau of Investigation for proper investigation,” Teodoro said.

“This is yet another episode of foreign interference and malign influence that is intended to discredit the legitimate and lawful efforts of the Philippine government to assert its national sovereignty and territorial integrity,” he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Dizon denies cover-up in Taguig flood control probe: 'We'll go where evidence leads us'
articles.summary: Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon has vowed "no cover-up" in his department's probe into Taguig’s flood control works, an attempt to clear the air after his answer at a Senate hearing was…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:04pm
Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon on October 20, 2025.
STAR / Jesse Bustos

MANILA, Philippines — Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon has vowed "no cover-up" in his department's probe into Taguig’s flood control works, an attempt to clear the air after his answer at a Senate hearing was construed as a clearance for the Cayetano stronghold.

Dizon's recent categorical denial of "ghost projects" in Taguig has landed him in the thick of the feud between Sen. Ping Lacson and Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano after it drew a sharp warning from Lacson against covering up anomalies.
Lacson on Monday revealed that an apologetic Dizon called him over the weekend and shared he felt "set up" into a flat denial of ghost projects in Cayetano's bailiwick.

The senator in a radio interview said he warned Dizon: "Vince, mag-ingat kayo, kasi pag nagco-cover up kayo, magiging criminally liable kayo (Vince, be careful, because if you cover this up, you'll be criminally liable)."
On Wednesday, Dizon told reporters Lacson was "correct" in saying that an attempt to cover up anomalous projects would make one criminally liable.
"But we would never do that. I won't allow it. No way that we would cover up. Where the evidence leads us, that's where we'll go. It's as simple as that," he said in mixed English and Filipino.
Dizon said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had set an example with having his own cousin, former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, arrested and detained for flood control charges.
"We need to follow the leader. Whether it's a relative or a friend, it doesn't matter," Dizon said.
"But there is a process. I've repeatedly said, the process is ongoing now with the Ombudsman," the DPWH chief said.
Conclusive answer
Dizon on Monday clarified his remarks in an interview with reporters and said his answer at the Senate hearing was a narrow and limited response to a specific question.

The DPWH chief explained that he was asked about how many projects have been found to be "conclusively" a ghost project in the whole country, and if any have been identified in Taguig. "My answer was 'none.' That's the full context," Dizon said.

Lacson has cited the DPWH's own inspection reports in alleging anomalies in Taguig's flood control works. He said the DPWH's audit has pointed to geotagged billing photos for Taguig works that were located 600 kilometers away in Leyte.
Cayetano has denied any involvement in alleged ghost projects in Taguig and has accused Lacson of raising accusations that are politically motivated.

articles.title: Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45m for every hour they halt businesses
articles.summary:
Figure cited by minister highlights trade-offs Kyiv faces as it tries to keep normal life moving amid Russian strikes

Missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every…

blocks.text: Missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every hour they bring business to a halt, according to the country’s economy minister, as Kyiv searches for ways to keep the economy running under an intensifying Russian bombardment.

Russia has increasingly targeted the infrastructure underpinning Ukraine’s economy, striking industrial sites, warehouses, logistics hubs and datacentres in what Oleksandr Kravchenko, the minister for economy and the environment, described as an effort to “destroy pretty much the entire economy”.

“What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,” he said, referring to Russia’s use of the new weapons that have pounded Kyiv in recent weeks.

Speaking from the heavily protected government building in Kyiv, Kravchenko, a former McKinsey executive who joined the government in the summer, said the attacks were forcing large parts of the economy into repeated standstills as workers were sent to shelters, with sirens lasting up to 10 hours a day.
“If people are in a bunker, business stops,” he said.
To ease the economic costs, the government recently introduced a new two-tier warning system designed to keep businesses operating during prolonged air raid alerts.
A “red” alert warns of a missile threat and requires people to seek shelter, while a “yellow” warning is used for drone threats, allowing many businesses to remain open.
More than half of businesses were continuing to operate during yellow alerts, Kravchenko said.

But a yellow alert is no guarantee of safety. That danger was made clear on Monday, when a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv during a yellow alert, killing two people while staff were still inside working.
It is one of the difficult trade-offs Ukraine faces as it tries to keep normal life moving while protecting people from an escalating campaign of Russian strikes.

Kravchenko said Russian attacks this year alone had caused an estimated $10bn in damage to fixed assets, with steel plants, warehouses, logistics infrastructure and, most recently datacentres, among the targets. Russia has also effectively blockaded Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, which before the blockade carried the bulk of the country’s exports.

The minister believed the government was better prepared this year for what could be the “hardest, the harshest winter” of the war, with further pressure expected on energy supplies, infrastructure and businesses already weakened by months of strikes.

To protect against future strikes, the government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukraine’s air-defence system, the minister said, although he cautioned that businesses could never fully protect themselves from Russian missiles and drones.
The ongoing damage from strikes has added to an already severe strain on the state’s finances.

The president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has recently put Ukraine’s remaining budget shortfall this year at about $27bn, a figure that has prompted questions among some European governments over how the gap emerged, despite the EU having already agreed a €90bn loan package for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027.
Kravchenko said the government had since narrowed the shortfall to $20bn through spending cuts and by identifying additional domestic reserves.
Kyiv was now seeking further support from the EU, Japan, Canada and the UK, including potentially bringing forward loans that had been earmarked for next year, Kravchenko said.
“There is very active work with all our international partners to get additional sources of funding,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

Kravchenko dismissed suggestions that the shortfall was the result of mismanagement or corruption. He also said it was not due to excessive spending under former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, whose drive to overhaul military procurement and rapidly expand Ukraine’s drone programme had made him one of the government’s most prominent reformers before his dismissal in July, a move that triggered street protests.
Instead, he said the gap reflected both weaker-than-expected state revenues and the rising cost of waging the war.

“The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said, pointing to the need for more air-defence systems and for Ukraine to accelerate development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered weapons.
But high-profile corruption scandals have also reached Zelenskyy’s inner circle, straining trust in the government both at home and among western donors.

A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that corruption in government was the most cited concern among Ukrainians, named by 50% of respondents, ahead of mass missile and drone strikes at 40%. The same survey found that 72% believed Zelenskyy bore personal responsibility for corrupt actions by people around him.
Kravchenko said progress had been made to tackle the issue but admitted that Ukraine faced both corruption itself and a persistent perception problem both inside Ukraine and abroad.
“I very much appreciate the pressure of European partners on reforms,” he said, adding that Ukraine also needed to tackle perceptions of corruption at home and abroad.

Ukraine’s external financing needs for 2027 are estimated at $52.6bn, but only about $20bn has so far been secured, according to the minister, with further tax rises and spending cuts under discussion.
Asked whether the rise of parties sceptical of support for Ukraine in France and Germany could weaken western commitment to Kyiv, he said: “Am I worried? I think I should be, probably.”
“The overall fatigue is increasing in Europe,” he added.

articles.title: South Korea demands apology from Pyongyang for landmine blasts that injured three
articles.summary: Blasts in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) injured three South Korean personnel earlier this month.

blocks.text: South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month.
Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September.

South Korea said on Tuesday that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, were "highly likely" from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what it said was a violation of a decades-old armistice.
North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation".

Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea.
Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making."

South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border.
South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War.
That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5mi) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas.
In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ.

In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied.
Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now.

The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms".
"UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said.

MANILA, Philippines — The transport strike by Pinagkaisang Samahan ng mga Tsuper at Operator Nationwide (PISTON) has proceeded for a second day on Wednesday, September 30, in protest against rising oil prices.

According to the transport group’s national president, former senatorial candidate Mody Floranda, the two-day transport strike was launched in protest against the continued implementation of the Oil Deregulation Law, which he said burdens jeepney drivers and the general public by allowing oil companies to dictate fuel prices unilaterally.
“Nawawala naman yung maliit na kita ng ating mga driver at mga operator dahil nga sa mataas na presyo ng petrolyo,” Floranda said.

PISTON, which started the transport strike on September 29, is also urging the government to reevaluate existing policies and laws, specifically targeting the excise tax on fuel and the Oil Deregulation Law.
The group anticipates that drivers and operators across different regions will participate in the strike, potentially disrupting public transit in several areas.
In Metro Manila, PISTON said that they will march from Welcome Rotonda to Mendiola Peace Arch in Manila on Wednesday afternoon.

articles.title: Marcos institutionalizes gov't spending tracking platform 'COMPASS'
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has institutionalized a centralized platform that will allow the public to track government budget, spending, and the implementation of projects.

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 10:50am
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has institutionalized a centralized platform that will allow the public to track government budget, spending, and the implementation of projects.
Marcos signed Executive Order No. 126 on September 28, institutionalizing the Centralized Open Monitoring Platform for Appropriations and Spending Statistics (COMPASS).

“Kapag pera ng bayan ang pinag-uusapan, dapat malinaw kung saan ito napupunta. Hindi dapat mahirap alamin kung magkano ang inilaan, saan ginastos, at ano ang naging resulta. COMPASS lets the public follow every peso,” Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said in a statement.

(When public funds are involved, it should be clear where they go. It should not be difficult to find out how much was allocated, where it was spent, and what the result was. COMPASS lets the public follow every peso.)

From tracking budgets, Malacañang said COMPASS will now provide information on the actual implementation of projects, including their financial performance, implementation and completion status, procurement information, and other transparency-related data generated throughout the national budget cycle.
Further, the order directs government agencies to submit and update relevant information through COMPASS while local government units are encouraged to use the platform.

COMPASS will also be linked to existing digital systems, including the integrated Financial Management Information System, Budget and Treasury Management System, Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System, Digital Information for Monitoring and Evaluation, and the E-Gov PH App.
Meanwhile, the COMPASS Council will oversee the platform.

Malacañang said the council will be chaired by the DBM and co-chaired by the Department of Information and Communications Technology. The Department of Finance and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) will serve as members. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
articles.summary: The president also signed an executive order requiring his government to refer to AI as Super Intelligence.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Trump met with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AI
US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".
The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.

The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI and a slowdown in developing the technology, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.
Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.
1. AI 'self-regulation' pact
Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson and top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.
The president told reporters that the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.
Under the agreement, which Trump posted on social media, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.
The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues, the document said.
They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."

The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday

blocks.text: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images
Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday
Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.
The president has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks, dismissing them as a "hoax".
He has said the only "guardrails" the industry needs is a "smart" president.
OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent weeks called for tighter oversight of the industry and foe a slowdown of development of the technology.
On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.

The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.
2. Doubling down on data centres
Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI.
The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the country over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on from communities.
Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas.
Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres.
"These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters.
Trump previously said on social media that the only reason communities in the US should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".
"The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame," he said.
Huang from Nvidia, which produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories".
These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added.
3. It's now 'Super Intelligence'

Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch," the order said.
"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.
During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".
Some tech leaders and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.
Zuckerberg said on social media on Monday: "We believe superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for all people and businesses."
On Wednesday, Musk reposted a clip of tech executives gathered around Trump at the White House, with the words: "Super Intelligence."
But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction in the industry because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

articles.title: Judge ends federal oversight of Oakland police department after 23 years
articles.summary:
Group of officers known as ‘riders’ in 2000s prompted longest arrangement of its kind in US history

After 23 years, a district judge has released the Oakland police department (OPD) from…

blocks.text: After 23 years, a district judge has released the Oakland police department (OPD) from federal oversight, marking the end of the longest arrangement of this kind in US history.

In the early 2000s, a group of police officers known as the “riders” were exposed for offenses like planting evidence, falsifying reports and using excessive force against primarily young Black men. These actions led victims to file more than 100 civil lawsuits against the department. In 2003, as a part of the settlement of these cases, OPD was put on a federal court-ordered reform program.

OPD was given more than 50 tasks to complete including collecting and analyzing data on racial profiling, dealing with complaints against officers more quickly and updating their community policing practices. Despite this, issues remained and the department’s reforms were put under the direct control of a federal judge in 2012.

Since then, the department has still had its share of scandals including allegations that several OPD officers sex-trafficked a teenage girl; nearly a dozen officers were either fired or suspended. The investigation into the trafficking of the teenager began in 2015 and OPD issued her a nearly $1m settlement in 2017.
For organizers against police misconduct and brutality, the decision to end the federal oversight scheme does not mean that the department should be free of scrutiny.

“Police cannot police themselves. Oakland’s history has already taught us that lesson,” the Anti Police-Terror Project (APTP) said in a statement following the judge’s decision. “The end of federal oversight does not mean the end of police misconduct. It does not erase the history that brought OPD under federal supervision. And it certainly does not mean Oakland should simply trust OPD to hold itself accountable.”

articles.title: Prosecution legal spox Tolosa receives impeachment court warning over comments
articles.summary: House prosecution legal spokesperson Benjamin Tolosa said that he also received a warning from the Senate impeachment court over comments on the case’s merits.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 9:32am
Atty. Benjamin Tolosa Jr.
House of Representatives
MANILA, Philippines — House prosecution legal spokesperson Benjamin Tolosa said that he also received a warning from the Senate impeachment court over comments on the case’s merits.
In a press conference on Tuesday, September 29, Tolosa said that there is "no express finding" that he violated the court's sub judice rule.
"Based on my reading, there's no express finding there that I violated Rule 18," Tolosa said.
“I would assume that the reason for this is that the court listened and considered the explanation that we gave in our answer,” he added.
According to Tolosa, the Senate's order did not contain any discussion disputing his defense that his public remarks fell under the "fair, true, and accurate reporting doctrine.”
Furthermore, he noted that the court did not contradict his assertion that the matters he had publicly discussed were merely procedural and therefore fell outside the restrictive scope of Rule 18.
Rule 18 of the impeachment rules prohibits parties from commenting on the merits of the case.

Despite the absence of an explicit finding of a violation, Tolosa said that the Senate impeachment court concluded its order with an admonition, directing the prosecution to exercise greater restraint when making public statements that could affect the merits of the case.
However, Tolosa disagreed with the warning, as there was no express mention that he violated a rule.
“Nonetheless, while I respectfully disagree, of course, I respect the authority of the impeachment court as an institution,” Tolosa said.
House Prosecutor Rep. Terry Ridon (Bicol-SARO) was also issued a stern warning by the Senate impeachment court over his comments.

The impeachment court also cautioned Ridon to observe the difference between merely informing the public about what occurred in the trial and “telling the public what the evidence proves or why it supports a party’s position.”

“This is to ensure that any decision made by senator-judges is based not on statements publicized outside the court but upon evidence and arguments presented and tested within its established parameters,” the order read.
In an interview with reporters, Ridon said that he accepted the warning from the impeachment court.
“Tinatanggap po natin ang warning na ito, at nagpapasalamat tayo sa Senate impeachment court sa kanilang graciousness sa bagay na ito,” Ridon said.
“We are committed to exercise greater restraint on particular details on the impeachment proceedings moving forward,” he added.

The National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) is investigating the alleged involvement of an off-duty police officer in a brawl during a basketball game in Tondo, Manila last September 27.
A young player was reportedly placed in a headlock during the altercation, according to a report on GMA News’ Unang Balita on Wednesday.
The mother of another minor who was involved in the incident alleged that the police officer punched and choked her son.

Calinisan said the commission will establish the facts and ensure that anyone found to have violated the law or police standards is held accountable, in accordance with due process.
“Hindi dahilan ang pagiging off-duty para makaiwas sa pananagutan. Ang bawat pulis ay inaasahang maging tagapagtanggol ng mamamayan, hindi dahilan ng kanilang takot,” he said.

articles.title: ICC rejects Duterte bid for expert verification of evidence
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court has rejected former President Rodrigo Duterte’s request to require expert verification of open-source and user-generated evidence in his crimes against humanity…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 8:39am

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on September 16, 2026, during a preparatory session as he faces charges over his “war on drugs,” which killed thousands.
AFP / Pool / Piroschka Van De Wouw

MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) has rejected former President Rodrigo Duterte’s request to require expert verification of open-source and user-generated evidence in his crimes against humanity case, saying the additional requirement could unnecessarily delay the start of his trial.
ICC Trial Chamber III, in a seven-page decision dated September 28, denied the defense’s request to amend the court’s E-Court Protocol to include an “expert verification field” for evidence listings.
The request was filed last month by Duterte’s defense team, led by British lawyer Peter Haynes, amid concerns over the volume and quality of evidence disclosed by the prosecution.
The proposed amendment would have required another layer of authentication for evidence obtained from open sources or generated by users.

“Given the large volume of evidence that has been made available by the Prosecution in the present case, as well as the breadth of open-source and user-generated evidence, such obligation, if implemented, may in the event be unnecessary and could well have the effect of causing a needless delay to the start of the trial,” the chamber said.
The chamber noted that it had already issued multiple orders during the third status conference to address concerns over the volume of evidence.
Instead, the ICC granted the prosecution’s request to amend the E-Court Protocol by adding a URL metadata field for open-source evidence.
The field will allow the parties to identify the URL associated with the evidence at the time it was captured.
The proposal was agreed upon by the prosecution, defense and common legal representatives of the victims.
“Under these circumstances, the chamber is satisfied that it is appropriate to grant the request and decides to amend the E-Court Protocol as requested,” the chamber said.
The ICC Registry, the court’s administrative arm, was ordered to implement the changes by October 2, less than two months before Duterte’s trial is scheduled to begin.
Defense flags volume of evidence

Duterte’s defense team has separately asked the ICC to cap the prosecution’s evidence at 10,000 items, saying the case record has grown to 62,130 from an initial 5,275. The defense said the disclosure includes more than 320,000 pages of documents and over 1,000 audio-visual materials.
Duterte’s lawyers have described the prosecution’s evidence disclosure as being in a “terrible mess.”
The prosecution has disputed the characterization, saying the defense’s claims were not entirely accurate and were “really exaggerated, in [his] view.”
Duterte faces crimes against humanity charges over alleged killings during his time as Davao City mayor and president of the Philippines.

The 81-year-old former president appeared before the ICC in person for the first time on September 16 during the third status conference, when the chamber also heard arguments concerning his health and ability to stand trial.
Philippine authorities arrested Duterte in Pasay City on March 11, 2025, before turning him over to the ICC. He was flown to The Hague, Netherlands, where he remains in ICC custody.
Trial Chamber III later ruled that Duterte should remain detained, citing the likelihood that he could abscond or obstruct or endanger the investigation or court proceedings.
His trial is scheduled to begin on Nov. 30, 2026.

articles.title: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.summary:
Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022

The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a…

blocks.text: The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.

The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children.

The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor.

Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee.

“While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”

Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022, and the senators say none of the cases has resulted in accountability. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad.

Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen.
The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him.
Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it.

“If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.”
In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank.

The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025.

A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes.
Many of the Democrats, who have historically been lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years.

When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000-pound bombs.
The measures failed because every Republican voted against it.

articles.title: ‘He’s unbearable’: bear that went viral for living under LA home is back
articles.summary:
‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces, but he just keeps coming back

He’s back: the 550lb bear made famous after he took up residence under an Altadena…

blocks.text: He’s back: the 550lb bear made famous after he took up residence under an Altadena home in November 2025 is wandering the Los Angeles neighborhood again after he moved in and out of the crawlspace of another home.
“Yellow 2120”, as the black bear has been tagged, was spotted in the crawlspace of a home on Minoru Drive on Monday.

Steve Clark, whose in-laws live in the house, told NBC LA that they monitored their new neighbor through security cameras, and tried to scare him away by playing loud music and turning on a leaf blower.
“I didn’t even realize that the bear could get all the way back to that access point. He has to rip out ductwork and do a bunch of damage to get there,” Clark said.

Although those attempts to oust “Yellow 2120” from his adopted den failed, the bear later left on his own. While the homeowners have sealed up their crawlspace, their neighbors are on alert in case the bear decides to move in with them next.
“Yellow 2120” made headlines last year when he took up residence under another Altadena home for two months.

In November 2025, homeowner Ken Johnson noticed the bear leaving the crawlspace and later contacted California’s department of fish and wildlife for assistance removing it from under his home. Despite sweet-scented lures and ammonia-doused towels, “Yellow 2120” remained in place until January – when Johnson sought assistance from members of the Bear League, a volunteer organization that aims to help humans live in “harmony” with the animals, that was able to force the bear out with paintball guns.

“He’s a nuisance and he’s living under my house rent-free,” Johnson told the Orange County Register at the time. “We call him … unbearable, but he’s so cute. Once he gets out, we’ll call him bearable, but for now it’s unbearable.”

After the Eaton wildfire tore through the Angeles national forest and scorched parts of Altadena in January 2025, wildlife – including several bears – sought shelter in the community. In the weeks following the fire, at least two 500-plus-pound black bears sought refuge in homes evacuated during the wildfire. Although it’s unclear whether “Yellow 2120” was one of them, he had previously taken up residence under another Altadena home, said Cort Klopping, a fish and wildlife spokesperson.
after newsletter promotion
As cities encroach closer on bear habitats, bear sightings are growing more common. In 2017, California registered 28 bear sightings in Los Angeles county. In 2023, that number rose to 455.

This month Alex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters, told the Guardian that human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation feeding period. This year is on track to be record setting when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said.

Black bears – the only species of bear living in California – are largely non-confrontational, having killed only one person in the state in recorded history. The population is estimated to be between 49,000 and 71,000, with 50% living in the north coast and Cascade regions, and 40% in the Sierra Nevada.

articles.title: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
articles.summary: Ukraine's remaining steelworks, a vital part of its economy, have all but ground to a halt because of relentless attacks.

blocks.text: Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city.
"Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says.

Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September.
"All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains.
Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded.
"We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC.
At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again.
Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times.
This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia.

Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another.
Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko.
Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action.

"Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far."
Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs.
The situation, he admitted, was very difficult.

"It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things."
Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center.
"In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC.

"This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (£1.5bn-£2.3bn) a year on average."

If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming."
The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction.
Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia.
Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware.
"We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv.
There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added.
Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon.
Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery.
"Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't."
EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine.
But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat.
His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed.
"This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

articles.title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
articles.summary: Mindgard said it discovered in July that Kimi models K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade developer's safety limits.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByChris Vallance
Senior technology reporter

Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.
Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.

It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.
Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".
The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.
Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning.
"Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.
Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.
These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.
While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.
Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.
Cyber-attack launchpad
Mindgard has not proven whether the answers supplied by Kimi on concerning topics would work.
But it argued guardrails should have prevented the models in question from entering into discussion with users on such subjects.
The firm said it was also confident a jailbroken Kimi 2.6 could allow hackers to run code on its computing resources and connect to the internet - making it a potential launchpad for cyber-attacks.

Garraghan defended Mindgard's decision to publicly discuss its jailbreak of Moonshot's systems, saying it had informed the developer and was not revealing key details about how it got the firm's models to ignore guardrails.
Mindgard alerted Moonshot to the jailbreak in an email on 27 July, following up about a week later.
It then published a blog about the issue on 12 September.
But the company said Moonshot only made contact recently, after it was approached by the BBC for comment.

In part of an email to Mindgard asking for more details, shared with the BBC by Moonshot, it said its model had generally shown "a high refusal rate for these types of requests" in internal evaluations.
Preventing jailbreaks

The findings come as the AI industry continues to be split on whether closed, proprietary models - like those powering ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude systems - or open-source tools are the best or safest way forward.
Kimi is an open-weight model, meaning someone could in theory take the model and run it themselves on their own computing infrastructure.
Prof Alan Woodward, of the University of Surrey, told the BBC there was a risk open-source models might end up in the wrong hands, but they could also be harnessed for cyber-defence.
He noted that AI firm Hugging Face used a Chinese open-source model to understand a hack later revealed to have been carried out by OpenAI agents.
Prof Woodward said international regulation was unlikely to match the pace of AI development, saying: "It's taken us decades to agree on the format of telephone numbers."
Like Mindgard founder Garraghan, Prof Woodward believes there should be a greater focus on identifying and prosecuting humans who misuse AI.

articles.title: Trump says AI companies agree to 'self-police'
articles.summary: Donald Trump said the US won't "stifle" the development of AI, which he sees as "bigger than the Industrial Revolution." The agreement comes amid mounting concerns over AI safety after recent hacking…

image.caption: Trump has dismissed AI safety concerns as a 'hoax'Image: Tierney L. Cross/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said a group of CEOs of Artificial Intelligence (AI) companies had signed an accord to "self-police" the technology's development.
Trump met with AI leaders at the White House, where he doubled down on his support for the technology.

The agreement comes as public scrutiny has grown over the risks posed by the emerging technology, following reports that OpenAI and Anthropic's AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies' systems.
Concerns are also mounting over the industry's growing footprint in communities, particularly with the growth of data centers.
Prior to the meeting, Trump reiterated that the US government would not limit the development of AI or support calls for "guardrails" or other restrictions on the sector.
"I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said. "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot."
Trump also announced that he would officially rename the technology "super intelligence" because "it's not artificial."
Which AI leaders were at the White House meeting?

House Speaker Mike Johnson joined the meeting, which included top AI executives like Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Elon Musk, whose X social media platform includes its own AI model, Grok.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also attended.
Data centers face backlash from US communities
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.
Later, the US president posted a copy of the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" on his Truth Social platform.
What does the AI accord say?
"Every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the accord begins.

The document affirms that tech companies will implement "robust internal controls to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated."
They are to "empower an internal team" to ensure "control, monitoring, and detection" are working as intended.

AI companies are also expected to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments," as well as "designate an independent committee of the board of directors" to oversee and receive reports.
Trump said the agreement is "morally binding" but not legally enforceable.
The accord does, however, leave the door open "to codify these steps into laws or regulations."
