articles.title: 77-year-old man put to death in Florida, 16th person to be executed in the state this year
articles.summary:
Curtis Wilkie Beasley was executed for the 1995 killing of Carolyn Monfort, after supreme court declined to intervene

A 77-year-old

blocks.text: A 77-year-old Florida man was put to death on Tuesday for his conviction in a deadly hammer attack on a woman decades ago, becoming the 16th person executed to date this year in the nation’s busiest death chamber.

Curtis Wilkie Beasley was pronounced dead at 6.12pm following a lethal injection at the Florida state prison near Starke, authorities said. He was convicted of first-degree murder, robbery and grand theft auto in the 1995 hammer attack on Carolyn Monfort at her home south of Orlando.

The Florida supreme court recently rejected arguments that executing a man Beasley’s age who is suffering from cognitive decline would amount to cruel and unusual punishment, and the US supreme court declined to intervene on Tuesday. Beasley is Florida’s seventh prisoner over 70 to be executed this year.

Beasley also was the 29th person, all men, who have been executed around the US this year. On Wednesday, Tennessee plans to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years by giving a lethal injection to Christa Pike, 50, for killing a classmate in a jealous rage when both were teens.

Court records show that Beasley had been staying at Monfort’s home in Dundee in August 1995 while he was pressure-washing and painting nearby apartments owned by her son-in-law. Monfort’s daughter went to her home after being unable to reach her for two days and found her body in a blood-splattered laundry room.
Monfort had suffered multiple blunt-force trauma injuries to the head, and a bloody hammer head was found wrapped in a towel nearby, according to investigators.

Authorities began searching for Beasley after a witness reported seeing him driving what turned out to be Monfort’s car. Investigators determined Beasley had traveled to Miami and later relocated to Alabama, where he was arrested while working under a false name for an electrical company, officials said. He was convicted and sentenced to death in 1998.

The state is getting closer to last year’s total of 19 executions, which was a record in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.
Two more executions are scheduled for this year, but the Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has temporarily paused the next one.

William Lee Thompson, 74, is scheduled to be executed 13 October for raping and fatally beating a woman at a Florida motel in 1976. After a doctor this month determined Thompson might be suffering from dementia, DeSantis ordered a panel of three psychiatrists to examine him to determine if he is competent to be executed.
DeSantis issued similar stays in 2023 and 2025 but both executions proceeded after evaluations.
William Reaves, 77, has a 20 October execution date. He was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy outside a convenience store in 1986.
All Florida executions are carried out via injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the state’s department of corrections.

articles.title: UN Security Council extends mandate of anti-gang force in Haiti into 2027
articles.summary: The United Nations Security Council on Tuesday extended by six months the mandate of an international security force in Haiti intended to fight powerful armed groups that have taken control of much…

image.caption: An armoured police vehicle that is part of the Gang Suppression Force is seen on patrol in the Haitian capital of Port-au-Prince on Tuesday. (Odelyn Joseph/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The United Nations Security Council on Tuesday extended by six months the mandate of an international security force in Haiti intended to fight powerful armed groups that have taken control of much of the country.
Gang Suppression Force staffing stands at just 30 per cent of what was intended

Twelve nations voted ​to renew the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) ​and none voted against. Three nations, however, abstained: China, Russia and Pakistan, whose representatives cited concerns over insufficient funds, personnel and efficacy.

The extension is intended to ​provide security ahead of Haiti's first election in a decade in December. Armed ⁠groups continue to control ⁠large parts of the Caribbean nation despite successive ‌international deployments, and the force has struggled to deploy enough troops to carry out its mandate.
Haiti, whose leaders first called for international security support in 2022, had urged nations to renew the mandate for the force, which is currently at less ⁠than 30 per cent of its intended size.

U.S. ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, representing one of the countries that proposed the motion, said that around 1,500 GSF troops are now deployed in Haiti. ‌Waltz said the remaining 4,000 are expected to arrive in the coming months.
"Seven missions have been dedicated to Haiti over the previous decades and obviously to limited success," Waltz said.
"We're trying to do something genuinely different."
11 dead in most recent violence

The vote came hours after ​gang members in Haiti's breadbasket region burned homes and killed at least 11 people in what a local mayor said was ⁠retaliation after a GSF unit killed three gang members in a push against illegal toll ⁠booths.
A month ago, another massacre in the hillside town of Kenscoff near the capital left ⁠at ⁠least 47 people dead and around ​50 more kidnapped.
UN-backed force aims to break gang-war siege in Haiti
The GSF was launched a year ago after the prior Kenyan-led mission similarly struggled to ​reach its goals with ⁠voluntary contributions. Its troops withdrew early this year.
The mandate was renewed until March 31, 2027. Haiti is scheduled to hold elections on Dec. 13, and final results are due on March 7.
Successive transitional governments have long delayed elections due to worsening insecurity, which has now forced close to 1.5 million ⁠people to flee their homes.

articles.title: South Africa to clean up high-risk areas after 12 women killed
articles.summary: The deaths sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country.

blocks.text: South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday announced a clean-up of high-risk areas across the country, after the bodies of 12 women were discovered in an area east of Johannesburg in just two months.
The deaths sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in South Africa, which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Ramaphosa announced what he called a multidisciplinary, national-level emergency response to the murders, for which there have been four arrests.
He said gender-based violence "cannot be accepted as a normal part of life in South Africa" and admitted the country has "not done enough" to protect women and girls.
"There has understandably been widespread fear that the discovery of these women in close proximity could indicate the work of a single perpetrator," Ramaphosa said in an address to the nation.
"At present, the police have not found evidence establishing that these killings were committed by a single perpetrator."
Admitting the government has not done enough in recent years to prevent gender-based violence, he announced a new wave of measures to help protect women and girls.
"Every municipality must begin a women's safety audit without delay," he said. "High-risk areas must be identified" and addressed.

"These audits must identify broken streetlights, overgrown public spaces, abandoned buildings, unsafe transport routes and facilities, poorly secured parks, and other conditions that place women at risk."
Ramaphosa also announced an "enforcement package" to reduce alcohol-related violence.
"Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator," he said.
"But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence, and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort."

The South African president also said a deeper change, beyond policing and legislation, must take place to reduce violence against women and girls, saying it "does not begin when a fist is raised" or when a woman is raped or murdered.
"It begins much earlier," he said. "It begins in attitudes that regard women as inferior… with the belief that a man has the right to control a woman.
"It begins when jealousy is mistaken for love, when control is mistaken for protection and coercion is mistaken for affection.
"It begins when a man refuses to accept the word no."
He went on to call on men and boys to take the lead in ending gender-based violence.
"We have placed the burden of male violence on women," Ramaphosa said. "That must change."
"The solution to violence against women cannot be to make women less free."
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.

While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said recently that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year.

articles.title: Six Flags shuts down X2 rollercoaster after hundreds allege brain injuries
articles.summary: The announcement comes after multiple lawsuits alleged that hundreds of riders suffered brain injuries from X2, a ride with seats that spin 360 degrees.

blocks.text: Six Flags Magic Mountain, an amusement park in California, has announced it will permanently close a popular rollercoaster after hundreds of riders alleged they suffered brain injuries.
The X2 rollercoaster, one of the park's main attractions, with long wait times to ride and seats that spin 360 degrees, has been closed since July.
Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do".

The decision comes after lawsuits and news reports alleged that hundreds of riders suffered brain injuries after riding X2. A law firm representing some of the plaintiffs said the decision had come "too late" for its clients.

Announcing the closure on Tuesday, , external Six Flags Magic Mountain Park President Brian Oerding said: "Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously."
Dordick Law Corporation, who filed civil lawsuits against the park, said it had been contacted by hundreds of people who alleged they had injuries they believed were caused by the ride.

"They got on X2 expecting a thrill. Instead, they left with catastrophic brain injuries," the firm said in a statement. "Some needed emergency brain surgery. Some are still fighting to get their lives back."
The law firm said that while it welcomed the closure of the ride to protect future guests, "it does nothing for the people who have already been hurt".

Originally called X, the ride first opened in 2002 but was closed months later for repairs to design flaws, the Los Angeles Times reports. It was then closed again in 2007 to replace its trains with lighter versions.
It reopened the following year as X2 and since then has been ridden by more than 16 million people, the park said.
A law firm that represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding X2 in 2022, said the closure was not enough.

While the Hawley family is "relieved to hear that Six Flags is finally closing the X2, it does not change the fact that Christopher Hawley was killed by a dangerous roller coaster that was allowed to operate for nearly two decades," attorney Brent Wisner of Wisner Baum LLP said in a statement to the BBC.
Hawley's family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August.
"That tragedy cannot be undone," Wisner said, calling for legal reform, proactive regulation and proper governmental oversight.
"We cannot rely on profit-centered corporations to do the right thing only after enough people have been hurt," he added. "We hope that whatever replaces the X2 is safe."

articles.title: Matthew Mayich's Arizona teammates dispute school report on workout before Hamilton NHL prospect's collapse
articles.summary: An anonymous letter by Arizona State University hockey players that was sent to the school's president disputes aspects of ASU's official review into events that led up to Matthew Mayich's collapse.…

image.caption: Through their lawyer, seven Arizona State University hockey players sent an anonymous letter to the university president related to an outdoor workout involving Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich, shown on the right in a St. Louis Blues sweater. The 21-year-old remains in stable but critical

blocks.text: Hamilton·New

An anonymous letter by Arizona State University hockey players that was sent to the school's president disputes aspects of ASU's official review into events that led up to Matthew Mayich's collapse. The letter alleges the Hamilton-born NHL prospect "received no water" during the outdoor workout on a hot day last month and calls for an independent investigation.
Arizona lawmakers also call for independent investigation into ASU training session last month

An anonymous letter by members of Arizona State University's hockey team that was sent to the school's president disputes aspects of ASU's official report into events that led up to Canadian NHL prospect Matthew Mayich's collapse.

In the review released last week, ASU official James Rund wrote that the Hamilton-born 21-year-old collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during Aug. 20 training at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus. It also determined ASU hockey coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.
The players said in the letter that they had it sent anonymously Monday to ASU president Michael M. Crow through their lawyer, Timothy J. Casey, as they feared retribution.

It alleges that Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout on a hot day last month, and calls for the university to place the trainers "responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the session" on leave pending an independent investigation.

items: Hockey coaches didn't submit training plan before Matthew Mayich collapsed in workout: Arizona university
Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout

blocks.text: The players' letter says that, to "our knowledge, no one involved has been placed on leave, suspended or disciplined. The head coach who selected the instructor and scheduled the session continues to lead our program."

It urges that the team's coaching staff be replaced "for the period of the investigation if the facts set out in this report, together with what the investigation finds, indicate that step is appropriate."

Also on Monday, the Arizona State Legislature's House and Senate education chairs, Republicans Matt Gress and Hildy Angius, announced on X that they're calling for an independent investigation into the Aug. 20 training session. In a news release, they said they have asked the state's Board of Regents to retain an independent investigator.
Mayich struggled near end of workout, ASU report says

According to Rund's report, during the workout, a "break was taken approximately 20 minutes into the event for the student athletes to drink water." However, the letter from the players alleges "Matthew, and many of us, did not get water at any point."

Rund, ASU's senior vice-president of educational outreach and student services, said coaches asked permission for Timothy Ziesel, who was there for the workout and had "spoken with the ASU hockey team in the 2025-26 season about topics of leadership and teamwork," to speak to the team.
However, the coaches didn't "submit a plan of training activities for review by ASU’s strength and conditioning coaches" before training began, Rund said.

items: Hamilton NHL prospect Matthew Mayich 'needs a miracle' after training collapse, family lawyer says
Parents of NHL prospect hospitalized after collapse at team workout say he's a 'fighter'

blocks.text: Near the end of the workout, "Matthew appeared to struggle, and then in rapid succession stumbled, dropped the medicine ball and fell to the ground," Rund wrote. "He attempted to get up and resume running, but fell to his knees."
Rund also announced that ASU would have a panel of experts provide best-practice recommendations.
The players' letter alleges that when "those of us who reached the water drank, Ziesel stood behind us and declared that he did not get water in combat."
The players also ask for answers to 19 questions, including:

items: Who approved Ziesel to work with the team and when?
Why was the strength and conditioning coach, who head coach Greg Powers says runs the team’s workouts, excluded from planning or reviewing the Aug. 20 session, and who made that decision?
Why was no one assigned to monitor each player for signs of heat illness, including altered consciousness?
Was the team physician contacted? If not, why not?
Why did the review [by Rund] rely on an off-site weather station?
Did anyone verify Ziesel’s first-aid, CPR and automated external defibrillator (AED) certifications?

blocks.text: Mayich family 'grateful' to teammates

In a statement shared with media Tuesday afternoon by Rob Carey, the Mayich family's lawyer, Matthew's parents, John and Christina, said they were “so grateful to Matthew's teammates. A lot of you have come by, sent messages, and kept Matthew in your thoughts every day. It means more to us than we can say."

The Mayichs said they "want this team to have a great season, and we'll be cheering for you. But the coaches who ran that workout on August 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn't have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day."
The players also made several requests, including that:

items: Written findings be issued on whether each requirement of the Outside Consultants and Exertional Heat Illness policies was met on Aug. 20.
The staff responsible for approving, conducting, and supervising the workout session be placed on administrative leave pending an independent investigation.
The investigation be referred to an agency outside the university.

There be confirmation in writing that no player will lose a scholarship, roster position or playing time for participating in any investigation or in this report, and that each will be protected from retaliation if their identities are revealed.

blocks.text: When asked for comment, Chris Fiscus, ASU vice-president of media relations and strategic communications, told CBC News on Tuesday afternoon that the university "will respond later today." At the time of publication, no response had been provided.

Last week, Carey said "Matthew is in stable but critical condition still. The family is still praying for a miracle, but nothing has significantly changed. But even if that happens, we will never have the young man who came to Arizona last month, a hockey star and ... a wonderful person."
Carey said that "when Matthew went down [during the workout], there was no plan and no preparation, so he was treated in a way that hurt his chances rather than helped them."
"A month later, nobody's been named, nobody's been suspended, nobody's been fired for violating the very policies ASU published today, and the university wants to appoint a committee."
Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020. He was selected in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft by the St. Louis Blues.

Doug Armstrong, the Blues' president of hockey operations, said in a news release in late August, "The entire Blues organization is keeping Matthew Mayich close to our hearts as we pray for his comfort and recovery while he continues to undergo medical treatment in Arizona."
The organization also extends its "deepest support" to his family, friends and teammates during this difficult time, Armstrong said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Conrad Collaco is a CBC News producer for CBC Hamilton with extensive experience in online, television and radio news. Follow him on Twitter at @ConradCollaco, or email him at conrad.collaco@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Transport strike to continue for second day, PISTON says
articles.summary: The Pinagkaisang Samahan ng mga Tsuper at Operator Nationwide (PISTON) said its transport strike will push through for a second day to press the government to act on the plight of jeepney drivers…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 6:14am Updated September 30, 2026 7:57am

The Pinagkaisang Samahan ng mga Tsuper at Operator Nationwide (PISTON) said its transport strike will push through for a second day on Wednesday to press the government to act on the plight of jeepney drivers amid rising oil prices.
The group said they expect drivers and operators from various areas to continue joining the strike, which could affect public transportation in parts of the country.
PISTON is calling on the government to address their concerns and review existing laws and policies, including the Oil Deregulation Law and the excise tax on fuel.
In a social media post, PISTON said its members will hold a strike at protest centers before they gather at Welcome Rotunda at 2 p.m. for a march to Mendiola in Manila.
Authorities, meanwhile, are expected to monitor the situation and deploy assistance to commuters affected by the strike.
Several universities have also suspended face-to-face classes in light of the transport strike.
According to a report of James Agustin on GMA News’ Unang Balita, PISTON members held a program along Aurora Boulevard corner West Point Street in Cubao, Quezon City on Wednesday morning.
One of its members Celso, who operates the Cubao-Divisoria route, said he was willing to sacrifice two days of income to bring their concerns to the government.
During his last day of operation, Celso said he earned only P200.
Despite the strike, commuters were still able to find jeepneys operating along routes from Cubao to Divisoria and Quiapo.
Meanwhile, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) said jeepney fares could be reduced if fuel prices decline in the coming months.
A fare rollback could be considered if a petition is filed, noting that a similar reduction was implemented in 2018 when fuel prices significantly dropped, according to the LTFRB.
The minimum fare for traditional jeepneys is currently P14.

However, PISTON is opposing a possible fare rollback. The group has a pending petition before the LTFRB seeking a P10 fare increase, saying the amount is needed to help drivers cope with rising fuel costs and provide for their families.
Another transport group, Manibela, is separately seeking a P2 fare increase.

Some commuters, including minimum-wage earners and students, meanwhile expressed support for lower fares, saying higher transportation costs add to their daily expenses. —with a report from Joviland Rita/LDF/KG, GMA News

articles.title: More than 400 detained as France student protests escalate
articles.summary: Students have been protesting conditions and resources in high schools since last week.

blocks.text: "We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old female student told the AFP news agency. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason. We're here precisely to say that the education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible. The teachers are overworked."
Taking to X, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said students have the right to protest, but condemned reports of violence as "indefensible".
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told BFMTV 440 people were detained, adding: "We don't have the final tally yet, but I'm told two thirds led to police custody."
French media reported that protesters hurled projectiles at police, who responded with batons and tear gas.
Speaking to AFP, Ryad Rani, president of Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, accused the French government of "repression" and police of using excessive force.
When pressed on the police response to the protests, which has been criticised by several French politicians, Nuñez said it had been "carried out in an extremely proportionate manner".
Writing on social media on Tuesday evening, education minister Geffray said: "The right to demonstrate is a fundamental freedom that cannot serve as an excuse for such actions.
"To legitimise them or, in this context, to call for extending the blockades is to endanger our students as well as public employees. It is irresponsible."
The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.
On Monday, France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned any escalation in the student protests would be "irresponsible" following the arrest of 164 people.
Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."

The continuing student demonstrations on Tuesday coincided with nationwide walkouts by unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions.
Nuñez said these protests, with at least 200,000 participants reported, mostly went without incident.

articles.title: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to 'self-police' AI development
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump has signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence companies to "self-police" the technology's development.

image.caption: President Donald Trump speaks at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

blocks.text: World·New
U.S. President Donald Trump has signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence companies to "self-police" the technology's development.
AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton says Trump 'doesn't really understand AI'

U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence company leaders signed a voluntary accord during a White House meeting that will include internal and external reviews of the technology.
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters outside the West Wing.

The announcement followed an extensive meeting between Trump and numerous leading executives from top tech firms. These companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centres in communities across the country that have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition. Many of the executives gathered in Washington have called for a slowdown in the development of the technology after several hgh-profile incidents where AI agents have gone rogue.
But earlier Tuesday, Trump promised that the U.S. government wouldn't limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for "guardrails" or other restrictions.

"I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution," Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot."

Top AI executives met with Trump at the White House Tuesday, including: Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic; Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI; Jeff Bezos, founder of Amazon; and Elon Musk, whose X social media platform includes its own AI model, Grok.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sat to Trump's right at Tuesday's White House lunch, according to a seating chart the president posted on Truth Social. Musk sat to Trump's left. Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also attended.

Trump's bullishness on AI contrasts with the alarms sounded recently by some AI executives, including Amodei, who earlier this month called for leading firms to slow down their development of the technology. Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also called for allowing safety measures to catch up as companies reported mounting examples of AI agents going rogue.
Other executives, particularly Huang and Zuckerberg, have downplayed concerns about runaway AI and underscored the responsibility of each company to ensure the safety of its products.
Vice-President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Republican Speaker of the House, Louisiana Rep. Mike Johnson, also attended.

The unveiling of the AI chatbot occurred at a daylong event in Washington during which multiple Trump administration officials celebrated a "Golden Age" fuelled by what Trump insists on calling "super intelligence," rather than artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio highlighted that America.gov could soon be used to apply for a first-time passport fully online, without an in-person visit to a processing centre.
Trump praises 'self-regulation' by AI industry

Speaking to reporters after the lunch with tech CEOs, Trump said there had been widespread agreement on "self-regulation" by the AI developers, "and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that."

He also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centres cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.
"You're going to see, data centres are going to be very popular," Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, "they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations."
Also Tuesday, Altman said in a television interview that the company is increasingly focused on safety. The day before, his company halted the rollout of a new model over safety concerns.

"We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model," he said on CNBC. "We have to do these in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don't have a bunch of anxiety."
Trump is 'ill-advised' about artificial intelligence, says 'godfather' of AI

Canadian-British artificial intelligence pioneer Geoffrey Hinton questioned the U.S. president's grasp of the technology when asked what he expected as Trump met with American tech executives on Tuesday.
"I think Donald Trump doesn't really understand AI, and I think he's ill-advised about AI," Hinton told CBC News, speaking hours prior to Trump's announcement.
Hinton linked the danger posed by AI today to owning a tiger cub as a pet.
"It's going to grow up, and unless you can figure out how to prevent it [from] ever wanting to kill you, you're in trouble," he said.
He said AI safety in the U.S. ought to be overseen by the federal government via an official agency akin to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

Trump portrayed the race to develop AI as largely a global competition between the United States and China, with the U.S. in the lead. He said there would be a winner and a loser, with no "second place."

The two countries agreed last week to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington. But Trump underscored Tuesday that he didn't want to co-operate too much with China: "I didn't want to do anything, because we're leading. Why would I want to do anything?"
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Fires and blockades as students stage school protests across France
articles.summary: More than 400 people, mainly minors, were arrested on Tuesday, the country's interior minister says.

blocks.text: More than 400 people, most of them children, were arrested in France on Tuesday during a wave of school protests across the country.
The country's interior minister Laurent Nuñez told broadcaster BFMTV that 440 people in total had been detained, while 48 law enforcement members had been injured.
Students are demonstrating over issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. France's education ministry said 400 schools were impacted by protests or disruptions on Tuesday.
The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.
The protests on Tuesday came the same day as professionals from public sectors - including teachers and firefighters - also demonstrated against planned budget cuts in France.

articles.title: Conservative MP Scott Aitchison expected to resign this fall: sources
articles.summary: MP and former Conservative leadership candidate Scott Aitchison is expected to resign his seat later this fall, sources tell CBC News.

image.caption: Conservative MP Scott Aitchison has represented the Ontario riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka since 2019. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking
MP and former Conservative leadership candidate Scott Aitchison is expected to resign his seat later this fall, sources tell CBC News.
Ontario MP and former mayor made bid for Conservative leadership in 2022
MP and former Conservative leadership candidate Scott Aitchison is expected to resign his seat later this fall, two sources tell CBC News.
A senior Conservative source said Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was told last week that Aitchison plans to leave at the end of the fall sitting.
The MP's departure was going to be announced next week, the source said. CTV News first confirmed the news of his departure.
Aitchison joins a list of Conservative MPs looking to exit electoral politics in recent months.
Prime Minister Mark Carney appointed former Conservative MP Richard Martel to the Senate early in the summer. Martel was sworn into the Red Chamber earlier this week.
Former MPs Cathay Wagantall and Larry Brock both stepped down in the past month.
Aitchison has been the MP for Ontario's Parry Sound-Muskoka riding since the 2019 election.
The former Muskoka mayor launched a leadership bid in the 2022 Conservative campaign that saw Poilievre chosen as the party's chief. Aitchison finished fifth.
Housing was a key feature of Aitchison's leadership campaign and Poilievre named the MP as his housing critic.
Aitchison's office did not immediately return a request for comment.
The resignation would create another vacancy in the House, where six seats are currently empty.
In addition to Brock and Wagantall, former Liberal cabinet minister Steven Guilbeault officially resigned last month. Former Liberal MP Shaun Chen resigned in mid-August.
Former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice and the Bloc Québécois's Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay both left federal politics to run in Quebec's provincial election.

articles.title: Sask. drone company says no 'special rights' attached to $10M US investment linked to Trump Jr.
articles.summary: Saskatoon-based drone maker Draganfly Inc. is receiving a US$10M "strategic investment" from two U.S. firms, including one linked to Donald Trump Jr., but says there are no board seats or other perks…

image.caption: Draganfly drones are used around the world for search and rescue missions, crop science and military operations. (Submitted by Draganfly Inc.)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New

Saskatoon-based drone maker Draganfly Inc. is receiving a US$10M "strategic investment" from two U.S. firms, including one linked to Donald Trump Jr., but says there are no board seats or other perks attached to the agreement.
2 U.S. companies investing in Saskatoon-based Draganfly

Saskatoon drone maker Draganfly Inc. says there are no "special rights" attached to a $10-million US investment from an unnamed U.S. investment fund and Unusual Machines Inc., a company linked to Donald Trump Jr.
Draganfly is headquartered in Saskatoon and was founded in 1997. Unusual Machines and the unnamed fund are each investing $5 million US.
Unusual Machines, a supplier of drone components, named the U.S. president's son to its advisory board in November 2024.
"No board seats or special rights are attached to these investments," a Draganfly spokesperson said in a statement emailed to CBC News.

"In response to rising demand for Draganfly's proprietary products and technology in Canada and other allied countries, we have recently attracted investment to facilitate new hires and expand manufacturing capability."

The investment took the form of a purchase of 1,869,159 common shares of the company at a price of $5.35 US, according to a news release by Draganfly. As of market close on Tuesday, the stock was trading at $6.20 US on the NASDAQ, a one-day increase of $0.60 US.
The stock also trades on the Canadian Securities Exchange. As of closing Tuesday, it was trading at $8.81, a one-day increase of $0.92.

items: Sask. drone maker Draganfly has high hopes for Ottawa’s defence spending spree

blocks.text: The company said it plans to use the investment money to accelerate development and fund general working capital.
Draganfly manufactures drones in Saskatoon and Vancouver, and is planning expansions in Edmonton and Ottawa. It also operates in Tampa, Fla.
The drones are used around the world in search and rescue operations, agriculture and by the U.S. military. In 2025, Draganfly won a contract to provide the U.S. Army with drones.

Earlier this month, Draganfly secured a five-year contract with Ottawa to supply the Canadian Armed Forces with up to 5,000 drones. The deal includes a firm commitment to buy 100 drones, with the option to purchase another 4,900.
The federal government approved Draganfly as a qualified supplier under Ottawa's Defence Drone Initiative.
In 2015, Draganfly was acquired by TRACE Live Networks, California-based tech firm.
Draganfly has a market capitalization of about $285 million, according to the company's statement.
The company is often cited as the maker of the first civilian drone to be credited with saving a life. A Draganfly drone was added to the collection of the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeremy Warren is a reporter in Saskatoon. You can reach him at jeremy.warren@cbc.ca.
With Canadian Press files

blocks.text: Home Affairs orders rapid review of government-wide cyber systems after OpenAI hack
OpenAI’s Medicare breach has prompted a government-wide assessment of cyber systems to bolster Australia’s public sector against further AI threats – deliberate or not.

Home affairs directed all government departments and agencies to undertake a “rapid” stocktake of legacy systems, to formulate risk management for legacy technology and to report their compliance back to the department.
The directive prioritises systems of government significance – the government’s critical systems – with a review due by the end of the year, while other systems will be assessed by March.
The acting home affairs minister, Richard Marles, said AI is “changing the environment in which we operate at extraordinary speed.”
double quotation markWe can’t wait for an old system to fail before replacing it. We need to identify vulnerabilities and deal with them before they can be exploited.

articles.title: U.S. Supreme Court says Trump can continue deportations to 3rd countries — for now
articles.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday let President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the ‌harms they may…

image.caption: The U.S. Supreme Court voted to allow President Donald Trump to resume swift deportations to third countries while it considers if the policy is legal. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday let President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the ‌harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.
High court voted to allow deportations to resume while it considers legality of policy

The court granted the Justice Department's emergency request to put on hold Boston-based U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling that the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful. The court also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on policy to follow.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three ​liberal justices dissented from the decision to let the deportations immediately resume pending the final outcome of ​the litigation.

Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the U.S. government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.
More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 ​countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.
Colombia agrees to accept U.S. deportation flights after Trump tariff threat

The policy is ⁠one of a number of measures the ⁠administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation. The Republican president has enforced ‌a sweeping crackdown on immigration — among his top priorities — since returning to office last year.

The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the U.S. State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic and other nations.

The Supreme Court previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the ⁠removals. In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.
The case began in 2025 after the DHS moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.
Migrants with legal protection being sent home

The policy provided that migrants could be ‌swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and U.S. authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.

In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process protections under the U.S. Constitution's Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government to provide ​notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.
In its emergency filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."
But both Murphy and critics ⁠of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.

The policy has resulted in deportees being ⁠unlawfully transferred by third countries back to their home countries from which the U.S. had already granted them protection, while others have been beaten, sexually assaulted, detained or have disappeared, ⁠the plaintiffs said ⁠in a court filing.

The administration is ignoring "the significant harm resulting from ​deporting thousands of longtime U.S. residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there," the plaintiffs said.

The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the administration "repeatedly violated, or attempted to violate" his orders. Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated another order he issued requiring additional steps before attempting to send a group of migrants to South Sudan.

More than a dozen United Nations human rights experts have written to the U.S. government urging a halt to policies that they said on Monday were putting migrants at heightened risk of abuse, including torture and persecution, by deporting them to third countries.

"At gravest risk are children, women, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking, ⁠LGBT persons, human rights defenders, stateless persons and other people ‌in extremely vulnerable situations," they said, without documenting individual cases.

articles.title: Morocco: King appoints first woman prime minister
articles.summary: The appointment of Fatima Zahra Mansouri comes after her center-right party won last week's parliamentary elections in Morocco. She had previously served as mayor of the city of Marrakesh.

image.caption: Fatima Zahra Mansouri said her premiership would be a source of pride for all Moroccan women [FILE: September 24, 2026]Image: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP

blocks.text: Fatima Zahra Mansouri became Morocco's first female prime minister, the country's royal cabinet announced on Tuesday. King Mohammed VI has tasked her with forming the next government.
Under the Moroccan constitution, the country's king has the power to appoint the prime minister, but he must choose someone from the party that wins the most seats in parliamentary elections.
Mansouri's appointment comes after her center-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won last week's parliamentary elections.
PAM raked in 97 out of 395 seats in the House of Representatives, 31 more than the next closest competitor. The vote was, however, marred by the lowest turnout in two decades.

"For the first time in our country's history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government," Mansouri said. "This is a source of pride not only for me but for all Moroccan women."
Mansouri is now the second woman in the Arab world to serve as prime minister, after Najla Bouden, who served in that position in Tunisia from 2021 to 2023.
Moroccans head to the polls amid rising voter apathy
First female mayor of Marrakesh

Her government will now need to deliver on voter's most important issues, such as fighting inflation, raising wages and creating jobs. At the same time, Mansouri is expected to oversee billions of dollars in investments linked to Morocco co-hosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup during her tenure.

"We are fully aware that this period will be significant and marked by high expectations from Moroccans, particularly young people," Mansouri said. "That is why we will have a program offering concrete and realistic solutions to citizens' concerns," she added.

Mansouri is also the first woman to serve as mayor of the city Marrakesh. She became mayor in 2009 for six years. She retook the job again in 2021. In addition to her mayorship, she has also been member of parliament.

The 50-year-old has been a member of PAM since 2008, the year the party was founded by current royal adviser Fouad Ali El Himma. PAM was formed to serve as a counterweight to the country's Islamist movement.
By 2024, Mansouri was one of the party's top leaders.

Her task now will be to form a government and for that, PAM has expressed willingness to work with all parties. Some, however, including the moderate Islamist Justice and Development party and left-wing Federation of Democratic Left, have said they plan to remain in the opposition.
Morocco's youth between hope and resignation

articles.title: Hurricane Polo makes 2nd landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
articles.summary: Hurricane Polo made a second landfall on Mexico's northwestern Pacific coast on Tuesday after drenching the southern Baja California peninsula.

image.caption: A street in Puerto San Carlos, Mexico, which was flooded by Hurricane Polo, is seen Tuesday. (Carl de Souza/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
Hurricane Polo made a second landfall on Mexico's northwestern Pacific coast on Tuesday after drenching the southern Baja California peninsula.
Made landfall near port city of Guaymas in Sonora state

Landfall was near the port city of Guaymas on the Sea of Cortez in ​Sonora state. State authorities ordered emergency evacuations in southern ​municipalities including Guaymas, Empalme, Benito Juarez and Vicam. Officials said 543 people hunkered down in shelters as the storm rolled in.
Polo, a Category 1 hurricane, ​was inland at 10 a.m. local time, and the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) reported ⁠maximum sustained winds of around ⁠120 km/h.
"Rapid weakening is expected as ‌the center of Polo moves farther inland," the NHC said in its bulletin.
While the hurricane was forecast to weaken over land, private forecaster AccuWeather warned its moisture-laden remnants could trigger a deluge across the U.S. Southwest and Plains.
PHOTOS | Hurricane Polo hits Mexico:
Hit Baja California as Category 2 storm
Polo earlier battered the Baja California peninsula as a more powerful Category 2 storm, turning streets into rivers and snapping trees.
However, Baja California Sur Gov. Víctor Manuel Castro said no lives were ‌lost due to the storm.

The storm was expected to dump 10 to 15 centimetres across southern and central portions of Sonora, with isolated maximum totals of 20 centimetres. Baja California Sur could face a further two to five centimetres ​of rain and the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, according to the NHC.

items: Hurricane Polo threatens Mexico's Pacific coast
Hawaii readies for arrival of Hurricane Nolo amid risks of catastrophic flooding

blocks.text: "At my house we tied all down. ⁠We prepared very well. We expected it to be stronger, but thank God it wasn't ⁠so disastrous," Bertha Lopez, a resident of Loreto in Baja California Sur, told Reuters.

Nearly 700 people ⁠sought ⁠refuge in emergency shelters in Baja ​California Sur, and will be returning to their homes throughout the day, the head of Mexico's civil ​protection agency, Laura Velázquez, said ⁠at a news conference.
In a post on X, Mexico's Secretariat of the Navy said a ship brought 2,000 food baskets, 8,000 litres of drinking water and machinery, among other things, to the region.

articles.title: Premier Scott Moe goes big on nuclear with plans to explore 2 large nuclear reactors in northwest Sask.
articles.summary: Saskatchewan says it wants to have a large nuclear reactor online by 2042. It has also narrowed down the location of further study for its construction of Small Modular Reactors (SMR) to the Rafferty…

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New

Saskatchewan says it wants to have a large nuclear reactor online by 2042. It has also narrowed down the location of further study for its construction of Small Modular Reactors (SMR) to the Rafferty site near Estevan.
Goal is to have 1st large nuclear reactor online by 2042
Premier Scott Moe announces new details of Sask.'s nuclear power plan
Saskatchewan is going big on nuclear, announcing plans to explore building two large nuclear reactors in the province's northwest, with a goal of having the first online by 2042.
The Government of Saskatchewan also confirmed it has narrowed down the location of further study for its construction of small modular reactors (SMRs) to the Rafferty site near Estevan.
Premier Scott Moe said the province's new Delivering Energy Security Through Nuclear Power plan establishes an initial target of 2,600 megawatts (MW) of nuclear power generation by 2050.
"With our world-class uranium resources, skilled workforce and growing nuclear expertise, Saskatchewan has everything we need to be a global leader in nuclear energy," Moe said.
"This ambitious plan turns that potential into action — strengthening our energy security, attracting investment, and building a strong nuclear future right here at home.”

items: As Sask. pushes nuclear power, questions raised about costs, other options
Did Sask. pick coal to power its energy future for financial reasons, or political ones?

blocks.text: Crown Investments Corporation Minister Jeremy Harrison said the plan focuses on four priorities for nuclear development:

items: Building electricity capacity for long-term growth.
Incorporating large nuclear reactors into the province's electricity supply planning.
Continuing nuclear development in Estevan.
Building on established nuclear capabilities.

blocks.text: “This plan gives SaskPower a clear path to meet growing demand and support the investment and industries that keep our province strong," Harrison said.
Large nuclear reactors
The 2,600 MW goal for nuclear power generation is a massive expansion of the province's nuclear plans, which had previously been restricted to SMR development and construction.
For context, SaskPower reported that the total power system demand at 10:30 a.m. CST on Tuesday was 2,829 MW. The record for most power use in the province was 3,910 MW on Dec. 30, 2021.
The SMR technology selected by Saskatchewan, the Hitachi BWRX-300, produces approximately 300 MW from a single unit.
Although SaskPower has previously said it wanted to pursue large nuclear technology, Tuesday's announcement is the first time the government has provided firm details.
The province did not confirm where the two large nuclear reactors would be constructed on Tuesday, but Moe has previously alluded to potential locations along the North Saskatchewan River.
SaskPower said it will evaluate potential locations while having "meaningful engagement with local communities and Indigenous peoples."
Sask. government wants to build a large nuclear reactor

The provincial government did not explicitly say what type of nuclear reactor it would use for the large scale reactors, but Westinghouse's CEO is included in the news release and references Westinghouse and Cameco's AP1000 Gen III+ reactor.
Some of those large scale reactors are already up and running in China and the U.S., with each reactor producing approximately 1,100 MW.

items: Canada wants to build up to 10 new nuclear plants. Will our pension funds pay for them?

blocks.text: SMR site selection
SaskPower also confirmed it has further narrowed down the locations for SMR deployment in southeast Saskatchewan.

The Crown corporation has previously indicated it was down to two possibilities: a site on the Boundary Dam Resevoir in the Rural Municipality of Estevan, and a location on the Rafferty Resevoir in the rural municipality of Cambria.
SaskPower confirmed Tuesday that it has selected the Rafferty site for "further study."
SaskPower says Estevan remain a key part of nuclear power plans, with the the goal of delivering at least 600 MW of nuclear power, or two Hitachi BWRX-300 units.
A final site decision is expected sometime this year, according to a SaskPower project schedule.
The first SMR is scheduled to be operational by the mid-2030s according to the same document.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexander Quon is the provincial affairs reporter for CBC Saskatchewan. He has been a reporter with CBC Saskatchewan since 2021 and is happy to be working in his hometown of Regina after half a decade in Atlantic Canada. He has previously worked with the CBC News investigative unit in Nova Scotia and Global News in Halifax. Alexander specializes in freedom of information requests and data reporting. He can be reached at: alexander.quon@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 'It's devastating': Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke face uncertain future due to layoffs
articles.summary: Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont. are facing an uncertain future after the company announced it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton…

image.caption: Aerial shot of Stelco Hamilton Works production facility at the Hamilton Harbour. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont. are facing an uncertain future after the company announced it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant.
Union says up to 500 workers could lose their jobs as company idles cold-rolled and coated operations
Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton are facing an uncertain future after the company announced Monday it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant.
Ron Wells, the president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, says the wind-down is expected to begin Oct. 9, with about 350 workers from the Hamilton plant expected to be laid off.
He said the total layoffs could be up to 500 in total, between the Hamilton and Lake Erie Works plant in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has also said up to 500 workers could be affected.
"I hate using 'we're disappointed' — we're disgusted," Wells told CBC Hamilton Tuesday morning.

items: Hamilton steel plant to lay off hundreds of workers as U.S. tariffs prompt 'survival' move

blocks.text: For families connected to the plant, the uncertainty is already taking a toll.
Jillian Watt's husband is a line worker, and has worked at Stelco in Hamilton for 21 years. She said he has not yet been told whether he will be among those laid off.

"They haven't spoken to individuals, so it's kind of still up in the air," she said Tuesday morning. Watt, who is a union representative for a Canadian Union of Public Employees heath workers local, spoke to CBC from the entrance to National Steel Car, just down the road from Stelco.
National Steel Car workers have been on strike for a 48 days and have been regularly joined on the picket line by other unionized workers.

Watt is particularly concerned about whether her husband's experience with the company is enough if layoffs are decided by seniority. She said the possibility of losing the family's main source of income is particularly stressful.
"It's a breadwinner for a family. We have four kids, you know, trying to make it by," she said. "It was a bit of a kick to the gut for both of us."

Watt said her husband had already been concerned about the plant in recent months, as operations were idled and orders slowed. Now, they are awaiting the verdict of what happens next. "It's very stressful," she said.
Union questions job commitments
Wells said the union was told about the layoffs during a meeting with the company Monday morning.
He said he has been talking with workers concerned about how long the layoffs could last because the company has not provided an end date.
"They're asking how long is this going to last? Should we start looking for another job?" Wells said. "People are concerned."
The company has said some affected workers could be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke.
But Wells said the union was told there are only roughly 40 to 45 openings there — a number he says falls well short of the potential layoffs in Hamilton.
Wells is also questioning the commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it acquired Stelco in 2024.
He said the agreement included a commitment to maintain the number of unionized employees for five years, and he wants the federal government to enforce it.
"You have people making these decisions in Cleveland and they have no ties to our community," Well said. "If 350 Hamiltonians lose their jobs, they don't care."

items: Hamilton steelmaker Stelco sold to Cleveland-Cliffs for $3.4B

blocks.text: Pat Persico, the senior director of corporate communications for Cleveland-Cliffs, told CBC News in an emailed statement that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.

"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in an email. "We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."
'Devastating' news for Hamilton
Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said the city has been working with the federal and provincial governments in response to the announcement.
"The fight is not over," Horwath told CBC's As It Happens radio program on Monday.
LISTEN | Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath reacts to layoffs:
As It Happens6:54Hamilton steelworker layoffs 'painful for our community,' says mayor
She said she believes Cleveland-Cliffs is not living up to commitments made to workers and that she has asked city staff to review commitments made during the company's restructuring process.
"We're going to fight tooth and nail to have them basically live up to their commitments and protect these jobs," she said.

items: Hamilton steelworkers union, business leaders warn of harder times ahead as Ford promises tariff relief

blocks.text: Karina Gould, the Liberal MP for nearby Burlington, called the decision "devastating news" for Hamilton and said the federal government is prepared to provide support to maintain operations and protect jobs.
"This is a very difficult time," Gould said.
Hamilton mayoral candidate Keanin Loomis, who is the president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, also called the announcement "devastating."
"Steel jobs have supported generations of Hamilton families and remain vital to our local economy," Loomis said in a statement on social media.
The impact of tariffs has been a discussion topic on the municipal election campaign trail, with several candidates sharing proposals on how to respond to trade uncertainty.

items: Hamilton mayor announces 7-point tariff-response plan

blocks.text: For Watt, the announcement represents another difficult moment for a city where steel means so much.
"My grandfather, my dad, my uncles, they all worked at Stelco," she said. "My husband and my brother are there, and this is going to have a huge impact."
"It's scary times."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeffery is a reporter with CBC Hamilton. He previously worked as a reporter at CBC Saskatchewan in Regina, and was an associate producer at CBC Toronto. You can reach him at jeffery.tram@cbc.ca.
With files from Meagan Fitzpatrick

articles.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on defense company
articles.summary: The Estonian government accused Moscow of an "act of sabotage" that is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe. The Baltic state has received support from EU and NATO leaders.

image.caption: Milrem Robotics makes autonomous unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine [FILE: December 2022]Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: NATO and EU leaders rallied behind Estonia on Tuesday, after the Baltic country accused Russia of being behind an arson attack in its capital Tallinn.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Moscow was found responsible for the August 15 arson attack against defense company Milrem Robotics, after the government conducted an investigation into the incident.
Milrem Robotics develops ground drones that are used in Ukraine.

"We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," Tsahkna said on X, adding that the perpetrators had been arrested, and Russia's ambassador had been summoned.
"This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," Tsahkna said.
NATO chief Mark Rutte backed Estonia, accusing Russia of furthering "its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies."

"It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine," Rutte said, adding that Russia is "failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine."
Kremlin says links to arson are "baseless"
Estonia has a population of 1.2 million and it borders Russia to the east.

The incident took place on the night of August 15, when a fire broke out in a building used by Milrem Robotics in Tallinn. According to a statement from the Estonian government, authorities were on the scene right away and no injuries were reported.
Three suspects were later detained in Latvia in connection with the arson attack and were handed over to Estonia this month.
The Kremlin responded to the arson investigation findings by dismissing them as "baseless" and with "absolutely no relation to reality."
"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow.
How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare
EU and NATO leaders rally behind Estonia

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pledged Germany's "full solidarity" with Estonia. "Russia's reckless hostilities will not divide us. They only strengthen our resolve to bolster NATO deterrence and support Ukraine," Wadephul wrote on X.
The EU said it stood by Estonia, saying the arson attack was "reckless" and would not deter the bloc in its support for Ukraine.
"Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen," European Commission spokesman Christian Wigand said.
French President Emmanuel Macron labeled the attack a "dangerous escalation" by Russia. He said it represented another in a "multiplication of these hostile acts."
"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron wrote on X.
Lithuanian foreign minister Kestutis Budrys said "Russia's fingerprints are all over" the arson attack, adding that it was proof that Moscow's "hostile activities do not stop at Ukraine's borders."
Neighboring Latvia's President Edgars Rinkevics said in response to the incident that "more support for Ukraine ... will be needed and must be provided."
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also commented ont he matter, saying attribution of the arson attack was "extremely serious" and "directed against Europe as a whole."
Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats

articles.title: Police investigating after 10K litres of diesel stolen from 3 Calgary gas stations
articles.summary: BG Fuels says it's had 10,000 litres of diesel stolen from three Mobil gas stations in Calgary, with surveillance footage suggesting the fuel was pulled directly out of underground tanks.

image.caption: BG Fuels says it's had 10,000 litres of diesel stolen from three Mobil gas stations in Calgary, with surveillance footage suggesting the fuel was pulled directly out of underground tanks. (Nate Luit/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
BG Fuels says it's had 10,000 litres of diesel stolen from three Mobil gas stations in Calgary, with surveillance footage suggesting the fuel was pulled directly out of underground tanks.
Footage suggests fuel was pulled directly from underground tanks
Sam Babcock didn’t think much of it when he got a call that his company’s fuel inventory was missing a massive amount.

Typically, the BG Fuels territory manager in southern Alberta would chalk up the dip to a simple input error. Babcock didn’t realize the loss was the first in a string of thefts equalling a loss of roughly 10,000 litres of diesel fuel, costing the company approximately $20,000.
“We’ve never seen this. Never across the country as well. At least in my time here, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” said Babcock.

BG Fuels is a Canadian wholesaler operating under the Mobil, Esso and Waypoint Convenience brands around the country. It's raising alarm after three Mobil gas stations in Calgary were hit with thefts in the last few weeks, with diesel fuel pulled directly out of underground tanks.
Most of the total was sucked up in an initial incident where the company lost about 8,000 litres of fuel, Babcock said.

After reviewing surveillance footage of the first theft, Babcock said it showed a truck arrive at around 4 a.m. while the station was closed and remain for roughly 25 minutes while removing diesel from the site, before driving away.
Given that a large commercial truck was used to store the fuel, Babcock pointed out anyone driving by at that hour wouldn't have thought anything suspicious was amiss.
But the thefts are creating a lot of stress for station agents, he said.
“A lot of them have come at nighttime to check in on their sites. They can’t sleep,” said Babcock, who oversees 28 gas stations in southern Alberta.

Surveillance footage shows something went wrong for the perpetrators during the second theft, resulting in only about 50 litres taken. About 2,000 litres was stolen during the final theft, Babcock said. The company said it believes the same perpetrators were involved in all three thefts, judging from the footage.
The thefts present a large safety concern, Babcock said, as the amount of diesel stolen is a lot of flammable material that needs to be handled correctly.
Police investigating thefts
The Calgary Police Service confirmed on Tuesday that it is investigating the incidents.
Nick Wilsher, a sergeant with the service’s crime prevention team, said that while smaller thefts involving siphoning fuel are more common, thefts like what BG reported are unusual.
Wilsher compared the market for fuel to other online marketplaces where a consumer may see a cheap product, know its low price may be because it’s stolen, and “pretend ‘well, maybe it’s not.’”
“It’s not a victimless crime ... Those costs are passed on to you as the consumer," said Wilsher.

“You might think you're getting a deal, but you’re actually making it more expensive for everybody else, including yourself when you can’t buy this cheap diesel anymore. You’re going to have to get it at the pump.”

items: Poilievre urges tax cuts to make diesel fuel more affordable
If Trump bans U.S. diesel exports, global prices will go even higher, experts say

blocks.text: Wilsher said retailers could look to increase security, improve locks and introduce tamper-proof alarm systems and more video surveillance to protect against thefts.

He added that the surveillance footage recovered by BG is helpful to show police the kind of vehicle used in the thefts, where they came from and drove to, and to potentially give them a closer look at the people involved.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Andrew Jeffrey is a multimedia journalist with CBC Calgary. He previously worked for CBC News in his hometown of Edmonton, reported for the StarMetro Calgary, and worked as an editor for Toronto-based magazines Strategy and Realscreen. You can reach him at andrew.jeffrey@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 'Keep demanding space:' Marcos highlights ASEAN women's role in economy, innovation
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. underscored on Tuesday the significance of women"s leadership and representation in driving ASEAN's economy and innovation, urging them to keep asserting their place in…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 1:31am

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. underscored on Tuesday the significance of women’s leadership and representation in driving ASEAN's economy and innovation, urging them to keep asserting their place in leadership.
In his speech at the 4th ASEAN Women Leaders’ Summit, Marcos pointed out that women remain underrepresented in the Cabinets and parliaments of ASEAN member states.
“For decades, women across Southeast Asia have sustained our families, strengthened our communities, driven our economies, and yet their contributions have too often been undervalued,” Marcos said.

“That must change. Women are not simply beneficiaries of our progress. They are leaders and innovators, shaping ASEAN’s future, and our policies, institutions, and investments must reflect this,” he added.

Marcos said the underrepresentation of women in national and regional dialogues reflects not only a gap in representation, but a gap in the perspectives that shape key policy decisions across the region.

“Our work is far from complete. Women remain underrepresented in the Cabinets and Parliaments of ASEAN member states. This is not simply a gap in representation; it is a gap in leadership in whose voices shape the decisions that affect our region,” the President said.
He urged women leaders to never stop leading and pushing forward their sector’s regional agenda and calls.
“To our women leaders in governance, civil society, business, and technology: Keep leading, keep demanding space, keep pushing our region forward,” Marcos said.
“Together, let us shape an ASEAN where equality is not just a policy target, but a lived daily reality for every woman and child,” he added.
Marcos also mentioned the ASEAN Women, Peace, and Security Agenda, emphasizing that having women at the decision-making table makes peace agreements “more durable and rebuilding is more inclusive.”
To further expand women's economic inclusion, Marcos pointed out that the care economy should no longer be overlooked, noting its vital function in sustaining overall economic growth.

“Unpaid care work falls disproportionately on women, restricting their time and opportunity to lead in the formal workforce, especially in the so-called non-traditional fields,” the President said. —LDF, GMA News
“By investing in care infrastructure and redistributing care obligations, we do not just support women, we unlock billions of dollars in economic potential across our region,” he added.
The Philippines holds this year's ASEAN Chairmanship. Last May, it hosted the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu, and is set to host the 49th Summit in November. (END)

articles.title: First female prime minister named in Morocco after winning elections
articles.summary: Her appointment by the king makes her only the second woman to lead a government in the Arab world.

blocks.text: At a victory press conference, prior to her announcement as prime minister, El Mansouri was asked whether the state would need to make changes to accommodate her in Muslim religious ceremonies attended by the king, including Friday and Eid prayers, where men and women pray in separate sections.
She did not directly answer the question, instead praising the king as "the biggest advocate for women" in the country.
"His Majesty is the holder of wisdom… If I am entrusted with the responsibility of head of government, it will be a great honour," she said.
El Mansouri is one of Morocco's most prominent female politicians.
A lawyer by training, she studied at Mohammed V University in the capital, Rabat, before continuing her education in France and the US, specialising in business and corporate law.
She entered politics after Pam was founded in 2008 and became the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh in 2009. She returned to the post after the 2021 elections.
In the past five years, she served as a minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under former Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
In February 2024, she became the co-ordinator of Pam's leadership coalition.
El Mansouri has rejected her portrayal as an "iron woman", telling Pam's magazine in 2021: "I am neither a woman of steel nor iron... I am a free activist."

During her political career, El Mansouri has rarely spoken publicly about women's rights or gender inequality, despite ongoing debates in Morocco over issues such as whether polygamy should be banned and whether men and women should have equal inheritance rights.
Under Morocco's constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the party that comes first in elections to the House of Representatives.
Pam has been led by a collective leadership since February 2024, rather than a single secretary general.
After the results were announced last week, El Mansouri said the decision was ultimately up to the king to choose between her and Lekjaa.
In the past, the appointment was largely a formality, as most Moroccan parties were led by a single secretary general, making it clear who would be nominated to head the government.
With 97 seats, Pam does not have a majority and will need to form a coalition to reach the 198 seats required for an absolute majority in the 395-member parliament.
It is not clear which party it will work with as it has fallen out with the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which led the outgoing government in which Pam was a junior partner.
The Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) ⁠rebounded with 54 seats, from only 13 in the previous election - buoyed by the return of party leader Abdelilah Benkirane, a former prime minister.
After the vote, Benkirane said the party would stay in opposition, refusing a partnership with Pam.
