articles.title: Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in Yemen
articles.summary:
Relations between the two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudi Arabia in Yemen

Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates over Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back.

Relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia in Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which it had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently effectively quit Yemen.

But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthi drive to the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait against pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed.

The future role of the UAE in Yemen was discussed at a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday attended by the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, UAE president Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan and a group of other Arab states, including representatives of Saudi Arabia.

Netanyahu reportedly offered to help Saudi Arabia defeat the Houthis, an offer that Riyadh would probably find near impossible to accept, even though Donald Trump has failed to answer the Saudi call for US help in Yemen.
A further meeting to discuss Yemen took place on Tuesday in Riyadh between Prince Khalid bin Salman al Saud, the Saudi defence minister, and Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE vice president.
It is part of a range of signs from the two sides suggesting they may want to find a path to reconciliation, even if only on energy.
Following the Houthi push to the Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint on Saudi oil exports, its forces are now trying to consolidate their gains and take the south-western city of Taiz.

“The Houthi forces are mounting simultaneous waves of attacks on the city trying to exhaust the Taiz Axis force defending the city. The Houthis are pushed back, but then the next day they come again on a different front,” said Baraa Shiban, a Gulf and Yemen specialist at the defence think tank Rusi who has just spent a week in Taiz.

“Efforts are being made to try to end the rift between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and there may be some confidence-building measures. But the UAE has left Yemen, and it is unlikely that Riyadh would let them back in since they are aligned with the STC, and that would spell trouble … the UAE and Saudi Arabia are fundamentally on opposite sides.”
The STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, fled into exile following the Saudi attack on its forces and the movement became marginalised as a political force.

But the former Yemen foreign minister and STC supporter Khaled Alyemany told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia may have to reconsider its political approach to the southern issue since the Giant Brigades, the UAE-trained southern forces once associated with the STC, provide some of the most reliable, well-equipped forces on the ground to stem the Houthi advance.
The Giant Brigades, however, have been urged by the STC to resist merging with Yemen government forces, arguing to do so will set back the separatist cause.
“We cannot fight and wage wars in the north against the Houthis if we do not have a horizon for our independence,” Alyemany said.

“The UN recognised government … operating from exile in Riyadh, insists that southerners fight to retake the capital, Sana’a, on its behalf, but without any promise of the south’s right to self-determination,” he said. “The problem is so long as the Yemen government derives its legitimacy from its Saudi funders rather than its people, the outcome is not Saudi Arabia’s stated goal of security along its southern borders.”

The White House has also been privately urging the UAE and the Saudi to bury their differences and allow a unified military command including the Southern Giants Brigades to challenge the Houthi advance. An additional proposal is to use Israeli intelligence and hire Israeli private security firms, something the UAE has done sometimes to brutal effect in the past in Yemen.

Saudi Arabia, reluctant to be seen cooperating with Israel, has also always resisted helping the southern separatists since division of the country might entrench Houthi rule in the north along its border. The Houthis have used drones and missiles to attack Saudi energy installations.

Despite Saudi air cover and support, the current battle to prevent the Houthis consolidating their gains is such that the parliament of the UN-recognised government has sanctioned a general mobilisation of the Yemeni people to fight the Houthis.
The World Health Organization stated that 838 people were killed and 3,643 others were injured due to the recent escalation in Yemen from 6 August last year until 26 September this year.

The Houthis insist they are not seeking to block general commercial shipping in the strait, but only that linked to Saudi Arabia. On Monday it published figures showing commercial shipping was flowing as normal.
The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia is in effect a colonial power, and the UN-recognised government based in Aden is a creature of Riyadh with no independent ability to govern the country.

April Longley Alley, senior fellow at Washington Institute, told an International Crisis Group seminar that the war is existential for the Saudis, but the Houthis are not going to compromise. “We will have to see if they hold these territories, but what the Houthis learned from the Iran war is that Saudi under pressure and attack will seek de-escalation,” she said. “The Houthis are demanding a victor’s peace.”

articles.title: Digger review: Tom Cruise is fantastic, but you might hate the film
articles.summary: This climate morality tale suggests that director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and his audience are engaging in the same self-satisfied ritual that got us into this real-life mess in the first place. Of…

image.caption: Tom Cruise, left, and Riz Ahmed appear in a scene from Digger. The topsy-turvy dark comedy follows Cruise's Digger as he attempts to save the world from a catastrophe he caused. (Warner Bros. Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

This climate morality tale suggests that director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and his audience are engaging in the same self-satisfied ritual that got us into this real-life mess in the first place. Of using high-minded entertainment to point out, and joke about, our impending doom, as if that alone is admirable. As if that could change anything at all.
Alejandro G. Iñárritu's dark comedy tells the story of an evil oil tycoon and the end of the world
Rise early. Work hard. Strike oil.

Those words are etched into the wood on a mantel, in all caps, below a reverently displayed 10-cent shovel — a shovel that oil baron Digger Rockwell's grandfather purchased around the turn of the century and used to start the empire Digger himself now steers to global domination.

As the film opens, Digger (Tom Cruise) stands next to it while screaming down a trio of his walleyed climate-expert subordinates about their general lack of resolve. He is delivering a diatribe for the ages about his grandfather's legendary work ethic, about toiling in the dust and the dirt and nearly dying under the blistering sun and — wait a second. Why aren't they listening to his story?

Well, there are a few good reasons. The first being that the purpose of his tirade was to keep those experts from shutting down his oil rig in Greenland due to a widening crack in the ice shelf upon which it sits. But as of a few minutes ago, Dr. Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) explains, the crack itself ceased to be a problem. It is now a crater.

The result is a smouldering methane explosion directly caused by Digger's willful negligence that is sure to, at least, raise a few eyebrows from the families of all those dead oil workers. As well as from a few world governments.

The second reason no one feels like listening to Digger's personal history: U.S. President Compson (John Goodman) has just arrived, and will probably want to know why this accident now implicates him in a cascading climate catastrophe that could drown Norway — and that's just to start.

That's not to mention the ambitious, destabilizing narrative twist that elevates Alejandro G. Iñárritu's newest beyond-farcical fable into what it is — a surprise second strand to the story that, without giving away the game, has us questioning why we're watching this at all. It suggests that Iñárritu and his audience are engaging in the same self-satisfied ritual that got us into this real-life mess in the first place. Of using high-minded entertainment to point out, and joke about, our impending doom, as if that alone is admirable. As if that could change anything at all.

At least, that's what you could get from it. The winding, tongue-in-cheek story is typical Iñárritu in a way that makes its basic worldview feel self-evident: like the ego-destroying reckoning with our own insignificance in Biutiful; the fascinating futility of perseverance in The Revenant; or the vulnerable self-criticism against egotistical legacy-building in Birdman.

It’s all there as Digger freewheels between a madcap Cruise caring for his dying, 30-year-old corpse of a cat and screaming down pussy-footed eco-activists still blindly dependent on fossil fuels. Or as he delivers self-aggrandizing, Shakespearean monologues about his own virility in a lecture hall inexplicably populated by mannequins in wigs.

The story about a self-obsessed, self-mythologizing opportunist pillaging a dying planet for his own profits unravels into something stranger, more confusing, more barbed and angry and ultimately defeatist. Digger is a comedy in the way one could find their own funeral funny.

Explaining exactly why would probably be a mistake (though we can confirm this is unequivocally not a musical) Without quite getting close to M. Night Shyamalan territory, going in blind to Digger’s actual format is probably for the best. (For example, revealing how Jesse Plemons’s red-haired Svengali fits into all this would probably spoil the fun.) Because the befuddling delight in discovering exactly how Iñárritu has chosen to make his demoralizing point about where we’re all headed is one of the movie’s few uplifting spots.

Suffice it to say, this and Birdman — Iñárritu's Oscar-winning 2014 examination of a man at war with his pathetic and inescapable impulse to matter — share serious DNA. And without the reprieve offered by the surprise reveal, the rotating cast of idiot oligarchs, preening politicians and sad-eyed scientists steering the Earth straight off a cliff in search of endless profits would be a bit too on-the-nose.

Which is not to mention the stilted, infinitely self-aware style — anyone who felt Wes Anderson fell a little too in love with his own schtick in the relentlessly obscure Asteroid City should probably steer clear of this one.

Digger is built for smug unpacking and film-critic scene analyses — "inaccessible," "artifice" and "up-its-own" are the three descriptors you could most readily use to describe it. Alienatingly ambitious, as is often seen in works by esteemed directors late in their careers, Iñárritu's latest does perform like a riddle he expects you to solve. A uniformly colour-graded cartoon for pretentious, beige-loving children, the film's deliberate mix of vomit humour and metaphor-laden philosophizing seems to scream all three descriptions at you the whole time. Imagine Megalopolis if it was, somehow, actually good.

items: Megalopolis is one of the worst big-budget movies ever made
Asteroid City is a masterful puzzle — and likely to be Wes Anderson fans' most hated movie

blocks.text: Which raises the question of why Tom Cruise would want to take this project on. The 64-year-old actor's last movie that wasn’t a franchise-focused blockbuster came nearly a decade ago: 2017’s American Made. The last time he made such an obviously transgressive and politically relevant movie was — being generous — 2007's Lions for Lambs or 1989’s Born on the Fourth of July. Realistically, the actual answer is "probably never."

Cruise is fascinating here, delivering searing, complex, southern-inflected line after line, reminding you that he was once one of the most talented and interesting leading men in Hollywood. But why re-enter the critical limelight with this, a movie that seems to intentionally attack the current U.S. administration? Especially when he chose to avoid criticizing that same government when it proposed instituting tariffs designed to limit American productions' abilities to film abroad — a move that could easily have tanked his globetrotting Mission: Impossible series?

Maybe Digger allows Cruise to have his cake and eat it, too. Maybe the meta turn later on allows him to do something that equally doomeristic films like Don’t Look Up, Silent Night, Greenland or even the upcoming Musk documentary can’t.

Because even while partaking in the indulgent wave of multimillion-dollar films openly claiming capitalism has killed us all, Digger does something decidedly more Iñárritu. It turns inward, and then out at the audience. It acknowledges the situation, pointing to a likely future when stepping outside means stepping into a roiling cloud of poison and autonomous police bots with guns.

But it also asks: If we’re not going to do anything about it, what are we accomplishing here? Are we doing anything but stroking our own egos, distracting ourselves, by showing we understand a reality we’re powerless to fix? As it directly asks, are we so enthralled by our own opinions that we’ll happily keep arguing about them as the world crumbles around us?
Maybe. Maybe not. Either way, they’re maybe less politically dangerous questions for Cruise to ask. And newer ones for us to answer.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Ethiopia: No regard for civilians as fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region continues
articles.summary: Fighting has returned to northern Ethiopia, shattering a fragile peace in the region. DW spoke to civilians caught in the crossfire amid communication blackouts, as rebel and federal forces keep…

image.caption: Prices in Tigrayan towns like Mekelle have surged since the onset of the fightingImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: As fighting keeps spreading across northern Ethiopia, civilians find themselves caught in the crossfire between opposing forces. Little information is emerging from the affected area as the internet and other communication services remain largely disrupted.
However, DW managed to speak to eyewitnesses whose accounts point to a growing toll on civilians.
A 22-year-old woman from the small town of Selenwuha told DW that her relatives were sheltering at home when heavy weaponry shelling struck their residences.
"I have lost six family members," she said. "Those who survived the attack, including the wounded, are currently confined to their homes.
"They have no access to medical facilities or vehicles, and the nearest treatment center is far away."
Strategic town of Alamata reported taken by ENDF

According to local residents, several violent incidents took place in recent days, especially in the border region between the Tigray and Amhara regions, with multiple further reports of civilians being killed by artillery fire.
The overall strategic situation on the ground meanwhile remains difficult to assess, with both rebel and federal forces reportedly making advances in different areas.
DW heard from a source in Tigray that the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) keeps advancing towards the regional capital Mekelle. The ENDDF is the country's official military force.
Tigrayan forces are reportedly fighting to defend other towns, including Mekoni and Maychew in southern Tigray, the source told DW on the strict condition of anonymity.

blocks.caption: TPLF fighters are patroling Mekelle — far from the frontline of the present conflictImage: AFP

blocks.text: Pro-government militia and affiliated media outlets in the country had reported earlier that the ENDF had made significant progress by seizing control of Alamata in southern Tigray on September 27.
The purported takeover was also recorded by the US-based conflict-monitoring organization ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data).
Located about 120 kilometers south of the regional capital Mekelle, the strategically important town is situated on a major highway.
During the 2020-2022 war, Alamata changed hands several times between the two warring parties.
Residents accuse federal forces of deliberate attacks
A 40-year-old resident of Alamata told DW that civilians had deliberately been targeted, citing the account shared by militia members in the region.
"The attacks… were acts of retaliation against the people of Alamata," the local said. "The militias told us that government forces had fired the artillery at us."

Another resident, aged 45, said he believed the attack had deliberately been timed to maximize civilian casualties during the opening hours of a market, "when large numbers of people would be gathered there."
"At the Saturday market in Alamata, 11 people were killed and 15 others were wounded", he told DW.

blocks.caption: Alamata has changed hands several times during the 2020-22 civil war (archive picture from January 2021)Image: Alemnew Mekonnen/DW

blocks.text: It's important to note that these claims could not be independently verified.
An ENDF spokesperson was also contacted by DW for comment; by the time of the publishing of this article, the spokesperson had not responded to the request.
Shifting alliances and mutual blame
Large-scale fighting erupted on September 23, when Tigrayan forces seized the airports of the regional capital Mekele as well as the regional hubs of Aksum and Shire.
Three days earlier, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups had announced a new alliance aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.

Unexpectedly, the alliance was joined by the Amhara Fano National Movement, which had supported federal forces against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, but has since then switched side and turned to fighting the federal government.
The federal government and Tigrayan forces meanwhile have accused each other of starting the latest escalation, both sides portraying their military actions as defensive in nature.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict
The unraveling of Ethiopia's fragile peace accord
Depending on the source, between 162,000 and 600,000 people were killed in the brutal 2020-2022 war, which was fought over the political status of the northern province of Tigray.

The war ended in November 2022 with the Pretoria Agreement, under which the TPLF agreed to the disarmament, demobilization and reintegration of its combatants, and to respect the federal government's constitutional authority.

However, key provisions remained unimplemented and major disputes unresolved, including the status of contested territories, the return of displaced people and the full demobilization of Tigrayan forces.
Meanwhile, a power struggle within the TPLF ended with the more hardline faction around Debretsion Gebremichael reasserting control in Tigray, further straining relations with Addis Ababa.
The TPLF also reinstated Tigray's pre-war regional council, a move the federal government viewed as a violation of the Pretoria framework.
Concerns mounted even further when the TPLF lost its legal party legislation, thus excluding the party from participating in national elections in June this year.
Tensions steadily increased, culminating in renewed clashes between Tigrayan and federal forces beginning in August 2026.

blocks.caption: The headquarter of Tigray's state broadcaster was reportedly hit in a drone strike earlier in SeptemberImage: AFP

blocks.text: Fears grow over civilian toll and rights violations

Local residents meanwhile are bracing for further fighting, as organizations like the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) have managed to evacuate only few people caught up in the conflict.
According to the ICRC, the global NGO got to evacuate only around 160 individuals from Tigray, including Ethiopian Federal Police personnel, Ethiopian Airlines staff and African Union monitors.

With reports of damage to civilian infrastructure, disruptions to essential services and interrupted communication and transport routes, observers are worried about the situation of residents not only in Tigray but all across northern Ethiopia.

Amdegebreal Admassu, an Ethiopian lawyer focused on political and legal affairs, told DW he had received reports of fighters impacting public facilities including hospitals, schools and religious institutions.
"We observe instances where these facilities — which also serve as shelters for residents — are either accidentally hit or deliberately targeted.
"Under both international law and our country's penal code, such actions are classified as war crimes," Amdegebreal further explained.
Nearly everyone in Tigray impacted by fighting
Mebrihi Birhane, vice director for the NGO Human Rights First Ethiopia, told DW that many of those civilian facilities had already been impacted during the 2020-22 war.
"The population must have access to essential services even in times of war. Ensuring this is an obligation for all armed forces involved in the conflict," he said.

Meanwhile, the prices of goods are reported to be increasing dramatically, as supply routes are disrupted, affecting residents of Tigray whose communities had so far been spared from the direct fighting.

blocks.caption: According to local journalists, residents of Tigray have rushed to buy flour and other productsImage: AFP

blocks.text: The latest reports indicate that Tigrayan forces have advanced into the Afar region and were said to be controling the area around Erebti.
Analysts say this advance could be aimed at threatening Ethiopia's main trade corridor — a vital route used for imports and exports and a lifeline for the country's economy.

The renewed conflict meanwhile could spread beyond the confines of Ethiopia to the Horn of Africa and beyond, as Prime Minister Abiy has already accused neighboring countries of picking sides and supporting rebel forces.
Several DW journalists contributed to this report.

articles.title: ICC rejects Duterte camp’s request on digital evidence
articles.summary: Trial judges of the International Criminal Court have rejected the request of the defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte to adopt a stricter protocol in verifying digital materials.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
Photos courtesy of the International Criminal Court show former president Rodrigo Duterte during his first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025.
Photos / ICC | via Janvic Mateo

MANILA, Philippines — Trial judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have rejected the request of the defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte to adopt a stricter protocol in verifying digital materials.

In a seven-page decision dated Sept. 26, the ICC Trial Chamber III denied the defense’s request for an additional “expert verification” field to accompany all forms of open source and user-generated evidence.

It said such an amendment to the ICC’s protocol would not align with the framework set by the Trial Chamber, which states that it is the defense’s primary responsibility to identify and raise issues for individual evidence presented by the prosecution.

“To the contrary, the requested amendment, if implemented, requires the prosecution to prepare additional materials that contain information regarding the relevance and admissibility of open-source and user-generated evidence, before the defense analyses evidence and raises any abovementioned issues,” read the decision.
Defense lawyer Peter Haynes earlier recommended the amendment to E-Court Protocol, citing the need for extra caution to ensure that evidence is properly verified before it is submitted to the court.

“The current case operates in a uniquely challenging information ecosystem, in which a large volume of misinformation, or ‘fake news’ has circulated and will continue to circulate, online,” Haynes said.
“The defense is concerned that the evidentiary record in the present case risks being overwhelmed by material of dubious relevance, authenticity and reliability,” he added.
The ICC prosecutor, however, described the request is “unreasonable, unnecessary and against the interests of judicial efficiency.”
“Open source and user-generated evidence are extremely broad categories of documents that capture numerous types of evidence,” wrote ICC acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang.

“As such, whether open source or user-generated evidence requires an accompanying expert report should be determined on a case-by-case basis by the submitting party that has the burden of establishing its relevance, probative value and assessing its potential prejudicial effect,” Niang added.
The Trial Chamber III instead granted the prosecution’s request to add a URL (uniform resource locator) metadata field for each of the open source or user-generated evidence submitted in the case.
The prosecution said the additional field will allow parties to easily identify the URL or link “associated with the open source evidence at the time it was captured.”

articles.title: ‘VP can’t be compelled to admit bank accounts’
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court yesterday denied the prosecution’s request for admission to compel Vice President Sara Duterte to admit to some pieces of evidence, including the ownership of bank…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court yesterday denied the prosecution’s request for admission to compel Vice President Sara Duterte to admit to some pieces of evidence, including the ownership of bank accounts, as it will be equivalent to self-incrimination.

In his ruling read in open court on Day 31 of the trial, presiding officer Francis Escudero denied the prosecution’s request for the Vice President to admit to “104 matters concerning respondent’s personal circumstances and former public offices, her spouse Manases Carpio’s business interests and various Bureau of Internal Revenue and bank records.”

The court agreed with the defense panel’s opposition to the prosecution’s request for “admission by adverse party” under Rule 26 of the Revised Rules of Civil Procedure, with Escudero saying it cannot prevail over Section 17, Article III or the Bill of Rights of the 1987 Constitution, which reads: “No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.”
Escudero cited the Bill of Rights, which protects even impeached officials’ “right against self-incrimination.”
He added that if the request is allowed, the respondent’s failure to answer a request for admission “will be ‘deemed as an admission of the fact requested to be admitted.’”

“That Rule 26 requires the answer be under oath exposes the party requested to ‘the additional peril of being held liable for perjury’ and thus, constitutes compulsion that is not allowed under the Constitution,” Escudero said

Escudero said while the court welcomes the prosecution’s bid to narrow the issues for trial, “any such measure to expedite the proceedings must always yield to the protection of the substantial rights of the respondent under the Constitution.”

While the court sided with the defense camp’s objections, Escudero said it is denying the Vice President’s move to “expunge” the request for admission, saying it will remain in the court’s records but with “no evidentiary or prejudicial
effect against Respondent.” Escudero also assured the Vice President that “her failure to answer (the Request for Admission) shall not be deemed an admission.”
The court also no longer tackled the Vice President’s camp’s “objection based on marital and filial privileges.”
Sought for comment, the prosecution panel said it does not consider the ruling a setback and would still present its case through witnesses and documents.

“Even if the ruling was adverse to the prosecution, I think we will still continue with the strategy, the plan of the prosecution. This is not a setback,” House prosecutor and San Juan Rep. Ysabel Zamora said.
Trillanes ready to testify
Even without a subpoena, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV said he is ready to take the witness stand before the impeachment court.
In a chance interview as he attended yesterday’s hearing, Trillanes said the prosecution has tapped him as an alternative witness in case Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte will not appear.
Duterte did appear yesterday and took the witness stand as prosecutors drilled down on the alleged ill-gotten wealth of his sister, the Vice President.
Trillanes said it was a coincidence that he and Mayor Duterte were both present before the Senate impeachment court yesterday.
“I hope to be presented as a witness after Mayor Baste, that’s all,” Trillanes added.
“The subpoena is issued if you need to be summoned, but I am willing and ready even if they don’t issue a subpoena. I am ready to be presented,” he added.
He was, however, mum on the testimonies of Mayor Duterte.
“Even if I want to answer that, I can’t…,” he said.
Trillanes is expected to reveal before the court details of the alleged sources of the reported P6.7-billion wealth of the Duterte couple.
Investigate own turf

Meanwhile, Sen. Erwin Tulfo advised Mayor Duterte to investigate his inner circle for failing to flag local government contracts awarded to a company linked to his sister, warning that the local chief executive could face legal liability for his staff’s oversight.
Tulfo pointed out that the mayor signs documents based on the approval of his subordinates, leaving him highly vulnerable to irregularities.
However, when asked if he would initiate the probe on his own accord, the mayor deflected to the justice system.
“As long as my sister’s name, the Vice President’s name was not on the contract, then there’s nothing,” he stated.

The exchange stemmed from Duterte’s admission that he signs between 50 to 300 documents daily, including payrolls, ordinances and contracts, relying entirely on the countersignatures of his city administrator and legal team. — Bella Cariaso, Neil Jayson Servallos, Daphne Galvez

articles.title: N.S. senior killed ailing wife after promising to help her take her own life, court hears
articles.summary: Douglas Smith, 75, was sentenced Tuesday for killing his wife in their home four years ago after she had asked for help taking her own life, according to court documents.

image.caption: Douglas Smith, 75, has been senteced to six years in prison for the death of his wife Iris Dodd in their home in Kingsport, N.S. on April 30, 2022. (Jeorge Sadi/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New
Douglas Smith, 75, was sentenced Tuesday for killing his wife in their home four years ago after she had asked for help taking her own life, according to court documents.
Douglas Smith, 75, sentenced Tuesday to 6 years for manslaughter
WARNING: This story includes references to suicide and details a killing.
A 75-year-old man smothered his ailing wife in their Kingsport, N.S., home more than four years ago after she made him promise to help her take her own life, a court was told Tuesday.

Douglas Smith was sentenced in Nova Scotia Supreme Court in Kentville, N.S., to six years in prison for the death of Iris Dodd, 72, on April 30, 2022. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter in April days before he was set to stand trial for second-degree murder.
Smith and Dodd, who had serious health issues, had been married for 33 years but faced eviction and had nowhere to go, according to an agreed statement of facts.
Court documents illustrate a harrowing situation the couple, who had a "long, supportive and happy life together," found themselves in that night.
Dodd’s health had been deteriorating since she suffered a stroke in 2018 and they were going to be kicked out of their home the next day, the documents say.
She used a wheelchair, was losing her eyesight and lived with chronic pain from arthritis and fibromyalgia — a long-term condition that causes muscle pain, extreme fatigue and sleep difficulty.
She had just had a long stay in hospital due to bouts of pneumonia.
On the night she died, court documents say Dodd told her husband she didn’t want to spend her final years in a health-care or long-term care facility.
She told Smith she planned to take all of her medication at once in an attempt to overdose and Smith should leave the house so he wouldn't be culpable.
The only thing she needed from her husband was for him to arrange the pills because she couldn’t see them very well.
Initially, the documents say, Smith didn’t support his wife’s plan when she raised the topic abruptly.
However, “The victim was very upset and made Mr. Smith promise to help her with her plan and he promised he would,” said the agreed statement of facts.
They couple agreed they’d go ahead with the plan the following day, which helped Dodd calm down and go to sleep.
Smith couldn’t sleep, though, worrying about his wife dying alone. He became increasingly concerned her plan might fail and leave her with permanent brain damage.
“Mr. Smith resolved all these thoughts and fears in his head by getting up and holding a pillow over the victim’s face,” the agreed statement of facts said.
‘She was in distress and I eased her distress’
The day after Smith killed Dodd, he drove to the local RCMP detachment to turn himself in.
After discovering the office was closed, he called 911 from the parking lot and admitted to taking her life.
A recording of Smith's 911 call was released by the court.
The call began with a dispatcher asking Smith what emergency he was reporting. The senior replied that he wanted to report a death.
The dispatcher asked if the death had been sudden or unexpected and Smith said that his wife had died and he was responsible.
Smith said he didn’t want to provide any details but the dispatcher said she required some information before an officer could be sent to meet him.
“She was in distress and I eased her distress,” Smith replied.
An officer came out of the detachment, arrested Smith and took him to a cell inside the building where Smith confirmed it was his voice on the 911 call, according to court documents.
Emotional day in court
Smith was emotional in court Tuesday, holding his head in his hands while the agreed statement of facts was read.
He wept when Crown prosecutor Daniel Rideout reached the part detailing how Smith had smothered his wife.
Smith was asked if he wanted a break but replied: "Let's get this over with."

items: More stories from the Annapolis Valley

blocks.text: During submissions, Rideout noted the case differed from the spate of domestic homicides in Nova Scotia in recent years.
Smith was driven by compassion when he took his wife's life, but he still broke the law and had other options available, Rideout said.

articles.title: Dutch police arrest suspected member of group that claimed FBI hack
articles.summary: The suspect, 24, was arrested before the alleged cyber attack took place.

blocks.text: Dutch police have arrested a suspected member of the ShinyHunters cyber-crime group that claimed to have stolen sensitive information on all FBI bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After the alleged attack last week, the group claimed to have every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address and phone numbers.
In a statement, Dutch police said it had arrested a 24-year-old man from Amsterdam on suspicion of being part of the group, which has also claimed other hacks.
The suspect was arrested on 15 September, before the alleged FBI attack. He is also suspected of attempted incitement to commit two murders, police said.

Police said they seized his devices and found a "large amount of information" on his laptop, including "details about two murders that were to be committed abroad" that they suspect he may have ordered.
The suspect has been held since his arrest. Dutch officials have not ruled out further arrests.
Stan Duijf, who leads Dutch investigations into cybercrime, said in a statement: "The ShinyHunters group is responsible for a large number of national and international victims.
"It is good that we have been able to arrest a suspect in the investigation into this group."

Taking to X, FBI director Kash Patel thanked Dutch partners and said: "As we speak, FBI teams are actively working with partners to obtain and execute more leads in the ongoing investigation based on this arrest."
Following the arrest, Brett Leatherman, assistant director of FBI Cyber, urged members of the group to hand themselves in "while the choice is still yours".
He added: "Other groups believed anonymity or their friends would protect them... but arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk.
"The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you, you know how to find us, we know how to find you."
ShinyHunters claimed to have breached the FBI's servers on 21 September and began contacting reporters the next day sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data.
The BBC has seen a small portion of the data, which appears to be genuine.

ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May.

The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records, and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information.
In its message on the dark web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money.
Instead, the cyber-criminals asked the agency to retract an advisory that it issued in May about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation.

The public service announcement, external, which is still up on the FBI's website, described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims".
"They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer now says there's lack of evidence she killed her children
articles.summary: In a shift from what was presented in her mistrial, Lindsay Clancy's lawyer now argues there's no evidence Clancy actually killed her three children.

image.caption: Lindsay Clancy sits in Plymouth Superior Court, on Tuesday, during a hearing set to determine the next steps after a mistrial was declared on Sept. 4, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
In a shift from what was presented in her mistrial, Lindsay Clancy's lawyer now argues there's no evidence Clancy actually killed her three children.
Clancy's defence didn't dispute the killings in earlier admission
WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.
In a shift from what was presented in her high-profile murder trial, Lindsay Clancy's lawyer now argues there's a lack of evidence that Clancy actually killed her three children.
"Where is the evidence that she did this?" defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said in a status conference Tuesday in part to determine whether there would be a retrial.

It appears to be a departure for the defence, which previously did not dispute that she caused her children's deaths but argued a lack of criminal responsibility based on postpartum psychosis. Earlier this month, after seven days of deadlocked jury deliberation, the highly divisive case ended in a mistrial after the 12-person jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
Reddington called the original investigation "ridiculous," adding "they just immediately assumed this woman was guilty."
He also questioned the accuracy of the statements Clancy made in the hospital after her apparent suicide attempt, saying it was "chilling" and that "she was told what happened."
"There is no evidence that she admitted she did this," he said.
"This entire case is based on speculation. Where is the admission? Where did she say that she did this?” he told Judge William Sullivan.

items: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer wants judge to investigate juror's conduct

blocks.text: "There is, there was, and there cannot be evidence under the Latimore standard that this woman killed those children,” he added, citing the Massachusetts legal test used to determine whether the evidence presented is legally sufficient.
A Nov. 2 date has been set for a hearing to consider Reddington's motion and several others Clancy's lawyers have filed seeking to avoid a retrial.
Case has captivated spectators

Clancy's high-profile murder trial, which ended Sept. 4 in a mistrial, has captivated spectators from the beginning. The case gripped the public, sparking debates about maternal mental health, creating dramatic moments both inside the court and out, and launching online conspiracy theories.

Clancy, 36, had been charged with murder in the killing of her three children in 2023 while her then-husband, Patrick, was running an errand. Jurors in Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., heard that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.
She then attempted to take her own life.

items: Patrick Clancy gives first TV interview after Lindsay Clancy mistrial

blocks.text: Previously, Clancy's defence didn't dispute the killings, but argued she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and little-understood mental health condition that can affect a new mom's sense of reality.
Prosecutors argued that Clancy was guilty of three counts of first-degree murder because she plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the killings.
CBC News has reached out to representatives for Patrick Clancy about Reddington's comments Tuesday. They said they would not be making a public comment.
Judge declares mistrial, what happens next? Legal analyst Melba Pearson talks with CBC News Network
'Voluminous' evidence: prosecution
In Tuesday's status conference, Plymouth County assistant district attorney Shanan Buckingham argued that there is "voluminous" evidence to suggest Clancy killed her children.
"We're hearing now for the first time in this argument that counsel is challenging first the sufficiency of the evidence as it applies to the three counts of murder," Buckingham said.
"I suggest to you that the entire record is voluminous as to the information supporting the fact that she did this."
She cited the DNA found on the exercise bands found around the necks of the children as an example, as well as the testimony from a hospital chaplain that Clancy said she had to kill them.
Speaking outside of court later, Plymouth County district attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters his office hadn't yet decided whether to retry Clancy.
"We're on for November 2. We're going to see what happens with the motions; we're still waiting for transcripts," Cruz said.
"We're doing a very thorough review right now, and we're going to continue to do our job to make sure that we do what's best in the interest of justice and the interests of the three children."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: French students and police clash as school blockades turn violent
articles.summary:
More than 200 arrested while teachers join protest over class sizes, exhausting timetables and staff shortages

French teenagers blockading their schools in protest at class sizes, teacher…

blocks.text: French teenagers blockading their schools in protest at class sizes, teacher shortages and long timetables have clashed with police, as politicians traded verbal blows over how to respond.
Demonstrations that began in Paris last week have escalated and spread across France, with the authorities reporting the arrest of 164 people on Monday.

On Tuesday, high school pupils in Lille, northern France, set fire to dustbins and threw bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at police, who responded with teargas after protestors vandalised bus shelters and advertising hoardings.

There were confrontations between children and police in Bordeaux, Rennes and Nantes in western France, and Marseille in the south. At the Lamartine lycée, in the north of Paris, students waved placards complaining they had exhausting timetables. One read: “8am-6pm. More hours of lessons than sleep”.
On Monday, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said protests had broken out at 180 schools, and 12 officers, 12 students and three school staff had been injured.
By midday on Tuesday, the education ministry was reporting protests at 300 high schools, a further 40 arrests and that 10 students and staff had been injured.

blocks.caption: Students face police at Baggio high school, Lille, on Tuesday. Photograph: Jean-François Badias/AP

blocks.text: The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said earlier that escalating the demonstrations would be “irresponsible”. He posted on X: “Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students staff or police.”

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) , responded to ministers’ instructions to police, posting on X on Monday: “The high school students protesting are harmless. The Lecornu government has ordered a crackdown. This brutality is irresponsible and has a clear racist undertone. Hands off our youth. Elected officials and France Unbowed activists, step in wherever you can.”

Lecornu, responding on X, called Mélenchon’s intervention an “irresponsible escalation”. “The duty of an elected official of the republic is to protect young people and call for calm. Exploiting their anger for partisan purposes is wrong,” he wrote.
He added that Mélenchon’s accusation of racism was “an insult”.

blocks.caption: Students blockade the entrance to Hélène Boucher school in Paris on Tuesday. Photograph: Paoloni Jeremy/Abaca/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The protests came as French unions went on strike over the government’s budget plans, which include €54m in public spending cuts. Many public sector workers stopped work on Tuesday, including an estimated 40% of primary school teachers.

Ryad Rani, president of the Union Syndicale Lycéene (the high school students’ union) had called for a total blockade of France’s high schools as a parallel action but urged protestors to “remain peaceful”. He said the union was protesting about a “general lack of resources, overcrowded classrooms of sometimes 32-35 students and the shortage of teachers and staff”.
after newsletter promotion
He said a circular sent by the interior and the education ministries to the police to maintain public order outside high schools “with a proportionate use of force”, was a “absolute scandal”.

blocks.caption: Students join a general protest in Paris on Tuesday against the release of next year's draft budget. Photograph: Teresa Suárez/AP

blocks.text: “We’re talking about pupils of 15-18 years old and the government’s only response is automatic and institutionalised repression. It’s unacceptable. High school pupils are taking action to demand fairer and more equitable conditions and they’re being met with the BAC [anti-criminal brigade] and the CRS [riot police],” Rani said.
He added that some teachers and school staff had stood in front of students to protect them from police. “Those are the images you should be showing,” Rani told BFM TV.

Caroline Chevé, secretary general of the main teachers’ union the Fédération Syndicale Unitaire (FSU – Unitary Trade Union Federation), who joined protestors at a march in central Paris on Tuesday, said she understood pupils’ frustration. “They’re facing the same challenges as we are. They’re in overcrowded classrooms. Sometimes they don’t have enough teachers because of staffing shortages. They see the same reality as we do, and they’re angry,” Chevé said.

blocks.caption: The blockaded entrance to Colbert high school, in Paris, on Tuesday. Photograph: Nicolas Garriga/AP

articles.title: National Rally’s Jordan Bardella rails at ‘war’ on party after antisemitism claims
articles.summary: President of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party faces calls to resign over comments he allegedly wrote as a teenager

blocks.text: Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN), has claimed a “total war” is being waged against his party as he faces a political storm after the publication of antisemitic comments he allegedly wrote as a young party member.

Bardella, who is facing calls from political opponents to resign, said on Tuesday that the report by the investigative website Mediapart was false. To a standing ovation from his party’s lawmakers and senators at a meeting in parliament, he said the report was an attempt to damage his party as Le Pen tops the polls before the 2027 presidential election.

“We are seeing the beginnings of a total war, an attempt to destabilise the presidential campaign,” Bardella said. He accused Mediapart of wanting “to kill my political career” and said he would take legal action for defamation. Le Pen, at Bardella’s side, said she had “absolute confidence” in him.

Journalists at Mediapart said they had independently authenticated the comments allegedly written between 2013 and 2015, including in email groups and on messaging services. Bardella was aged 17 to 18 at the time and was a member of the party that was then called the Front National.

The alleged comments included “the Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so”. He is also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”.

Mediapart’s investigation has shaken Le Pen’s presidential campaign. Since Le Pen took over the party leadership in 2011, she has sought to detoxify the party image and move it away from its antisemitic past in order to increase its electoral reach.
When Le Pen’s father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, co-founded the party in 1972, its ranks included former members of a Waffen SS military unit under Nazi command during the second world war.

Pierre Bousquet, a former member of the Waffen SS Charlemagne division, was the party’s treasurer for its first nine years. Another early member had been in the paramilitary militia under Philippe Pétain, the leader of the puppet Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis and ensured the deportation of one-quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps, about 76,000 people.

In 1987, Jean-Marie Le Pen described the Holocaust as a “mere detail” of the second world war. In the decades that followed he was convicted more than 15 times for hate speech and contesting crimes against humanity as he repeated negationist comments, including saying the Nazi occupation was “not particularly inhumane”.

Marine Le Pen, who expelled her father from the party in 2015 after he repeated antisemitic comments, has in recent years directly appealed to French Jewish voters. She said her party would protect them, describing the RN as “the best shield for our fellow French citizens of Jewish faith”.

blocks.caption: Bardella and Marine Le Pen at a rally in Lievin, northern France, in July. Photograph: Jean-François Badias/AP

blocks.text: Bardella made an unprecedented visit to Israel in 2025, the first by a French far-right leader, in an attempt to demonstrate the RN’s new credentials. In 2023, Bardella told a TV interviewer he did not think Jean-Marie Le Pen was antisemitic, before backtracking on his comments after criticism.

The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, responding to the Mediapart investigation, wrote on social media: “To all those with a short memory: antisemitism isn’t an accident in the RN, it’s that party’s history. That’s the real face of the far right.”

Aurore Bergé, the minister for equality and against discrimination, said the “antisemitic and conspiracy theory” content of the alleged messages “reminds those who might have forgotten the nature of the far right”.

Raphaël Glucksmann, a candidate in the Socialist presidential primary, wrote on social media that no public relations exercise would fundamentally change the RN. “Let us never forget that they all joined a party founded by antisemitic fanatics and out-and-out racists,” he said.

Yonathan Arfi, of the CRIF, the umbrella group of French Jewish organisations, told France Culture radio he was “stupefied by the virulence of the antisemitic comments” allegedly made by Bardella. He said that if true, the comments undermined the RN’s claims to have detoxified its image.
He asked: “How could a political party leader, having made such sickening comments, reach such a high position in a party that claims to have changed and now fights against the hatred of Jews?”

The Green leader, Marine Tondelier, said Bardella, an MEP, should resign from all his political positions. She said: “The man who presents himself today as the biggest defender of Jews … is in reality an obsessional antisemite.”

articles.title: TV journalist is crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom
articles.summary: Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has ascended to the throne after King Oyo died at the age of 34 due to a cancer battle. He previously worked for Ugandan broadcaster UBC as a TV anchor and editor.

image.caption: The new king (left in photo) took part in traditional rituals ahead of his coronationImage: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS

blocks.text: A TV journalist on Tuesday was crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom.
What do we know so far?
Edward Rukidi Kiganangoma has ascended to the thrown after his predecessor, King Oyo Kyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, died unexpectedly last month.
King Oyo was only 34 and had lost his cancer battle while receiving treatment in the US. Oyo had became king at only three years of age.
Oyo's death sparked a succession battle in Uganda, with Oyo's mother pushing for the late king's undisclosed son to be the next monarch.

blocks.caption: King Oyo was laid to rest earlier this month after a nine-day period of mourning [FILE: September 10, 2026]Image: Michael Muhati/REUTERS

blocks.text: However, the royal Babito clan chose Kiganangoma, now Nyabongo I, as the heir to the throne out of a group of eligible princes.
Kiganangoma took part in a coronation ceremony in the remote town of Fort Portal in western Uganda to ascend to the throne.
Coronation rituals included a mock battle and animal sacrifices. The ceremony in Fort Portal was televised and attended by thousands of people.
Kiganangoma, who is 56 years old, had worked as a journalist and editor for Ugandan public broadcaster UBC.
Tooro's new king vows to 'protect our culture, our traditions and customs'

"We have a big task to protect our culture, our traditions and customs and good conduct among our people," the new king said in his maiden speech. He had also told the New Vision newspaper: "My family never let me treat royal descent as an entitlement."
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni was present for the coronation ceremony of the new king.

While expressing sadness over King Oyo's passing, Museveni also said he congratulates "his Highness Nyabongo. I have been watching him on the news and he is a good newsreader. I am sure he will do a good job."
Uganda is a constitutional republic with a president voted in democratically.

However, the country's four major precolonial kingdoms still hold cultural influence over the East African nation, despite not wielding any political power. The kings are involved in maintaining social order and safeguarding the heritage of their respective kingdoms.

articles.title: Watch: US journalist Evan Gershkovich describes being detained by Russian agents
articles.summary: He was arrested in Russia in 2023 and later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges.

blocks.text: US journalist Evan Gershkovich has told the BBC's Today programme about the 16 months when he was detained in Russia.

In his first UK broadcast interview, the Wall Street Journal correspondent said he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in March 2023, and arrested him.
He was later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges, but released in 2024 as part of a high-profile prisoner exchange.
He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false, and following his arrest, then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.

articles.title: Judge tosses drug trafficking convictions for B.C. compassion club founders after constitutional challenge
articles.summary: A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has ruled in favour of two harm-reduction activists convicted of drug trafficking who argued they were doing it to reduce the harms caused by toxic drugs.

image.caption: Eris Nyx, right, speaks near Jeremy Kalicum, founders of the Drug User Liberation Front (DULF). (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has ruled in favour of two harm-reduction activists convicted of drug trafficking who argued they were doing it to reduce the harms caused by toxic drugs.
Judge says DULF founders 'selflessly' put their lives on hold during public health emergency
Justice Catherine Murray found parts of Canada's Controlled Drugs and Substances Act unconstitutional and stayed the convictions against Jeremy Kalicum and Eris Nyx.

Murray said Kalicum and Nyx's compassion club, the Drug User Liberation Front (DULF), reduced the harms associated with the toxic drug crisis and did not negatively impact the community or public safety.
Kalicum and Nyx were found guilty last year of drug trafficking after Vancouver police raided the club in 2023.

items: Drug User Liberation Front founders found guilty of drug trafficking
More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: Murray said in court on Tuesday that the pair "selflessly" put themselves to the side for the cause.
"Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx have borne the burden of bringing a successful constitutional challenge, thereby doing the public interest a service at considerable personal cost," Murray said.
She noted thousands of people have died due to toxic drugs since the public health emergency was declared in B.C. in 2016.

Murray put Kalicum and Nyx's convictions on hold last year to hear the constitutional challenge, where their lawyers argued that forcing drug users to rely on unregulated street drugs violates the Charter of Rights.

Murray said in her ruling then that Nyx and Kalicum's intentions were good as they tried to save lives, but that buying pure drugs on the dark web and selling them to members was not covered by an exemption that allowed for drug storage and testing.
She said the two were "agitators" who wanted to make change and were aware that they ran the risk of a trafficking prosecution.
Kalicum and Nyx's lawyers had argued that closing the club violated the rights of those who are disabled by addiction and raised their risk of death from an unregulated, illicit drug supply.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Satirist launches site naming Cornell students accused in gang-rape lawsuit
articles.summary: Writer Toby Morton is using a new website to amplify allegations in a high-profile sexual assault lawsuit involving seven Cornell students. The reopening of the case is causing an outcry on social…

image.caption: The Chi Phi fraternity was barred from campus in 2024Image: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Toby Morton, who wrote several episodes of the animated comedy series "South Park," launched a website seeking accountability in connection with an alleged 2024 sexual assault case involving seven Cornell University fraternity members. The site names seven men accused of sexually assaulting a 20-year-old woman who was allegedly unconscious after being given drugs and alcohol at a Cornell fraternity house and collects personal data and photos of the members involved.

"I've received messages reminding me I'm not a journalist, I'm 'just a satirist,'" Morton wrote in a September 27 Instagram post regarding the creation of his website TheCornell7.org. "This is true, but it makes me more dangerous," he added, saying he has "nobody to tell me I've gone too far."

The case has recently drawn a surge in public attention after the accuser, identified as Jane Doe to protect her identity, filed a lawsuit in mid-September. Her complaint alleges that she was brutally sexually assaulted in 2024 by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity while unconscious after being pressured to take ketamine, smoke marijuana and drink alcohol at the fraternity house on Cornell's campus in Ithaca, New York. The university, she said in the lawsuit, failed to protect her. Cornell conducted an internal investigation after the incident, but no one was charged.

blocks.caption: The reopening of the case has caused renewed attention on social mediaImage: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Since the lawsuit was filed on September 16, the case has generated widespread commentary on social media. Some have criticized Cornell and the district attorney's office, while others have questioned the allegations.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who handled the original case, said his office has reopened it and plans to present evidence to a grand jury amid public questions about why no criminal charges were initially filed.

Van Houten said in a statement that his office is considering bringing criminal charges related to the incident, though the allegations in the civil complaint are "dramatically different" from the woman's statement to police two years ago — in her statement to authorities, she did not allege she was drugged without her knowledge or that she did not consent to engage in sexual acts.
Justice sought
Cornell's Chi Phi chapter was barred from campus after the alleged incident in 2024. The accuser also dropped out of Cornell University, according to her attorney.

One of the most chilling allegations of the lawsuit is that a message was sent to a Chi Phi Snapchat group at about 1:42 a.m., inviting members to the room to abuse Doe, who was heavily under the influence of drugs and alcohol. The lawsuit alleges that more men then entered the room and that the assault continued for several hours until Doe lost consciousness.

"There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn't. I've never seen anything like it," an attorney for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, told CBS. Giuffra pointed out that two of the seven accused fraternity members were expelled, while the others received lesser disciplinary measures. "Not one of these guys was arrested," Giuffra told the network.

blocks.caption: Actress Florence Pugh described the allegations as 'horrific' on social mediaImage: Cover Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Politicians and actors speak out

Many people, from US politicians to Hollywood actors, have spoken out about the case in recent days. US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, condemned what she described as a "culture of rape" protected by elite institutions. "When I read what happened at Cornell, those men posted in a group chat. That means it was normal to them. That means it was acceptable to them. This is a culture, and what we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore," she said Sunday at a forum near Cornell's campus.

British actress Florence Pugh described the allegations as "horrific" on social media and expressed her support for the student involved. Pugh, who is also currently on a promotional tour for her upcoming Netflix series "East of Eden," wrote a lengthy statement on Instagram, saying that "Colleges/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world. You build men that get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and that they won't be harmed in return."
"Those who protect and impose light sentences on men who rape and destroy lives should be punished and closely scrutinized. Why are you protecting someone so fiercely?" she wrote.

American actor Josh Gad, best known as the voice of Olaf in Disney's"Frozen" films, also commented on the Cornell case, criticizing what he described as insufficient disciplinary consequences for the students accused of sexual assault. In an Instagram post, Gad said sexual violence should not be treated as a mistake or addressed with limited disciplinary action by a university, arguing that the alleged conduct had "destroyed a life” and calling for greater accountability.
Edited by Joshua Lang.

articles.title: Senegal's Youth Olympics makes Olympics in Africa 'logical'
articles.summary: The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.

image.caption: Senegal have refurbished some of their existing facilities rather than just building new onesImage: Cem Özdel/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: At the end of October 2026, the first ever Olympic event on African soil will take place as the Youth Olympics comes to Senegal.
Around 2,700 young athletes are expected to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports, with many qualifying through the African Youth Games last year.

"We were entrusted with hosting this event and that is why from Johannesburg to Nairobi, from Dakar to Djbouti, it is all of young Africa that is watching you and watching you with pride," Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said at the arrival of the flame.

The moment marks yet another step forward for global sport in Africa. In 2025, the first major road cycling event took place on the continent, and in September this year it was announced the first-ever World Athletics Championships would be held in Kenya in 2029. There are also on-going negotiations about Formula 1 returning. It appears that 16 years on since the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, global sport is finally returning to different parts of Africa.
"This is a victory for Africa. It opens the door for Africa to host major events," Malick Diouf, head of a marketing agency and founder of the Dakar Sport Summit, told DW.
"Africa is in the process of opening up to the world, hosting major events and everything. And all of Africa must celebrate this kind of victory."

blocks.caption: Malick Diouf believes Africa as an Olympic host is the logical next stepImage: DW

blocks.text: With more major events in Africa, the question around an Olympic Games being on the continent looms.
Sports scientist Kamilla Swart has said awarding Africa a Games would make the world "take Africa more seriously." Diouf believes it's the logical next step.
"The Youth Olympic Games, it's a major test for Africa. And I think this is where we need to succeed in organizing these Games and also in sending a message," Diouf said.

"We, Africa, are ready to host the Summer Olympics, and I think that would be the logical next step after the Dakar Olympics. We have Olympic champions; we have record holders; we have Olympians, so we deserve to host the Olympic Games."
Senegal an attractive option for many reasons
The move to re-use and refurbish existing facilities rather than build whole new ones is likely why Senegal's bid was so tempting for the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

The fear of the white elephant facility appears to have been considered here. The Iba Mar Diop Stadium, the track and field stadium, is expected to be used for athlete training ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

"It’s by using these facilities, by participating in and hosting international events, and by consistently maintaining them to the required standards, that we’ll be able to keep these stadiums up to the standards they currently meet," Diouf said.

There's also the social and economical impacts of the Youth Olympics. Diouf believes the impact is beyond just infrastructure, but into roads, the development of the hospitality, security and broadcasting sectors and the young athletes themselves.
"There's life after the Games. Now we need to figure out how to use the resources we have, we need to develop and capitalize on what we have showcased during the Games," said Diouf.
Future of Youth Olympics in doubt

The significance of these Games stretch beyond even the history they are making in Africa. In May of this year, IOC President Kirsty Coventry put the brakes on the future of the Youth Olympics, leaving real doubts as to whether there will be any more after the 2028 winter edition.

"We need to pause and have a real reflection on why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games and we realized that across the Movement it's very disjointed. There's not a true North Star of why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games," Coventry told reporters.
"So the EB (IOC Executive Board) decided to pause the 2030 process right now so there will not be an election in June, and rather we need to take a step back and develop a youth strategy."

blocks.caption: The Youth Olympics in Dakar might well be the last summer edition of the youth games, adding even more importance to the first ones in AfricaImage: Nicolas Remene/Le Pictorium/IMAGO

blocks.text: A lot has changed since the Youth Olympic Games were launched in 2010. Initially it was seen as a way to engage a younger audience (athletes were limited by age to between 15 and 18) by trialing new sports as well as testing host country's on a smaller stage. However, with the age of athletes decreasing and the challenges of engaging a younger audience in the modern sports entertainment landscape even more challenging, it appears clear the IOC are reconsidering their options when it comes to investment.
"My only wish is that Dakar be memorable and that people reconsider their decision not to host the Games in 2030," Diouf said.

"I don’t want these to be the last Youth Olympic Games, but if these are to be the last Youth Olympic Games, we need to go out with a bang. Dakar needs to show the world what Senegal is all about, what Africa is all about."
From October 31 to November 13 this year, Senegal will have the chance to do just that.

articles.title: Close-up look at Turner's '£50m' Rome painting on show in the city
articles.summary: Turner’s early 19th century painting - Rome, from Mount Aventine - will be on display in the Italian capital for the first time ahead of an auction in London in December.

blocks.text: A renowned painting by British landscape artist JMW Turner has returned to the city that inspired it nearly two centuries ago.
Rome, from Mount Aventine features a panoramic view of the Italian capital and will be on display at the Palazzo Rondinini for three days.
Dating back to the 19th century, the masterpiece was based on sketches made in Rome.
The work of art is remarkably well preserved and is believed to have never been restored. It even features traces of fingerprints and brush hairs are still visible.
The painting has only been to auction once before, selling for more than £30 million.
Sotheby's now expects it could fetch around £50 million when it goes under the hammer in London this December.
The BBC's Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Sarah Rainsford, had a close-up look at the painting in Rome.

articles.title: UK PM Burnham seeks 'hope again' at Labour Party conference
articles.summary: Andy Burnham is seeking a delicate balance between optimism and realism at Labour's annual party conference. He promised hope and an end to "politics as usual" but also an "honest conversation" about…

image.caption: Andy Burnham evoked surely Labour's most universally popular past government, the post-war adminstration under Clement Atlee, in his speechImage: Temilade Adelaja/REUTERS

blocks.text: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, only in the role for a few months after replacing Keir Starmer, has told the Labour Party conference in his native Liverpool that his government wants to restore hope and end "politics as usual."

But the UK's seventh prime minister in a decade is trying to balance a series of evidently conflicting fiscal goals: bolstering economic growth, reducing cost-of-living pressures, safeguarding pensions and making care costs more affordable, upgrading creaking infrastructure and significantly boosting military spending.

That's all while battling a populist challenge from Reform UK and Restore Britain on the right and the Green Party on the left. This led Labour to severe local and regional election defeats in May and ultimately spelt his predecessor Starmer's demise.

blocks.caption: Housing Secretary and party members' favorite Angela Rayner was among the speakers warming up the audience on Tuesday ahead of BurnhamImage: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Burnham say in his conference speech?

Burnham, a Liverpool lad who was mayor of Manchester prior to moving to take up Britain's top political job, repeated his most common mantra since coming to power, namely that "more of the same" will not solve the various issues facing the UK.
"We can't carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards," Burnham said. "More of the same isn't good enough and isn't going to get us where we need to be."
The conference's banner headline "hope again" was not incompatible with a more honest conversation, Burnham said.
"Hope comes from honesty ... and saying the things politicians usually avoid," he said.

He cited Labour's post-war government under Clement Atlee, famed for achievements like setting up Britain's National Health Service, as an example of his party past credentials, having "built the peace" in the public interest. He said that since the 1980s and the Conservative-dominated Margaret Thatcher era of his youth, this direction was lost.

"I will say it straight, Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialization, deregulation, privatization, austerity, Brexit, and what has it given us? A country run for vested interests, not in the public interest — with power held in too few hands, and too many places left to drift," Burnham said.

Burnham told the audience he would take on "the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long," including social care, high levels of youth unemployment, and greater public control of once-nationalized core interests like energy, water and housing.
"The British right talk about 'taking back control," Burnham said, evoking the slogan of the 2016 Brexit campaign. "Never forget that they are the ones who gave it away in the first place!"

blocks.caption: Major UK broadcasters are also on site in Liverpool for Labour's conference week, hoping for face time with the prime minsiter and other leadersImage: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why is Burnham, and Britain, in such a tricky bind?
Burnham said on coming to power that he wanted his premiership to be a "circuit-breaker for Britain" after years of rising prices and anemic growth.

He hit the ground with a handful of new policies like a cap on bus fares, temporarily removing value added tax from electricity bills amid the Iran war, and announcing a bid to stamp out rough sleeping.
But critics say his more grand stated strategy lacks detail and could prove economically unfeasible.

Burnham is constrained by a series of factors, including Labour's 2024 election campaign pledges under Starmer's leadership, Britain's strained public finances, and the suddenly risk-averse debt markets that have started heaping pressure on most developed economies of late.
Borrowing costs for his UK government, as it eyes a series of new banner spending plans, hit a 10-year-high on the morning of Burnham's speech.
In a sign of this lacking spending wiggle room, Burnham has already pushed back his stated aim to formulate reform plans for Britain's social care system.

He said on Tuesday that a "National Care System" would be put forward in time for the next election, currently scheduled for 2029. He said it would be a change "as significant" to the UK as the foundation of the state-funded National Health Service, and also essential to ensure the wider NHS' survival.
He said the plan would be "fully funded, and not by borrowing."

Burnham said that he did not expect such reforms to be easy, and acknowledged "I may pay a political price," but he said they were necessary steps and the kind of leadership he'd promised the party when seeking to replace Starmer this summer.

blocks.caption: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood addressed the conference on Monday, with the anti-migration Reform UK probably the biggest electoral threat to Labour — if not necessarily the party Labour voters are migratingImage: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: These challenging economic realities coincide with Labour facing multi-pronged political threats. They hail from right-wing populist parties like the anti-immigration Reform UK, from left-wing populists claiming to hold an economic magic wand like the Green Party, and from nationalist parties in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland advocating independence from the UK.
